findFirst-then-create upsert has a race that creates duplicate credentials

The handler does `prisma.credential.findFirst({ userId, appId })` and then either updates or creates. Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same user/app (retries are typical for webhooks) can both observe no existing credential and both execute `prisma.credential.create`, leaving duplicate credential rows for the same user and app. Other parts of the codebase use `findFirst` when reading credentials, so duplicates silently shadow each other and can cause the wrong (stale) credential to be used. Since `(userId, appId)` is not unique in the schema, this should at least be serialized (e.g. transaction with locking, or a unique constraint) rather than a check-then-act.

prisma is used but never imported — build-breaking error

The newly added token-refresh block calls `await prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, ... })` at lines 96–99, but the file's import list (lines 1–20) does not import `prisma` from `@calcom/prisma`. This is a compile-time TypeScript error (`Cannot find name 'prisma'`) and will fail the build/type-check for the whole app-store package.

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate detection and blacklist checks are case-sensitive

Duplicate filtering uses `guest === attendee.email` and the blacklist uses `blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)` where the blacklist entries are lowercased but `guest` is not. Email addresses differing only in case (e.g. `Alice@x.com` vs `alice@x.com`) are treated as distinct: the blacklist can be bypassed with mixed case, and `createMany` will insert a second Attendee row for an email that is already on the booking, producing duplicate attendees who then each receive emails. The dialog-side Set-based uniqueness check has the same flaw. Compare normalized (`toLowerCase()`/`trim()`) values on both sides.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isTeamAdminOrOwner requires admin AND owner (&&) instead of OR

The check `const isTeamAdminOrOwner = (await isTeamAdmin(user.id, booking.eventType?.teamId ?? 0)) && (await isTeamOwner(user.id, booking.eventType?.teamId ?? 0));` uses `&&`, so it is only true when the user is simultaneously a team admin AND a team owner. In Cal.com's membership model a user has a single role, so this expression is effectively always false. As a result, legitimate team admins and team owners of team event types are always denied with FORBIDDEN when trying to add guests — the feature is completely broken for team bookings. This should be `||`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sendAddGuestsEmails is called with the raw `guests` input instead of the deduplicated `uniqueGuests`

The handler computes `uniqueGuests` (excluding emails already on the booking and blacklisted ones) but then calls `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` with the original input. In `sendAddGuestsEmails`, any attendee whose email appears in that list is sent a full AttendeeScheduledEmail as if they were a brand-new guest — so an already-existing attendee who was (re-)submitted gets a fresh 'scheduled' confirmation email rather than the 'new guests added' notice. Pass `uniqueGuests` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sendAddGuestsEmails ignores the event type's disableStandardEmails settings

Every other sender in this file (sendScheduledEmails, sendLocationChangeEmails, sendCancelledEmails, etc.) accepts the event type metadata and skips host/attendee emails when `eventTypeDisableHostEmail`/`eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail` (metadata.disableStandardEmails) is set. `sendAddGuestsEmails` takes no `eventTypeMetadata` and unconditionally emails the organizer, all team members, and every attendee. Event types that explicitly disabled standard emails will still have emails sent whenever guests are added.

false_negatives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Any attendee can add arbitrary guests to a booking, enabling email spam through the platform

The permission check grants access to any existing attendee (`isAttendee`), and there is no limit on how many guests can be added or how often. Anyone who books a public event can then submit an arbitrary list of victim email addresses, and the handler will persist them as attendees and send them AttendeeScheduledEmail invitations containing the event details, organizer identity, and video meeting URL. This turns the endpoint into an unauthenticated-content email relay abusing Cal.com's sender reputation. The UI added in this PR only exposes the dialog on the organizer's bookings list, so the attendee permission appears broader than the feature requires; if attendee-added guests are intentional, they at least need rate limiting / a count cap.

Calendar update uses the requester's credentials instead of the organizer's

The handler builds `new EventManager({ ...user, credentials: [...credentials] })` from `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` — i.e. the credentials of whoever called the endpoint — even though the booking's organizer (with credentials) was already loaded via `booking.user.credentials`. When anyone other than the organizer adds guests (a team admin or an attendee, both of which the permission check explicitly allows), `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` attempts to update the organizer's calendar event using credentials that have no access to it. Worse, this call is outside any try/catch and runs after the DB update, so the attendees are already persisted but the mutation throws and the calendar event is never updated — attendees get no calendar invite on the real event and the client shows an error despite the guests having been added.

Guests added to seated (seatsPerTimeSlot) events get no BookingSeat reference

For seated events, every attendee is expected to have a BookingSeat record (seat reference) — the handler even copies `seatsPerTimeSlot`/`seatsShowAttendees` onto the CalendarEvent, but it only creates plain Attendee rows via `createMany` and never creates BookingSeat entries. Guests added to a seated booking will have no `seatReferenceUid`, won't be counted against seat availability (so the slot can be overbooked), and any flows that rely on seat references (joining, cancelling a seat, rescheduling a seat) will break or behave inconsistently for them.

No validation of booking status or time — guests can be added to cancelled/rejected/past bookings

After fetching the booking, the handler never checks `booking.status` or whether the booking has already ended. Guests can therefore be added to CANCELLED or REJECTED bookings (receiving CONFIRMED ics invites and scheduled emails for an event that does not exist) and to bookings in the past. The UI partially hides this (the edit menu is rendered for past confirmed bookings too, via the `isBookingInPast && isConfirmed` branch in BookingListItem.tsx), and the API itself enforces nothing, so cancelled/past events can have attendees appended and calendar/email notifications sent out.

Organizer email subject uses attendees[0].name, which may be an empty string

The subject is built with `name: this.calEvent.attendees[0].name`. The handler creates the new guests with `name: ""` and includes them in `evt.attendees`; since the ordering of `attendees` after the booking update isn't guaranteed, `attendees[0]` can be one of the new nameless guests, producing a subject like 'Guests Added: 30 min meeting with  at ...'. The scheduled-email flow this copies assumes attendees[0] is the booker with a real name.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount incremented via read-modify-write on a stale snapshot

Both failure paths set `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` using the value read at the start of the run. If two cron executions overlap (possible when a run takes longer than the cron interval), both read the same retryCount and both write the same incremented value, so a failure is not counted and deletion is delayed. Using Prisma's atomic `retryCount: { increment: 1 }` avoids the lost update without changing the logic.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount-based deletion is not scoped to SMS reminders

The new deleteMany uses an OR where the second branch is just `retryCount: { gt: 1 }` with no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter, unlike the first branch. `retryCount` lives on the shared `WorkflowReminder` table used by EMAIL and WHATSAPP reminders too. Today only this SMS cron increments the counter, but any other code path (e.g. the email reminder cron adopting the same column, or a backfill) that raises retryCount above 1 on a non-SMS reminder will cause those reminders to be silently deleted by the SMS cron before they are ever sent. The retryCount clause should include `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` to match the stated intent of the change.

false_positives.candidate:
No tests covering the new retry/delete behavior

This PR introduces user-facing behavioral changes — reminders are deleted after two failed scheduling attempts, including via the catch-all error path — but adds no tests. There is nothing verifying that a reminder is deleted exactly after two failures (retryCount boundary `gt: 1`), that a reminder that fails once is retried and can still succeed, or that deterministic errors (e.g. template rendering throwing) also count toward deletion. A regression here silently drops customer SMS reminders, so at least the retry-count boundary and the delete query scope should be covered.

retryCount update inside catch block can throw and abort the whole cron run

Previously the catch block only logged the error, so a failure for one reminder could never stop the loop. Now the catch block performs `prisma.workflowReminder.update` unguarded. If that update itself fails — e.g. the row was deleted concurrently by another cron execution or by a booking cancellation, or the DB connection is the very thing that failed — the exception propagates out of the catch, the for-loop terminates, all remaining unscheduled reminders are skipped for this run, and the handler returns a 500. The retry-count write in the catch should be wrapped in its own try/catch (or the loop should continue on failure) so one bad reminder cannot starve the rest.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

false_positives.candidate:
Integration tests never execute the generated SQL for org/team scopes

The org-scope (line 332) and team-scope (line 295) tests assert conditions via `expect(conditions).toEqual(Prisma.sql`...`)`, which only deep-compares the Sql object's internal `strings`/`values` arrays — it never runs the SQL against the database. The only test that actually executes a query (`getBaseConditions`, line 481) uses scope `"user"`, the one code path that contains no `ANY(...)` array interpolation. As a result the tests pass while the org/team SQL is syntactically invalid (Prisma expands `ANY(${ids})` into `ANY($1, $2, ...)`, a Postgres syntax error). At least one test per scope should execute the produced conditions with `$queryRaw` against the real database so invalid generated SQL is caught.

Org-scope expectation depends on nondeterministic row ordering for userIds

The org-scope test asserts exact equality with `Prisma.sql`... ("userId" = ANY(${[user.id, user2.id, user3.id]})) ...`. The service builds that array from `MembershipRepository.findAllByTeamIds`, a `findMany` with no `orderBy`, so Postgres does not guarantee the row order (the user also has two memberships — team and org — that get deduped via `Set`, preserving whatever order rows came back in). If the membership rows are returned in a different order, the Sql `values` array order differs and the deep-equality assertion fails spuriously. The assertion should compare order-insensitively or the repository query should impose a deterministic order.

Public `findMany` method removed without updating callers

The previous implementation exposed a public `findMany(findManyArgs)` method that combined authorization/filter conditions into a `bookingTimeStatusDenormalized.findMany` call. This PR deletes that method entirely and replaces it with `getBaseConditions(): Promise<Prisma.Sql>`, shifting query execution to callers via `$queryRaw`. No caller is updated in this PR (only the service and its test are changed), so any existing consumer that invokes `insightsBookingService.findMany(...)` — e.g. the insights tRPC procedures that fetch booking events/status/hourly data — will fail TypeScript compilation and lose functionality. Either keep a compatible `findMany` wrapper or update all callers in the same change.

`ANY(${array})` with Prisma.sql renders invalid SQL — org/team scope queries will throw at runtime

In `buildOrgAuthorizationCondition` (line 164 and 168) and `buildTeamAuthorizationCondition` (line 201) the code writes e.g. `Prisma.sql`("teamId" = ANY(${teamIds}))``. Prisma's tagged-template helper expands an interpolated JavaScript array into a comma-separated list of bound parameters — it does NOT serialize it as a single Postgres array parameter. So with `teamIds = [10, 20, 30]` the emitted SQL is `"teamId" = ANY($1, $2, $3)`, which Postgres rejects with `syntax error at or near "$2"` (ANY requires a single array expression or subquery). Every org-scope and team-scope query will therefore fail with a raw-query error at runtime; only the user-scope path (which has no ANY) is valid. The correct pattern is `"teamId" IN (${Prisma.join(teamIds)})` or passing a single array parameter with an explicit cast. The tests don't catch this because they only structurally compare Sql objects built with the same broken pattern.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Script uses macOS-only sed syntax and a CWD-relative .env path

`sed -i '' -E ...` is the BSD/macOS form of in-place edit; on GNU sed (Linux, including CI containers and most dev VMs) the empty string is interpreted as a file name and the command errors out, so the script silently fails to update GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL for Linux users. Additionally ENV_FILE="../.env" only resolves correctly if the script happens to be invoked from inside the scripts/ directory; running it from the repo root creates/updates a .env one level above the repository. Use a portable sed invocation (e.g. `sed -i.bak` plus cleanup, or detect GNU vs BSD) and resolve ENV_FILE relative to the script's own location.

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Handler throws a generic Error, surfacing as HTTP 500 instead of a proper tRPC error code

When the credential does not exist or belongs to another user, the handler throws `new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. In tRPC a plain Error is converted into an INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (500) response, which misleads clients and error monitoring into treating an expected authorization/not-found case as a server crash. The rest of the codebase uses TRPCError with code "NOT_FOUND" or "FORBIDDEN" for these cases; this should too.

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache timestamp is hardcoded to en-US formatting regardless of the user's locale

The 'Last updated' timestamp is formatted with `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)`, so every user — including those with a different app locale and different date conventions (day/month ordering, 24h clock) — sees a US-formatted date. The formatter should use the user's locale (available via useLocale / i18n.language) or the browser default by omitting the locale argument.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

false_positives.candidate:
No tests for the new deleteCache mutation's ownership check or the cache-status repository method

This PR adds a destructive, user-facing mutation (deleteCache) whose only protection is the userId ownership check in the handler, plus a new repository aggregation (getCacheStatusByCredentialIds) that drives what the UI displays. Neither has any test coverage: there is no test that a user cannot delete another user's credential cache (the security-critical path), nor any test covering the groupBy/mapping behavior. Given this is a security-sensitive destructive endpoint, at minimum the authorization failure case and the happy path should be covered.

deleteCache mutation never invalidates the connectedCalendars query, leaving stale cache status on screen

The deleteCache mutation's onSuccess only shows a toast and calls the optional onSuccess prop (onChanged). Unlike the disconnect mutation right below it (which explicitly invalidates viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars and viewer.apps.integrations in onSettled), nothing refetches connectedCalendars after a cache delete. The cacheUpdatedAt value that drives the 'Cache Status' display and the 'Delete cached data' menu item comes from that query, so after a successful deletion the UI will continue to show the old cache timestamp and offer deletion again until something else triggers a refetch — and in usages where onChanged is not provided it never updates. Add utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars.invalidate() to the deleteCache mutation's onSettled.

dev:cron now uses npx tsx but tsx is not a declared dependency

The script was changed from `ts-node cron-tester.ts` to `npx tsx cron-tester.ts`, but tsx does not appear in dependencies or devDependencies of this package (ts-node is still declared). `npx tsx` will fetch an unpinned tsx version from the registry on each fresh machine, which fails in offline/restricted environments, is non-deterministic across developers, and can break under yarn 3 PnP setups. Add tsx as a pinned devDependency and invoke it via yarn, or keep ts-node.

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds counts expired cache rows as active cache

The new groupBy query aggregates over all CalendarCache rows for the given credentials with no expiresAt filter. Everywhere else the cache is read (getCachedAvailability) rows are only served when expiresAt >= now, so an expired row is functionally dead. But connectedCalendars.handler uses this method to compute cacheUpdatedAt, which the UI uses to decide whether to show 'Cache Status: Last updated ...' and the 'Delete cached data' action. A credential whose only cache rows expired weeks ago will still be presented as having an active cache with a misleading 'last updated' timestamp. The where clause should include expiresAt: { gte: new Date() } to match the read path semantics.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reminder cancellation writes are fire-and-forget and may be lost before commit

Previously the cancel handler collected `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany(...)` promises into `remindersToDelete` and awaited them in `Promise.all`. The new code calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` / `deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...)` inside a `forEach` without awaiting anything. The `cancelled: true` update (or row delete) therefore happens in the background after the response may already have been sent; in a serverless deployment the lambda can be frozen once the response completes, so the flag may never be written — in which case the cron never cancels the SendGrid send and the reminder email is still delivered, re-creating the bug this PR fixes. The calls should be collected and awaited (the same applies to the identical new pattern in `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx` requestReschedule and `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/workflows.tsx`).

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reschedule path cancels SendGrid sends immediately and orphans the reminder rows, re-introducing the 100-pending-cancellations problem

When a booking is rescheduled, the old booking's email reminders are cancelled via `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)` with `immediateDelete=true`. That path POSTs the `status: "cancel"` to SendGrid right away — for reminders that may be scheduled days in the future — which is exactly the behavior this PR identifies as the root cause of hitting SendGrid's max of 100 pending cancellations (pending cancellations accumulate until the scheduled date). Additionally, the immediateDelete path neither deletes the `WorkflowReminder` row nor sets `cancelled: true`, so the row lingers with `scheduled: true` and is invisible to the cron's `cancelled: true` cleanup; it only disappears when the generic `scheduledDate <= now` deleteMany runs after the send date. For consistency with the fix, the reschedule path should mark `cancelled: true` (like the cancel path in handleCancelBooking) and let the cron perform the SendGrid cancellation inside the final hour. Also note the whole forEach is fire-and-forget, so the surrounding try/catch can never catch errors from these async calls.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
One failing SendGrid cancel aborts the whole cancellation batch and drops all DB deletes

In the new cancellation block of the cron handler, the `await client.request(...)` to SendGrid is inside the `for` loop but the whole loop is wrapped in a single try/catch. If the SendGrid request fails for any one reminder (e.g. a stale/invalid `referenceId` batch_id, which returns an error from SendGrid), the loop exits immediately: (a) all remaining `remindersToCancel` never get their SendGrid cancellation posted, so those emails will still be sent even though the bookings were cancelled — the exact bug this PR is meant to fix; and (b) the `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` promises collected in `workflowRemindersToDelete` are never awaited, and since Prisma promises are lazy, those deletes never execute. Because the failing row is never deleted, it will abort the loop again on every subsequent cron run (every 15 min), permanently blocking cancellations for all reminders that happen to sort after it (the query has no orderBy). Each reminder's SendGrid call and DB delete needs its own error handling so a single bad record can't block the batch.

Paid cancelled bookings return early and never cancel their workflow reminders

When a paid booking is cancelled, the handler refunds the payment, sets the booking status to REJECTED, and returns early at `return { message: "Booking successfully cancelled." }` — before reaching the new "Workflows - cancel all reminders for cancelled bookings" block further down (which calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` / `deleteScheduledSMSReminder`). As a result, workflow reminders for refunded/cancelled paid bookings are neither flagged `cancelled` nor deleted, and SendGrid will still send the scheduled reminder emails — the exact issue this PR is meant to resolve, still reproducible for any paid event type. The reminder cancellation should happen before (or independent of) the paid-booking early return.

requestReschedule cancels reminders without awaiting them

In the `requestReschedule` mutation, the old code collected `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany` promises and awaited them via `Promise.all(remindersToDelete)`. The new code calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` / `deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...)` in a `forEach` without awaiting. The mutation can complete and the serverless invocation can be torn down before the `cancelled: true` updates / deletes commit, leaving reminders active for a booking that was cancelled for rescheduling, so the cron never cancels them and emails may still be sent. The calls should be awaited.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Calendar/video deletions run un-awaited inside async forEach; surrounding try/catch is now dead

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) })` fires off async callbacks that nothing awaits, and the function proceeds to send the reschedule email and return immediately. Previously `getCalendar` was synchronous so `deleteEvent` was at least initiated synchronously; with the new `await getCalendar(...)` the deletion isn't even started until the dynamic import resolves, which races with the function returning (risky in serverless, where the process can freeze after the response). Additionally, errors thrown inside these async callbacks — including dynamic-import failures — reject outside the surrounding try/catch (lines 124–139), producing unhandled rejections rather than the logged errors the catch block intends. Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))` inside the try block.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Recurring-event calendar deletions are never awaited and may never start

In the recurring-event cancellation branch, the code does `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent); })`. Because `getCalendar` is now async (dynamic import), the entire body of the forEach callback — including the very first `calendar.deleteEvent(...)` call — is deferred until after the dynamic import resolves. Previously `getCalendar` was synchronous, so the first `deleteEvent` was at least initiated synchronously inside the callback. The handler later does `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` (line 652) using the contents of `apiDeletes` at that moment, which is still empty/partial because the async callbacks haven't run yet, and then returns the response. On serverless platforms the function can be frozen once the response is sent, so the external calendar events for all remaining recurring booking instances may never be deleted, leaving stale events on users' calendars. The pushed values are also the awaited results rather than promises, so they were never going to be awaited anyway. Use `await Promise.all(credentials.map(async ...))` and push the actual promises before awaiting.

false_positives.candidate:
Dynamic imports are evaluated eagerly at module load, so nothing is actually lazy-loaded

Each entry like `applecalendar: import("./applecalendar")` is evaluated when the `@calcom/app-store` module itself is first imported, which immediately kicks off loading of every app's chunk. Because the import() expressions run at object-literal evaluation time (not on property access), importing this module anywhere starts fetching all ~28 app bundles at once — there is no per-app deferral, only code splitting. If the intent of the PR is to defer loading apps until they are used, the values need to be lazy thunks (e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`) with call sites adjusted. As written, the change also converts app-module load failures into rejected promises stored in this object, which will surface as unhandled rejections for any app that is never explicitly awaited.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`end` in the working-hours check is a copy-paste of `start`

In the new working-hours block of checkIfIsAvailable: `const start = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute(); const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` — `end` should be computed from `slotEndTime` (i.e. slotStartTime + eventLength). As written, end === start, so the check `end > workingHour.endTime` only verifies that the slot *starts* before the working-hours end. A slot that starts inside the fixed host's working hours but finishes after their end time (e.g. host available 09:00–12:00, a 60-minute slot at 11:30–12:30 contributed by another round-robin host's wider availability) passes the check and is bookable, letting invitees book time the fixed host is not available.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
dayjs objects compared with `===` — always false

`if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes') === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, 'minutes'))` compares two distinct dayjs object instances by reference, which is always false (`.isSame()` was presumably intended). This branch exists to detect a blocked-day override (start === end, i.e. 'unavailable the whole day'). Because it never fires, a blocked day is only rejected incidentally via the before/after checks, and a slot starting exactly at the block's start instant satisfies none of them: the callback returns undefined, `dateOverrideExist` is already true, and the function returns `true` (available) — leaking a bookable slot on a day the host explicitly marked unavailable.

false_positives.candidate:
Date-override days skip the busy-time check, enabling double bookings

In checkIfIsAvailable, when any date override matches the slot's day, `dateOverrideExist` is set to true and, if the slot falls inside the override window (so the `find` callback never returns true), the function hits `if (dateOverrideExist) { return true; }` — returning 'available' before the `busy.every(...)` check at the bottom ever runs. This means that on any day where a host has a date override, that host's existing bookings and calendar busy times are completely ignored. A fixed host (or a regular solo event user, since they are also isFixed) with a date override who already has a booking/meeting inside the override window will be shown as bookable, producing double bookings — the exact problem this PR claims to fix ('prevents round-robin events being booked where the fixed hosts are unavailable'). The busy check must still run when a date override exists; only the working-hours check should be bypassed.

Multiple same-day date-override windows veto each other

The `dateOverrides.find(...)` logic treats 'slot is outside this one override window' as grounds to return false (unavailable), but a user can have several override windows on the same date (cal.com's UI allows adding multiple time ranges to one date override, stored as separate rows). For a slot that falls inside window B, window A's callback hits `slotStartTime.isAfter(date.end)` (or `slotEndTime.isBefore(date.start)`) and returns true, so the slot is marked unavailable even though it is within window B — and vice versa. Net effect: on a day with two or more override windows, every window is rejected by the other and the host shows no availability at all. The find should only return a 'reject' verdict after confirming the slot is outside *all* same-day windows for that user.

No test coverage for the round-robin fixed-host date-override fix

The PR's primary purpose is making date overrides (and working hours) of *fixed hosts* apply to round-robin events via the new logic in checkIfIsAvailable, and the PR description lists a round-robin fixed-host scenario as the main test plan. However, the only test added exercises a single-user personal event with a different invitee timezone. None of the new checkIfIsAvailable behavior — fixed host availability gating, override-window filtering per host, interaction with busy times — is covered, which is how the regression where busy checks are skipped on override days (and the multi-window veto issue) went unnoticed. A round-robin scenario with one fixed host having a date override should be added, including a case where the fixed host is busy inside the override window.

Offset-shifted override times discard the day component

The invitee-timezone conversion computes `startTime`/`endTime` as `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, 'minute').hour() * 60 + ...minute()`. Taking `.hour()/.minute()` after the offset shift drops any day rollover: when the invitee/organizer offset difference pushes the override across midnight (e.g. organizer Asia/Kolkata override 01:00–02:00 = 19:30–20:30 the previous UTC day, viewed by a UTC invitee: offset = −330 min lands on the previous day, but hour() yields 1170 minutes), the slot is materialized at 19:30 on the *current* invitee day instead of the correct adjacent day. Since the activeOverrides filter keys on the unshifted date, cross-midnight overrides are placed on the wrong day — precisely the timezone-adjustment scenario this PR is fixing. The shifted value should be carried as a full timestamp (or the day delta applied to startOfInviteeDay), not reduced to minutes-since-midnight.

Override decoding depends on the server running in UTC

The new code decodes the override's wall-clock-encoded Date back to a real instant with `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes')` and compares it against `slotStartTime`/`slotEndTime`, which are explicitly UTC (`time.utc()`). `dayjs(date.start)` parses the Date in the process's local timezone, so the decode math (wall time − organizer offset = real UTC instant) only holds when the Node process runs with TZ=UTC. On any non-UTC runtime (dev machines, some CI/self-hosted setups) the override window and day-matching comparisons are shifted by the server offset, making fixed-host override filtering silently wrong. Use `dayjs.utc(date.start)` for these comparisons, as the parallel code in packages/lib/slots.ts already does with `.utc()`.

override.timeZone is optional in the type but required by the conversion

`dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()` assumes `override.timeZone` is set, but the `TimeRange` type declares `timeZone?: string` as optional and getSlots is a shared library function — nothing at the type level guarantees every caller supplies it (the slots router happens to add it in this PR). With `timeZone` undefined, dayjs's tz plugin falls back to the host system's timezone when computing `organizerUtcOffset`, so the offset correction is silently computed against the server timezone and override slots are shifted by a wrong amount. Either make the field required for date overrides passed to getSlots or guard/default it here.

The PR's goal is to block linking a GitHub App installation when the OAuth-authenticated GitHub user differs from the user who installed the app. However, in GitHubInstallation.dispatch the check only runs when an Integration row already exists (the webhook-created path). An attacker who learns or guesses a victim's installation_id (these are sequential integers) can still attach that installation to their own Sentry org whenever the victim's Integration row is absent (webhook delivery failed or delayed, or installation predates webhook handling), which is the same hijack this PR intends to prevent. Only the body-parsing step is wrapped (and with a bare `except Exception`). Wrap the token exchange and user-info calls and render the error page on failure.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at class definition time

In a dataclass, a plain default expression is evaluated once when the class body executes, not per instance. `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` therefore freezes `queued` to the module import time for every `AssignmentSource` created without an explicit value, instead of recording when the assignment was queued. Dataclasses only reject list/dict/set defaults, so this fails silently. The fix is `queued: datetime = field(default_factory=timezone.now)`. The field is currently unused, so the impact is limited to incorrect data, but it is a latent bug for any future consumer of the timestamp.

true_positives.golden_comment: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
AssignmentSource.to_dict() puts a non-JSON-serializable datetime into the Celery task payload

`sync_group_assignee_outbound` passes `assignment_source.to_dict()` as a kwarg to `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async`. `to_dict()` is `dataclasses.asdict(self)`, which includes `queued` as a raw `datetime` object. Celery's default task serializer is JSON (and Sentry's task payloads are generally expected to be JSON-safe), and a `datetime` is not JSON-serializable, so `apply_async` will raise `TypeError: Object of type datetime is not JSON serializable` at enqueue time. This failure occurs synchronously inside `GroupAssignee.objects.assign/deassign` whenever an assignment was triggered by an inbound integration webhook (which is exactly the new code path that always sets an `AssignmentSource`), so every inbound-triggered assignment would 500 the webhook handler and never enqueue any outbound sync. Even with an encoder that coerces datetimes to ISO strings, `from_dict` would then produce `queued` as a string rather than a datetime. The `queued` value should be serialized explicitly (e.g. `isoformat()` / timestamp) and parsed back in `from_dict`, or dropped from the payload. Note the new tests run tasks eagerly via `self.tasks()`, so no real serialization round-trip is exercised and this would not be caught by CI.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
