false_negatives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

false_positives.candidate:
Redis memory check double-counts clusters shared by multiple per-process buffers, skewing the used/available ratio

Shards are assigned to processes round-robin (`process_index = i % num_processes`), so when `max_processes > 1` each per-process `SpansBuffer` typically holds shards that map to the same Redis cluster as other buffers. `submit()` now aggregates memory by calling `buffer.get_memory_info()` on every buffer and summing the results; a cluster's used/available memory is therefore counted once per covering buffer instead of once as before (previously a single buffer covered all assigned shards and could report each cluster once). If clusters are not counted a uniform number of times (e.g., cluster shard counts not divisible by the process count), the computed `used / available` ratio is skewed and `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage` hard backpressure will trigger too early or too late. It also multiplies the number of Redis INFO calls made on the consumer's submit path by the number of flusher processes.

Restarting a hung flusher in thread mode leaves the old thread running, producing duplicate segments for the same shards

When `produce_to_pipe` is set, flusher workers are `threading.Thread`s. In `_ensure_processes_alive`, if such a worker is judged hung (healthy_since stale), the restart path calls `process.kill()` only when `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`, so for threads nothing stops the old worker, and then `_create_process_for_shards` unconditionally starts a new thread for the same shards and overwrites `self.processes[process_index]`. The hung-but-alive thread and the replacement thread then concurrently call `buffer.flush_segments()` / `done_flush_segments()` for the same shards and both write to the same `process_backpressure_since`/`process_healthy_since` values, which can produce the same segment twice to the output and corrupts the health/backpressure bookkeeping. Either guard against restarting un-killable hung threads or document/handle the duplicate-flush window explicitly.

_create_process_for_shard is dead code and would leak a duplicate process if used

`_create_process_for_shard` is never called anywhere. Worse, if it ever were used, it calls `_create_process_for_shards` without killing the existing process for that shard's group and without incrementing `process_restarts`, leaving two live processes flushing the same shards (duplicate segments produced, conflicting health values). It should be removed or fixed to go through the same kill-and-track path as `_ensure_processes_alive`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts the opposite of what the implementation does and only passes by timing luck

The test's docstring says "errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages", but the final assertion is `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` — i.e. it asserts that nothing was committed. In the actual implementation, `OrderedQueueWorker.run` completes the offset in a `finally` block even when `result_processor` raises, so both offsets (100 and 101) become committable and the commit loop commits them on its next 1-second tick. The test only passes because it finishes (processing is mocked and instant) before the commit thread's first 1s wake-up; wait a second longer and the offsets of the "failed" message would be committed. The test should either assert that the failed message's offset *is* committed (matching the implementation and the existing at-least-once semantics of the other modes) or the implementation should be changed — as written it documents behavior that is false and is fragile to scheduling.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

false_positives.candidate:
Shared FixedQueuePool is shut down by the old strategy on rebalance, causing silent message loss

The `FixedQueuePool` is created once in the factory's `__init__` and shared by every `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` produced by `create_with_partitions`. Arroyo closes and re-creates the strategy on every partition revocation/rebalance: the old strategy's `close()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which shuts down all queues and worker threads in the shared pool. The new strategy created after the rebalance still references the same pool. From then on, `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` calls `work_queue.put()`, which raises `queue.ShutDown` on a shut-down queue; this is caught by the broad `except Exception` in `submit`, which then calls `add_offset`/`complete_offset` on the message's offset. The result: every message after a rebalance is silently dropped (never processed) while its offset is marked complete and committed to Kafka. Since consumer groups rebalance on every deploy/scale event, running this mode in production would skip uptime results without any error surfacing beyond a log line. The pool needs to be created per `create_with_partitions` call, or `close()` must not shut down a pool it doesn't own.

Worker queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure and memory can grow without limit

`FixedQueuePool` creates each work queue with `queue.Queue()` (no maxsize), so `submit`/`put` never blocks. The docstring on `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` (line ~253) claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but that never happens: the Arroyo consumer thread will keep polling Kafka and appending `WorkItem`s faster than slow workers can drain them, buffering an unbounded number of decoded results in process memory. This is exactly the failure mode the PR is meant to mitigate (one slow item/group clogging processing) — a slow group now grows its queue until the consumer OOMs. The queues should have a `maxsize` (or `submit` should otherwise block/apply backpressure) to match the documented behavior.

join() ignores its timeout and shutdown abandons all queued items instead of draining them

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(timeout)` ignores the timeout and just calls `close()`, which immediately shuts down the queue pool. In `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` each worker's `shutdown` flag is set to True before `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` is called, so a worker that is woken with pending items still in its queue processes at most one more item and then exits its `while not self.shutdown` loop — everything remaining in the queues is discarded without being processed and without a final offset commit. Standard Arroyo strategies drain in-flight work and commit during `join` on graceful shutdown; here every deploy or rebalance abandons the entire in-memory backlog (which, given the unbounded queues, can be large) to be redelivered and reprocessed. At minimum `join` should wait for queues to drain up to the timeout and perform a final commit of completed offsets.

test_stats_reporting is flaky: asserts total_items > 0 after workers may have already drained the queue

The test submits 10 trivial work items (the processor just appends to a list under a lock) and then immediately asserts `stats["total_items"] > 0`. The three worker threads start consuming as soon as the first item is put, so on a fast machine all 10 items can be processed before the main thread reaches `get_stats()`, making `total_items` 0 and the assertion fail intermittently. The non-zero-depth assertion needs synchronization that blocks workers (e.g. an event the processor waits on) to be reliable.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key is ambiguous: fields joined with '_' can collide for UIDs containing underscores

userPermDenialCacheKey builds the key by concatenating namespace, userUID, action, name, and parent with '_' separators and no escaping or length prefixing. Resource and folder UIDs in Grafana can contain underscores, so distinct (name, parent) pairs produce identical keys: e.g. name="dash_a", parent="fold_b" and name="dash_a_fold", parent="b" both yield the same key. Because a cached entry means 'deny', a denial recorded for one dashboard/folder combination will incorrectly deny access to a different, unrelated dashboard for up to 30 seconds (shortCacheTTL). Use a delimiter that cannot appear in UIDs, hash the individual fields, or encode lengths to make the key unambiguous.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache is checked before the new DB requery path, reintroducing stale denials for newly granted permissions

The stated goal of this PR is to let creators access dashboards/folders they just created by requerying the DB when cached permissions don't contain the resource. However, the denial cache is consulted first in Check and short-circuits before both the permission cache and the DB fallback. If a Check is evaluated and denied before the permission grant is visible (e.g. a check that races the permission write at creation time, or read-replica lag on the permission query), the denial is cached for shortCacheTTL (30s) and every subsequent check for that exact resource returns Allowed=false without ever hitting the DB requery logic added in this PR. The creator is then locked out of the resource they just created for up to 30 seconds — the same symptom this PR is meant to fix. Consider a much shorter TTL for denial entries, or falling through to the DB on denial-cache hit under a singleflight/throttle instead of returning immediately.

Denial-cache hits are counted as permission-cache hits in metrics

When the denial cache short-circuits a Check, the code increments s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage with label "true" (cache hit). This metric is meant to track usage of the permission cache (permCache); denial-cache hits are a different signal and will inflate the apparent permission cache hit ratio, making dashboards/alerts built on this metric misleading. Consider a separate metric or an additional label value (e.g. "denial") for this path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
GrafanaRuleListItem rendered in rules.map without a key prop

In the `rules.map(...)` switch in FilterViewResults, the 'grafana' branch now returns `<GrafanaRuleListItem rule={...} groupIdentifier={...} ... />` with no `key` prop — the previous code passed `key={key}` (the comment in this file explains the artificial `key` exists specifically to prevent key duplication). The 'datasource' and default branches still pass `key={key}`. React will log a missing-key warning and, more importantly, reconciliation of this infinitely-appended list can match/grafana list items incorrectly when the list grows or re-renders.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence menu item renders in the new list view but clicking it does nothing

In the new ruler-less list view, RuleActionsButtons is rendered with only `promRule` (no `rule`/RulerRuleDTO). AlertRuleMenu computes `canSilence` from `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(promRule, ...)`, which can be true, so the 'Silence notifications' menu item is shown and calls `handleSilence()` -> `setShowSilenceDrawer(true)`. However, the drawer is only rendered behind the guard `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) && showSilenceDrawer`, and `rule` is undefined in this context, so the SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer never appears. The user clicks Silence and nothing happens — a visibly broken action in the primary new list view.

false_positives.candidate:
Component doc comment still says it loads from Prometheus and Ruler endpoints

The JSDoc above GrafanaGroupLoader still reads 'Loads an evaluation group from Prometheus and Ruler endpoints' and the `expectedRulesCount` comment still says 'Ruler response might contain different number of rules', but this PR removed the `useGetGrafanaRulerGroupQuery` call and all ruler handling from the component. The comments now describe behavior that no longer exists and will mislead future maintainers.

Delete menu item can never render in the new list view despite prom-based delete ability

The Delete menu item is guarded by `{canDelete && rulerRule && (...)}`. This PR adds prom-based ability checks (`canDelete` can now be true via `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` even without a ruler rule), and RuleActionsButtons.V2's `handleDelete` only needs the identifier (`showDeleteModal(identifier, groupIdentifier)`), but in the new list view `rulerRule` is always undefined, so the `rulerRule &&` guard permanently hides Delete. Users cannot delete Grafana rules from the new alert list view even with full permissions. The same pattern at line 123 (`canPause && rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)`) also makes Pause unavailable in the list view.

Prom-based abilities use alertingRule check for ModifyExport/Pause, dropping support for recording rules

In `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`, ModifyExport, Pause and Restore use `isAlertingRule = prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` as the supported flag, whereas the ruler-based equivalent uses `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rule)` / `isGrafanaManagedAlertRule`, which matches both alerting and recording Grafana rules. In the new list view (promRule only, ruler abilities unavailable), Grafana recording rules therefore lose the Export menu item and pause support that they previously had. Modify-export and pausing are valid operations for Grafana-managed recording rules.

Refactor of useAllAlertRuleAbilities drops the federated rule group check, enabling edit/delete on federated Mimir groups

Before this change, `useAllAlertRuleAbilities(rule: CombinedRule)` computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` and used it to disable Update/Delete/Pause/DeletePermanently for federated (cross-tenant Mimir) rule groups. The PR rewrites `useAllAlertRuleAbilities` to delegate to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities(rule.rulerRule, groupIdentifierV2)`, which hardcodes `const isFederated = false` (with a TODO). Since `useAlertRuleAbility`/`useAlertRuleAbilities` still route through `useAllAlertRuleAbilities` and are used by existing components (e.g. the old RulesTable / RuleActionsButtons), edit, delete and pause actions are now offered in the UI for federated rule groups where they were previously disabled. The backend may still reject the operation, but this is a UI-level permission regression.

Rule link no longer includes the returnTo parameter

The deleted GrafanaRuleLoader's GrafanaRuleListItem built the view URL with `createRelativeUrl('/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view', { returnTo })` using `createReturnTo()`, so navigating back from the rule detail view returned the user to the list. The new GrafanaRuleListItem (used by both GrafanaGroupLoader and FilterView) builds the href without `returnTo`, silently regressing the back-navigation behavior for the new list views.

Stale comment and variable name reference ruler rule preloading that was removed

The comment 'This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules, but it improves the UX / Because the user waits a bit longer for the initial load but doesn't need to wait for each group to be loaded' and the variable name `cacheAndRulerPreload` remain, but the `alertRuleApi.util.prefetch('getGrafanaRulerGroup', ...)` dispatch they described was deleted in this PR. The remaining code only upserts the Prometheus groups cache, so the comment/identifier are now incorrect.

skipToken path computes Duplicate ability against Grafana permissions, wrongly enabling Duplicate for cloud rules

When `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`/`useGrafanaPromRuleAbility` is called with `skipToken` (e.g. in AlertRuleMenu and RuleActionsButtons.V2 for cloud/Mimir rules, where `prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(promRule)` is false), `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined)` still computes abilities: loading is false so `MaybeSupported = AlwaysSupported`, and `[AlertRuleAction.Duplicate] = toAbility(duplicateSupported=true, getRulesPermissions('grafana').create)`. AlertRuleMenu then ORs this with the ruler ability, so `canDuplicate` becomes true for a cloud rule whenever the user has the Grafana-internal rule create permission — even if they lack the external rule write permission that the ruler-based check requires. The Duplicate menu item appears and navigates to a clone flow that will fail.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Interpolating before querySupportsSplitting() defeats the $__range no-split guard

The new `.map((query) => datasource.applyTemplateVariables(...))` runs before `partition(queries, querySupportsSplitting)` on line 300. `querySupportsSplitting` deliberately excludes queries containing `$__range` (lines 285-287) because the range variable must be resolved against the full, unsplit time range. Since `applyTemplateVariables` substitutes `$__range` with the full-range duration up front, by the time `isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr)` is evaluated the token is already gone, so the guard never fires. Queries using `$__range` — previously sent as a single unsplit request — will now be time-split into daily chunks with the full-range duration baked into every sub-query (e.g. `rate(foo[3d])` executed against each 1-day window), and each chunk's lookback extends well outside its own range, returning wrong/inflated results. The range-variable check needs to run against the uninterpolated expr, or `$__range` queries need to be excluded before interpolation is applied.

Shard-split queries are now interpolated twice, duplicating ad hoc filters and re-processing interpolated values

`runShardSplitQuery` interpolates every target via `datasource.applyTemplateVariables` (line 52), and each shard sub-request is then executed through `runSplitQuery` (line 163), which after this PR interpolates the same targets again (querySplitting.ts:299). The updated test asserting `applyTemplateVariables` is called 5 times (once here plus once per shard group) confirms the double pass. Consequences: (1) `applyTemplateVariables` also injects `request.filters` ad hoc matchers into the stream selector, so with ad hoc filters configured those matchers are appended twice to every selector sent to Loki; (2) any variable replacement value that itself contains a `$`-style token (e.g. `${...}`) will be re-processed and potentially mangled by the second pass. Before this PR each query was interpolated exactly once. Consider interpolating only in one place — e.g. drop the interpolation in `runShardSplitQuery` since `runSplitQuery` now handles it — while noting the shard-values fetch (`fetchLabelValues`) needs the interpolated selector, so the fetch path must still receive an interpolated expr.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext returns a discarded instance, breaking log assertions

`TestLogger.FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()` instead of `f`. Any code under test that logs through `FromContext` — which the updated `LoggerMiddleware.logRequest` now does — will record calls on a throwaway logger instance, so tests that inject a `TestLogger` and then assert on its `InfoLogs`/`ErrorLogs`/etc. will see zero calls and no captured messages. The fake should return `f` (or record on the shared instance) so log output through `FromContext` is observable in tests.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.

false_positives.candidate:
FromContext doc comment is a copy-paste of the New comment and misdescribes the method

The doc comment for the new `FromContext` interface method reads "FromContext returns a new contextual Logger that has this logger's context plus the given context.", which is a verbatim copy of the `New` method's comment. `FromContext` takes a `context.Context` and (per its implementations) extracts/derives a logger from it — it does not merge variadic key/value pairs into the logger's context. The comment misleads implementers and callers about the method's contract.

FromContext never reads the context-bound logger, so Plugin Request Completed logs lose pluginId/endpoint/dsName/dsUID/uname

The new `FromContext` implementation calls the method `d.l.FromContext(ctx)` on the infra `*log.ConcreteLogger`. That method only derives a logger with the `traceID` from the trace span in the context; it does not return the logger that `log.WithContextualAttributes(ctx, p)` stores in the context. The new `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` (contextual_logger_middleware.go) attaches the pluginId/endpoint/dsName/dsUID/uname attributes to a context-bound logger via `log.WithContextualAttributes`, and `LoggerMiddleware.logRequest` now relies on `m.logger.FromContext(ctx)` to pick those attributes up (the explicit log params were removed from logger_middleware.go). Because the wrapper never retrieves the context-bound logger — it should call the package-level `log.FromContext(ctx)` — the "Plugin Request Completed" log line silently loses the pluginId, endpoint, dsName, dsUID and uname fields that were logged before this change whenever backend request logging (`PluginLogBackendRequests`) is enabled.

New ContextualLoggerMiddleware added without any test coverage

This PR introduces a new middleware that moves the `instrumentContext` logic (which endpoint/datasource/user attributes get attached and under which conditions, e.g. nil `DataSourceInstanceSettings` or nil `User`) out of the old instrumentation middleware, but adds no test for it. The only test touched is the renamed metrics middleware test, which covers metrics collection, not the contextual attributes. A regression in which attributes are attached — or in the interaction with `LoggerMiddleware.FromContext` — would go unnoticed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check is racy: COUNT then INSERT is not atomic

CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the limit by first running CountDevices and only inserting if count < deviceLimit, with no transaction or database-level constraint tying the two together. Two concurrent requests for distinct new devices can both observe count < limit and both insert, exceeding the configured limit. With multiple Grafana replicas each doing this independently (and per-instance local caches), the overshoot can be larger. If the limit is meant to be enforced (e.g., for licensing/abuse control), the check-and-insert needs to be atomic (single transaction with locking, or a conditional INSERT based on a subquery count).

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Local cache is populated before the DB write, so rejected devices bypass the limit on retry

In tagDeviceUI, the local cache entry for the device is set (a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})) BEFORE calling anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice. When the device limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, which now propagates up to Anonymous.Authenticate and rejects the request. However, the device's cache key has already been written, so for the next 29 minutes every subsequent request from that same device hits the cache and returns nil without ever touching the database — meaning authentication succeeds. The net effect is that a device over the limit is blocked exactly once and then freely allowed in on any retry, which defeats the feature. The cache entry should only be set after CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Device tagging moved onto the synchronous auth path without timeout or panic recovery

Previously TagDevice was invoked in a background goroutine guarded by recover() and a 2-minute timeout (timeoutTag), so a slow or panicking database call could not affect request authentication. This PR calls a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice synchronously inside Authenticate with no timeout and no panic guard. On every local-cache miss (at least once per ~29 minutes per device per instance) the anonymous authentication path now blocks on a COUNT plus an UPDATE/INSERT against the database, and any panic in that path will crash the request. Consider keeping the failure isolation (timeout/recover) while still propagating the limit error.

Device-limit rejection surfaces as a raw error, producing HTTP 500 for end users

When TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, Authenticate now returns that plain error (return nil, err). The authn layer has no typed handling for this error, so anonymous users who exceed the device limit will get a generic HTTP 500 Internal Server Error with the message 'device limit reached' instead of a deliberate status such as 429 Too Many Requests (or 401) with a user-facing explanation. The error should be wrapped in a typed authn/response error that maps to an appropriate status code and message.

New device_limit option is not documented in defaults.ini/sample config or docs

The PR adds a new configuration key `device_limit` under [auth.anonymous] (read via anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0)) but does not add it to conf/defaults.ini, conf/sample.ini, or the administration documentation, where all other auth.anonymous options (enabled, org_name, org_role, hide_version) are documented. Admins have no way to discover the setting, its default (0 = unlimited), or its semantics without reading the source.

No test that an existing device can still update when the limit is reached

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only covers the rejection path (a brand-new device being refused with ErrDeviceLimitReached when the limit is reached). There is no test for the complementary updateDevice success path: an already-registered device that is at/over the limit must still be able to refresh its row (client_ip/user_agent/updated_at), otherwise legitimate returning devices would be locked out. There is also no test covering the interaction with the service-level local cache (i.e., that a rejected device is not cached and is re-checked on retry).

anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined infers property type 'undefined'

In GrafanaBootConfig, the new field is declared as `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined;`. Under strictNullChecks this gives the class property the literal type `undefined`, so any TypeScript consumer reading config.anonymousDeviceLimit sees type `undefined` and cannot use it as a number without a cast. The neighboring fields use explicit annotations (e.g. `loginError: string | undefined = undefined;`). This should be `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined;` to match the GrafanaConfig interface. Note also that the Go DTO (FrontendSettingsDTO.AnonymousDeviceLimit, an int64 without omitempty) always serializes a number, so the value is never actually undefined in boot data.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup logs every successful batch at Error level, including full ID lists

The new batch callbacks log at Error level during normal, successful operation: lines 534, 537, 554, 557 (CleanAnnotations) and 576, 579 (CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags) all call r.log.Error(...). These fire on every cleanup cycle and every batch, and they dump the complete slice of fetched IDs into the log line (up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize entries, potentially tens of thousands of IDs per line). This produces massive log lines and constant false error-level noise that can trip alerting on error logs and bury real errors. The 'err', err key/value pairs log a value that is always nil at those points, indicating these are leftover debug statements. They should be Debug level (or removed) and should not serialize the entire ID slice.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute for all cleanup jobs, undocumented

The PR is about splitting the annotation cleanup queries, but it also changes the CleanUpService ticker from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This makes every cleanup job run 10x more often, not just annotation cleanup: filesystem scans of the images and CSV directories (cleanUpTmpFiles), expired snapshot/dashboard-version/image deletion, user invite expiry, short URL and query history cleanup. Each minute now scans directories and issues DELETEs against many tables, and since each run has a 9-minute timeout, a slow run means cleanup work executes essentially back-to-back with no idle gap. This behavior change is not mentioned in the PR description and affects operators' DB and I/O load; if the motivation is to compensate for the new split queries under-deleting annotations, only the annotation job cadence should change.

false_positives.candidate:
SQLite inline-ID path builds the IN list with quadratic fmt.Sprintf concatenation

In deleteByIDs, the SQLite fallback builds the ID list via values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) inside the loop, which copies the entire accumulated string on every iteration — O(n²) byte copying. With the large batch sizes this path exists for (the new test uses a batch size of 32767), that is on the order of gigabytes of transient copying per batch on every cleanup cycle. A strings.Builder plus strconv.AppendInt would make it linear. Related minor points: the comment 'SQLite has a parameter limit of 999' is outdated for SQLite >= 3.32.0 (which supports 32766 variables, as the new test's name acknowledges), and the branch is keyed off the configured AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize rather than len(ids), so even a final 5-row batch takes the string-building path when the configured batch size exceeds 999.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete installs the base logger into the context instead of the enriched one

Delete builds `log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method)` but then calls `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)`, dropping the name/kind/method values for anything downstream that logs via `klog.FromContext(ctx)`. It should pass `log`, as the other methods do.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
DeleteCollection records the legacy delete result against the storage metric

In the async goroutine of DeleteCollection, the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` instead of `recordLegacyDuration`. Legacy delete-collection latency/errors will be attributed to unified storage, corrupting both metrics (all other methods use `recordLegacyDuration` in this position).

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete success metric records the object name as the kind label, causing unbounded Prometheus label cardinality

In Delete, the success path calls `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` — passing the resource `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. This both mislabels the metric (kind label contains object names) and creates a Prometheus series per object name, which is unbounded cardinality that can blow up the metrics store. It should be `options.Kind`.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes are unordered, so create-then-update/delete sequences can diverge legacy storage

Each write method spawns an independent goroutine with its own 10s timeout and no serialization. A client that creates an object and immediately updates or deletes it will have the create's legacy write and the update/delete's legacy write racing in separate goroutines: the update can reach legacy before the create has been applied (failing with not-found, since forceAllowCreate is false), or a delete can be applied before the create lands, leaving a stale object in legacy. Because reads in mode 3 come only from unified storage, this divergence is invisible to users and only shows up as error counters. If ordering matters for the 'safe measure' copy, the legacy writes need a queue/serialization per object.

Async legacy writes derive their context from the request context, so they are canceled when the request completes

In Create (and identically in Delete line 110, Update line 135, and DeleteCollection line 163) the background goroutine does `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` where `ctx` is the incoming request context. The request context is canceled as soon as the API handler returns, which happens immediately after the synchronous unified-storage write — so the child context used for the 'safe measure' legacy write is typically canceled before or during the legacy SQL call. The legacy write will then fail with context canceled, silently diverging legacy and unified storage (only visible as a metric). The goroutine should detach from the request lifecycle first, e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)`, before applying the 10s timeout.

Create and Update record a legacy-storage error metric when unified storage fails and legacy is never called

In Create (line 45), when `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` even though the legacy store was never invoked — this both inflates legacy error counts and loses the unified-storage error metric. The same mistake exists in Update at line 129, which records `recordLegacyDuration` on a `d.Storage.Update` failure. Both should call `recordStorageDuration`, as the error paths in Delete and DeleteCollection correctly do.

New mode-3 integration subtests read the legacy API immediately after k8s writes, racing the async legacy write

The added 'with dual write (file, mode 3)' and 'with dual write (unified storage, mode 3)' subtests reuse `doPlaylistTests`, which asserts legacy `/api/playlists` results immediately after k8s creates/updates/deletes (e.g. comparing `/api/playlists` list right after `client.Resource.Create`). In mode 3 the legacy write happens in a background goroutine with up to a 10s window, so these assertions race the async write and will be flaky; combined with the request-context cancellation bug in dualwriter_mode3.go they may fail consistently. The test needs polling/retry on the legacy side or the async write needs to be made deterministic for tests.

TestMode3_Create error case configures the failure on the legacy mock, but mode 3 calls unified storage first

The case 'error when creating object in the unified store fails' sets up only `setupLegacyFn` returning an error and provides no `setupStorageFn`. In mode 3, `dw.Create` calls `d.Storage.Create` first; with no expectation registered on the shared mock for that call, testify will panic with an unexpected-call failure rather than exercising the intended error path. The error expectation needs to be on the storage mock (and this worked in mode 1 only because mode 1 calls legacy first).

Update passes the original objInfo to the legacy store, so UpdatedObject is invoked a second time against a different old object

The previous implementation fetched the old object, computed the updated object once, and wrapped it in `updateWrapper` so both stores persisted the same object. The new code passes the raw `objInfo` to both `d.Storage.Update` and, asynchronously, to `d.Legacy.Update`. This means `objInfo.UpdatedObject()` is invoked twice: the second time (in the goroutine) it runs against the old object fetched from legacy storage, which may have a different resourceVersion or may not exist yet (see the create-ordering race). `UpdatedObjectInfo` implementations are not guaranteed to be idempotent or reusable across calls, and the resulting legacy object can diverge from what was written to unified storage. The legacy call should receive a wrapper holding the object already produced by the unified update.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No re-check of cache after acquiring write lock causes duplicate loads

After the fast-path read returns nil, the code acquires the write lock and unconditionally reloads the assets from disk (or CDN) without re-checking `entryPointAssetsCache`. If several requests arrive before the first successful load (e.g. at startup), they will each take the write lock in turn and each perform a full file read/HTTP fetch, even though the first one already populated the cache. A simple `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` immediately after acquiring the write lock would avoid the redundant loads.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
Write lock held across file and network I/O serializes all callers

The write lock acquired at line 48 is held (via defer) across `readWebAssetsFromCDN` (an outbound HTTP request) and `readWebAssetsFromFile` (disk I/O). While the load is in progress, every other goroutine calling GetWebAssets — including ones that arrive after the load has started but before the cache write at line 69 — blocks on the write lock instead of doing their own I/O in parallel, and in dev mode every single request now serializes on this mutex. This is a behavior change worth being aware of; it is not a correctness bug, but a slow or hanging CDN call will now stall all callers on the mutex.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

false_positives.candidate:
Error message 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' is misleading

When a user submits a SQL expression query, ReadQuery now rejects it with the error "sqlExpressions is not implemented". The feature is in fact implemented but deliberately disabled as the CVE-2024-9264 mitigation, and the sqlExpressions feature flag still exists in the codebase. Users who explicitly enabled the flag will receive a message claiming the feature does not exist, which is confusing and makes support/debugging harder. The message should state that SQL expressions are disabled (e.g. "sqlExpressions is disabled") rather than not implemented.

No regression test covering the SQL expression disable

This PR disables SQL expressions as a security mitigation (CVE-2024-9264) but adds no test asserting that a query with type 'sql' is rejected by ReadQuery, nor that NewSQLCommand/SQLCommand.Execute fail with the stubbed DB now that go-duck is removed. Existing tests in pkg/expr/sql that exercised TablesList against a real DuckDB would now fail or have been silently affected, and there is no guard preventing a future change from accidentally re-enabling the execution path. A regression test verifying SQL expressions return an error would protect the security fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the build-wide lock allows concurrent duplicate builds of the same index

BuildIndex previously serialized all builds with cacheMu; now two goroutines can build the same NamespacedResource concurrently (getOrCreateIndex in search.go does a check-then-build with no synchronization, and its own comment acknowledges it does not block concurrent builders of the same key). Consequences: (1) for file-backed indexes (size > FileThreshold), both builders call bleve.New on the same directory path, and the second one fails on the bleve lock file, surfacing a spurious error to a search or watch-event request; (2) for memory-backed indexes both builds succeed and the second write to b.cache silently overwrites the first, leaking an open bleve.Index that is never closed and wasting the entire duplicate build. A per-key lock (or singleflight) is needed instead of the single global lock that was removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs reads b.cache map without holding cacheMu

TotalDocs() iterates over b.cache without acquiring b.cacheMu (it never did, but it matters now). Before this PR, BuildIndex held cacheMu for its entire duration and TotalDocs was effectively only reached after all init builds completed; now the lock is only taken for the final map insertion, and this PR adds a new call to TotalDocs in searchSupport.init (search.go line 216, the "search index initialized" log) that runs right after the watch-event goroutine is started. That goroutine calls getOrCreateIndex -> BuildIndex on events for unknown namespaces, which writes b.cache concurrently with the TotalDocs iteration. Concurrent map read/write in Go is a fatal runtime error ("concurrent map read and map write"), which will crash the process. TotalDocs should take b.cacheMu.RLock() before iterating.

false_positives.candidate:
BuildIndex starts a span but drops the span context, inconsistent with the PR's trace-propagation fix

The PR fixes trace propagation by assigning the context returned from tracer.Start back to ctx in search.go and sql/backend.go, but bleveBackend.BuildIndex still does `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)` and discards the span-scoped context. Any operation inside BuildIndex that could use the context (e.g. passing it to the builder callback or future instrumented calls) would be detached from the BuildIndex span, so the bleve portion of index-building traces remains disconnected from its children. Use `ctx, span := b.tracer.Start(...)` for consistency with the rest of the change.

Data race on shared err variable across errgroup goroutines in init

Inside searchSupport.init, every errgroup goroutine executes `_, _, err = s.build(ctx, ...)` assigning to the same outer `err` variable that is also read after group.Wait() and was previously assigned by GetResourceStats. With initWorkers > 1 (the exact scenario this PR is optimizing) these goroutines write err concurrently, which is a data race (flagged by -race) and can produce torn/ stale error values. Each goroutine should use a local error variable and return it, letting errgroup surface the first failure. The same loop also increments totalBatchesIndexed++ from multiple goroutines without synchronization (line 189), another race that can undercount the value reported in the span event.

NewResourceServer leaks resources when eager Init fails

When s.Init(ctx) fails, NewResourceServer returns nil, err but does not call s.cancel() to release the cancellable context created a few lines above, and does not close the blob bucket that may have been opened earlier in the function (OpenBlobBucket/NewCDKBlobSupport). Since Init now runs at construction time, init failures (e.g. index build errors) are a realistic path, and each failed construction leaks the context and the bucket handle. The error path should call cancel() and close any opened blob support before returning.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup in testCacheIDPForLogin registers removal of literal alias "alias" instead of the created IDPs

In testCacheIDPForLogin, both cleanup registrations use getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove) with the literal string "alias" instead of the actual alias variable ("idp-alias-" + i / "idp-alias-20"). As a result none of the ~21 identity providers created by the test are removed afterwards, and the deferred remove() calls will hit a non-existent IDP (404) during cleanup, which can fail the test class teardown and pollutes the shared test realm for subsequent tests. The same literal-alias copy/paste already existed in testCacheIDPByOrg and was duplicated here.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Login-cache invalidation on update uses the org-aware wrapped model, missing invalidations while the organization is disabled

update() fetches the 'original' IDP via getById(), which returns the model wrapped by createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel(). That wrapper overrides isEnabled() to also return false when the linked organization is disabled. registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate() then applies getLoginPredicate() (which includes isEnabled()) to this wrapped model. Consequence: if an organization is disabled and an admin updates one of its IDPs changing hideOnLogin or linkOnly (fields consumers of the login cache do not re-check), both 'original' (isEnabled=false due to disabled org) and 'updated' (hideOnLogin=true) fail the predicate, so no invalidation is registered. The .idp.login caches are not invalidated by organization enable/disable either, so when the organization is re-enabled, the stale cached ID list makes the IDP appear on the login page even though it is now hidden/link-only. The predicate comparison should be done against the unwrapped stored model (raw isEnabled) rather than the organization-aware wrapper.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default keystore provider (SUN), not BouncyCastle

The CryptoProvider contract states this method returns the BouncyCastle security provider. AuthzClientCryptoProvider instead returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which is the SUN provider on standard JDKs. BouncyIntegration caches the returned provider's name globally (BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER) and keycloak-core code uses that name for explicit-provider JCA lookups (e.g., KeyStore/Cipher/Signature.getInstance(alg, BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER)); pinning those lookups to "SUN" will throw NoSuchAlgorithmException/NoSuchProviderException for anything SUN does not implement (e.g., PKCS12 keystores, which live in SunJSSE), even though the algorithms are available elsewhere in the JVM. It also needlessly instantiates a KeyStore on every call. The correct behavior for an environment without BouncyCastle is to return null, as WildFlyElytronProvider does.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract method order() breaks all existing third-party CryptoProvider implementations

CryptoProvider is a public SPI loaded via ServiceLoader, and this PR adds a new abstract method `int order()` without a default implementation. Any existing out-of-tree implementation of CryptoProvider (custom crypto provider extensions compiled against the previous keycloak-common) will fail to compile against the new version and, worse, will throw AbstractMethodError at runtime when an old jar is used with the new keycloak-common, because CryptoIntegration.detectProvider now calls CryptoProvider::order on every ServiceLoader-discovered provider during sorting. This turns a previously working deployment into one that fails during CryptoIntegration.init. The method should be declared as `default int order() { return 0; }` (or similar) so existing implementations keep working.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
ES384/ES512 tests sign with a P-256 key and never verify the re-encoded DER with JCA

The test constructor creates a single key with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()`, whose default curve is P-256, and reuses it for all three tests. As a result testES384 and testES512 never process real 48-byte or 66-byte r/s values, so the padding/truncation logic in integerToBytes for those sizes is untested despite the test names suggesting otherwise. Additionally, the test only asserts that decode(encode(x)) == x, which is self-consistent by construction; the re-encoded DER signature is never passed to java.security.Signature.verify(), so an encoder bug that produces DER the JCA (or the server) rejects would still pass. Each test should generate a key for the matching curve (secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1) and verify the re-encoded signature with JCA.

Multiple equal-order providers are now resolved silently and arbitrarily instead of failing fast

Previously, having more than one CryptoProvider on the classpath was a hard configuration error ("Multiple crypto providers loaded..."). Now detectProvider sorts by order() descending and silently takes the first, only logging the ignored ones at debug level. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200, so if two server-side providers end up on the classpath together (a real misconfiguration, e.g. both elytron and fips jars present), the winner is determined by ServiceLoader encounter order, which depends on jar/classpath ordering and is effectively arbitrary — the server may run with the wrong crypto provider with no warning above debug level. Equal-order ties should still fail fast, or at least log a warning.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing null check and no migration for the new Clients resource/scopes on existing realms

In hasPermission(ClientModel, String), when no per-client resource exists the code loads the 'Clients' type resource via AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(...) and immediately calls authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource) without checking for null. getResourceTypeResource returns null whenever the admin-permissions resource server was initialized before this change: AdminPermissionsSchema.init() returns early when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() already exists, so realms that already had FGAP v2 enabled never get the new 'Clients' resource or the new scopes (configure, map-roles, map-roles-client-scope, map-roles-composite). For such realms every client admin operation that reaches this fallback throws an NPE (500), and creating any Clients-typed permission fails with 'Scope does not exist'. Add a null check here (mirroring the no-arg hasPermission) and provide an upgrade path that adds the new schema objects to existing admin-permissions resource servers.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
Client removal fails with UnsupportedOperationException when V1 and V2 fine-grained-authz features are both enabled

AdminPermissions.registerListener now gates the ClientRemovedEvent handler only on Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (the V1 flag), which can be enabled at the same time as ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. When both are on, the listener calls AdminPermissions.management(session, realm).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false); management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2, clients() returns the new ClientPermissionsV2, and setPermissionsEnabled unconditionally throws UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2"). The exception propagates out of the event listener during session.clients().removeClient(...), so deleting any client — and by extension deleting a realm, which removes its clients — returns a 500. The same landmine exists for isPermissionsEnabled/resource/getPermissions. Either make the V2 overrides graceful no-ops for these legacy management methods, or make the listener skip when the V2 feature is active.

Javadoc on void require methods incorrectly says "Returns {@code true}"

The newly added javadoc for requireView() ("Returns {@code true} if {@link #canView()} returns {@code true}.") and requireViewClientScopes() ("Returns {@code true} if {@link #canViewClientScopes()} returns {@code true}.") describes a boolean return, but both methods are void and throw ForbiddenException on failure. This contradicts the otherwise consistent 'Throws ForbiddenException if ...' wording used for the other require* methods and misleads implementers of the interface.

canMapRoles/canMapCompositeRoles/canMapClientScopeRoles ignore manage permission and MANAGE_CLIENTS role

These three methods only evaluate the explicit map-roles* scopes and, unlike canManage/canView in the same class, do not short-circuit on root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_CLIENTS) and do not treat a manage permission as implying map-roles. This is inconsistent with the rest of the class (canConfigure and canView both chain through canManage) and with UserPermissionsV2, where manage transitively grants map-roles (asserted by testTransitiveUserPermissions). Consequence: under V2, an admin holding the manage-clients role, or a manage permission on a specific client or on all clients, gets 403 when mapping client roles to users or adding composite roles — a regression compared to V1 behavior, where manage clients implied the ability to map its roles.

getResourceName does not resolve names for Clients-typed resources

getResourceName only special-cases the Users resource type, resolving the stored user id to the username. For the newly added Clients resource type it falls through to resource.getDisplayName(), which is never set for FGAP-created resources (getOrCreateResource only sets name/scopes), so admin REST responses and the admin console will show a null/empty name for client-typed permission resources instead of the client's clientId. Add a Clients branch mirroring the Users one that resolves ClientModel.getClientId().

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:
Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

false_positives.candidate:
CAUTION overstates when the rolling-updates feature is required

The new CAUTION block states that the `rolling-updates` feature must be enabled, 'Otherwise, the Keycloak Operator will fail.' This is too broad. The companion test change in `UpgradeTest.createInitialDeployment` enables the feature only when `spec.update.strategy` is explicitly set; the default case (no update strategy) deliberately deploys the Keycloak CR without the feature and still expects rolling-upgrade behavior for configuration changes (`testCacheMaxCount` with a null strategy asserts `eventuallyRollingUpgradeStatus`). So the Operator only fails when `spec.update` is used without the feature, not in general. As written, the doc will scare users into enabling a preview feature they don't need for the default upgrade behavior. The caution should say the feature is required only when setting `spec.update.strategy`.

Feature-disabled exit code 4 and the check command path are not tested

This PR introduces a new exit code `FEATURE_DISABLED = 4` (and renumbers the recreate exit code from 4 to 3), making the exit code the documented contract for automation ('they should rely only on the exit code of the check command'). However, `testFeatureNotEnabled` only asserts the error message text for the `metadata` subcommand; it never asserts that the exit code is 4, and it does not exercise the `check` subcommand with the feature disabled at all. A regression that returns exit code 0 or 1 when the feature is disabled — which would silently break GitOps pipelines that branch on this code — would not be caught. The test should assert `cliResult.assertError(...)` plus the exit code 4, and cover `update-compatibility check` without `--features=rolling-updates`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() grants manage rights to admins holding only the view scope on all groups

In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() the fallback permission check is `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`, i.e. it returns true when the caller has either the VIEW or the MANAGE scope on the all-groups resource. This appears to be a copy-paste of canView() directly above it. As a result, an admin who is granted only a 'view' permission for all groups (e.g. via an all-groups scope permission with the view scope) is treated as being able to manage groups globally: the no-arg canManage()/requireManage() is what GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup() uses to authorize creating top-level groups, so a view-only admin can create groups. Per-group manage (canManage(GroupModel)) correctly checks only MANAGE, so the no-arg variant should drop AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW from the expected scopes.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns authz resource IDs instead of group IDs

In GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission(), the granted set is populated with `groupResource.getId()`, which is the authorization-store Resource UUID. In the V2 schema the group ID is stored as the resource *name* (AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup returns group.getId() and getOrCreateResource creates the resource with that name). Callers of this method — UsersResource.searchForUser, BruteForceUsersResource.searchForUser and UsersResource.getUsersCount — feed the returned IDs into the UserModel.GROUPS session attribute / group-filtered count queries, which expect real group IDs. Concretely: an admin whose only user visibility comes from a view-members/manage-members permission on all groups will get a non-empty set containing a resource UUID, the GROUPS session attribute is set with it, and searchForUserStream filters by membership in a non-existent group, so the admin sees zero users. The method should add groupResource.getName() (the group ID), mirroring what the V1 implementation did by stripping the prefix from the resource name.

false_positives.candidate:
No upgrade path for realms that enabled admin permissions before the Groups resource type existed

AdminPermissionsSchema.init() creates the 'Groups' all-resource and the group-specific scopes (manage-members, view-members, manage-membership) only when the admin-permissions client is first created for a realm. Realms that already have admin permissions enabled (resource server initialized by an earlier version) will never get the new resource type or scopes, and this PR adds no migration. Consequences for such realms: AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceTypeResource() returns null for 'Groups', and GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission then calls `policyStore.findByResource(server, null)`, which dereferences the null resource in the JPA store implementation and throws (500 on group admin endpoints); likewise creating any group permission fails because the scope lookups in getOrCreateResource find no 'manage-members'/'view-members' scopes and throw ModelException("No scopes found."). A migration/initialization step that adds the new resource type and scopes to existing admin-permissions resource servers is needed.

Per-resource permission check in getGroupIdsWithViewPermission looks up resources by ID as if it were a name, and per-group resources are never typed

Inside the findByType visitor in GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission(), the code calls `hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), VIEW_MEMBERS, MANAGE_MEMBERS)`. However hasPermission(String groupId, ...) does `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)`, so it is passed a resource ID where a resource name is expected; the lookup returns null and evaluation silently falls back to the all-groups resource instead of evaluating the policies attached to that specific group resource. Additionally, resources created by AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource never have their type set (no setType call), so resourceStore.findByType(server, GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...) will not even iterate per-group resources — only the 'all groups' resource created in init() carries the type. Net effect: view-members/manage-members grants on individual groups are never detected by this method, and (combined with the getId() bug) the group-ID set used to filter user searches is wrong or empty.

getResourceName does not resolve names for the new Groups resource type

AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceName() resolves human-readable names only for the Users resource type; for everything else it returns resource.getDisplayName(). Group resources created via getOrCreateResource are named by group ID and never have a display name set, so anywhere this method is used to present resources of a Groups-type policy (e.g. permission listings in the admin UI), the entry will show null/empty instead of the group's name or path. A GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE branch resolving the group (e.g. its name or path) should be added, analogous to the existing Users handling.

true_positives.golden_comment: The translation is in Italian instead of Lithuanian. This should be translated to Lithuanian to match the file's locale (messages_lt.properties).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Lithuanian totpStep1 replaced with Italian text

The new value for `totpStep1` in the Lithuanian account message bundle is `Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:` — that is Italian, not Lithuanian. Lithuanian users will see an Italian sentence on the TOTP (mobile authenticator) setup screen of the account console. The English source is "Install one of the following applications on your mobile:"; the value should be a Lithuanian translation of that sentence (an existing Lithuanian wording for the same concept can be taken from the login theme), not the Italian one.

true_positives.golden_comment: The totpStep1 value uses Traditional Chinese terms in the Simplified Chinese file (zh_CN), which is likely incorrect for this locale. Please verify the locale‑appropriate translation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Simplified Chinese bundle contains Traditional Chinese text

The new `totpStep1` value in the zh_CN account bundle is `在您的手機上安裝以下應用程式之一：` which uses Traditional Chinese characters (手機, 應用程式) and Taiwan-style wording, while the rest of the zh_CN bundle is Simplified Chinese (e.g. `mobile=手机` on the previous line). zh_CN users will see a jarring mix of scripts.
