false_negatives.golden_comment: The anchor sanitization logic has a potential issue where it consumes English matcher groups without proper validation. If the translated text has more anchor tags than the English text, this could lead to incorrect validation results.
The method name 'santizeAnchors' should be 'sanitizeAnchors' (missing 'i').
Field HTML_TAGS should be declared as 'private static final' following Java naming conventions for constants

false_positives.candidate:
Java MessageFormat choice pattern used in i18next-based admin-ui bundle

The keycloak.v2 admin console renders this bundle with i18next, where positional interpolation is `{{0}}`. The changed `error-invalid-multivalued-size` message now uses `{0}/{1}/{2}` plus a Java MessageFormat choice pattern `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}`. i18next will not interpolate single-brace placeholders and knows nothing of Java choice syntax, so the user-attribute size validation error will be shown to administrators with literal placeholders and the raw choice string. The previous i18next form (`Attribute {{0}} must have at least {{1}} and at most {{2}} value(s).`) worked; the Java MessageFormat version should only be used in the server-rendered theme bundles.

Java MessageFormat syntax used in i18next-based account-ui bundle

The keycloak.v3 account console is a React app that renders this bundle with i18next, whose interpolation syntax is `{{0}}` (as used by all neighboring keys in this file, e.g. `error-invalid-length-too-short='{{0}}' must have minimal length of {{1}}.`). This change replaces `{{0}}/{{1}}/{{2}}` with `{0}/{1}/{2}` and appends a Java MessageFormat choice pattern `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}`. When the account UI displays `error-invalid-multivalued-size`, i18next will not substitute `{0}`, `{1}`, `{2}` and will print the raw choice expression literally, so end users see `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.` instead of a formatted message. The Java MessageFormat variant belongs in the server-side bundles (base admin/login themes); this JS bundle should keep the i18next syntax (the previous `{{0}} ... value(s)` form, or i18next pluralization).

Lithuanian loginTotpStep1 replaced with Italian text

The new value for `loginTotpStep1` in the Lithuanian login message bundle is `Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:` — Italian text pasted into a Lithuanian file. Users with a Lithuanian locale will see an Italian instruction on the login flow's Mobile Authenticator setup page. The English source is "Install one of the following applications on your mobile:" and the value should be translated into Lithuanian.

true_positives.golden_comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Constructor null-checks grantType twice and never validates rawTokenId

The constructor contains `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed");` — a copy-paste of the line above. It checks grantType a second time (with a misleading message about rawTokenId) and never null-checks rawTokenId. A null rawTokenId then silently propagates and would be rendered as the literal string "null" by DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId when concatenating the token id. The check should be `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, "Null rawTokenId not allowed");`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isAccessTokenId matcher has inverted condition and wrong substring offset

In the new isAccessTokenId(String expectedGrantShortcut) matcher, matchesSafely does `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`. Two bugs: (1) the condition is inverted — the matcher returns false exactly when the grant shortcut equals the expected one, and returns true (if the rest is a UUID) when it does NOT match; (2) the offset is wrong — in a token id like `onrtac:<uuid>` the 2-char grant shortcut occupies positions 4-5, so it should be substring(4, 6), not substring(3, 5) (which yields e.g. "ta"). The correct check would be `if (!items[0].substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`. As written, every event assertion switched to this matcher (expectCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectDeviceCodeToToken, expectAuthReqIdToToken) will fail against correctly-encoded token ids, breaking a large part of the integration test suite.

true_positives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getShortcut() javadoc contradicts the mandatory 2-character format

The javadoc says the shortcut is "usually like 3-letters", but DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromTokenId strictly requires the encoded context to be exactly 6 characters (2 per segment) and throws IllegalArgumentException otherwise, and the whole PR design assumes every shortcut is exactly 2 characters. A grant factory returning a 3-letter shortcut (as the javadoc suggests) would produce token ids that can never be decoded. The javadoc should state that the shortcut must be exactly 2 characters and unique, and ideally postInit should validate the length.

true_positives.golden_comment: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
testIncorrectGrantType passes for the wrong reason (NPE from null sessionFactory)

In testIncorrectGrantType, the factory's postInit() is never called, so its sessionFactory field is null. Decoding "ofrtac:5678" reaches DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.getGrantTypeByShortcut("ac"), which — not finding the shortcut in the manually populated map — calls sessionFactory.getProviderFactoriesStream(...) and throws a NullPointerException. The test catches plain RuntimeException, so it passes on the NPE rather than on the intended IllegalArgumentException("Unknown value 'ac' for grant type"). The test should assert the specific exception type/message (and ideally initialize the factory via postInit with a real or mocked session factory) so it actually verifies the unknown-shortcut handling.

false_positives.candidate:
Grant type only recorded for standard token exchange, not other exchange flows

The Constants.GRANT_TYPE attribute is set to the token-exchange grant type only inside StandardTokenExchangeProvider.exchangeClientToOIDCClient. Other token exchange providers built on AbstractTokenExchangeProvider (the legacy V1 token exchange behind the TOKEN_EXCHANGE feature, subject impersonation V2, federated exchange) never set this attribute, so access tokens minted through those flows will encode the grant type as "na" (unknown) even though they went through the token-exchange grant. Since recognizing the token-exchange grant is one of the stated goals of this PR (issue #37117), the attribute should be set in a shared place (e.g. TokenExchangeGrantType.process or AbstractTokenExchangeProvider) so all exchange variants are covered.

New abstract getShortcut() breaks existing custom OAuth2 grant type providers

getShortcut() is added as a new abstract method with no default implementation on the OAuth2GrantTypeFactory interface. Any existing custom OAuth2 grant type provider (compiled against the previous interface) will fail with AbstractMethodError at runtime — and it will be hit during server startup, because DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit() unconditionally calls gtf.getShortcut() on every registered OAuth2GrantTypeFactory. A default method (e.g. returning null, or a shortcut derived from getId()) combined with null-handling in the encoder factory would keep backward compatibility for third-party grant providers.

Public copy constructor Context(Context) removed from grant SPI class

The diff removes the public copy constructor OAuth2GrantType.Context(Context context). Nothing in the repository uses it anymore, but Context is a public static class of the OAuth2 grant type SPI, so any external custom grant implementation that built a derived context via this constructor will fail to compile or link after upgrade. Since the field set is otherwise identical, keeping the constructor (now also copying grantType) would avoid an unnecessary compatibility break for custom providers.

The exhausted credential then remains in user storage, isConfiguredFor keeps returning true, and the user continues to be challenged with recovery codes that can never succeed. false_positives.candidate:
Recovery codes validated against user storage are never consumed and remain reusable

When the recovery-codes credential lives in local storage, the code that was just used is consumed as a side effect of validation (RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.isValid removes the used code and persists the credential). When the credential lives in user storage (the new path added by this PR), validation is delegated to the storage provider's CredentialInputValidator.isValid, and nothing afterwards marks the code as used: there is no updateCredential/disableCredentialType callback with the remaining codes. The test provider added in this PR demonstrates the gap — BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid only checks membership in the stored raw-code list and never removes the used entry, so the same recovery code can be presented again on every subsequent login. This silently weakens the one-time-use security property of recovery codes for exactly the scenario this PR enables, and the new test (testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin) never asserts that a used code is invalidated. Either Keycloak should push the remaining codes back via updateCredential after a successful user-storage validation, or the limitation should be explicitly handled/documented.

Reader thread is never joined, so the test can pass without ever exercising the race

In createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti, the background thread that repeatedly calls managedRealm.admin().groups().groups(...) is started but never joined. The main thread deletes the 100 groups, sets deletedAll=true, and immediately asserts caughtExceptions is empty. Because there is no thread.join() (and no guarantee the reader thread has executed even a single iteration before the deletes finish), the test can pass vacuously on a slow or busy CI runner without ever reproducing the concurrent read-during-delete scenario this PR is fixing. Additionally, the reader thread performs one more iteration after deletedAll becomes true (the flag is only checked at the top of the loop), so any exception thrown in that final in-flight request happens after the assertion has already executed and is silently lost. The test should join the reader thread before asserting (and ideally ensure a minimum number of read iterations occurred).

false_positives.candidate:
Restarting a hung flusher in thread mode leaves the old thread running, producing duplicate segments for the same shards

When `produce_to_pipe` is set, flusher workers are `threading.Thread`s. In `_ensure_processes_alive`, if such a worker is judged hung (healthy_since stale), the restart path calls `process.kill()` only when `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`, so for threads nothing stops the old worker, and then `_create_process_for_shards` unconditionally starts a new thread for the same shards and overwrites `self.processes[process_index]`. The hung-but-alive thread and the replacement thread then concurrently call `buffer.flush_segments()` / `done_flush_segments()` for the same shards and both write to the same `process_backpressure_since`/`process_healthy_since` values, which can produce the same segment twice to the output and corrupts the health/backpressure bookkeeping. Either guard against restarting un-killable hung threads or document/handle the duplicate-flush window explicitly.

Redis memory check double-counts clusters shared by multiple per-process buffers, skewing the used/available ratio

Shards are assigned to processes round-robin (`process_index = i % num_processes`), so when `max_processes > 1` each per-process `SpansBuffer` typically holds shards that map to the same Redis cluster as other buffers. `submit()` now aggregates memory by calling `buffer.get_memory_info()` on every buffer and summing the results; a cluster's used/available memory is therefore counted once per covering buffer instead of once as before (previously a single buffer covered all assigned shards and could report each cluster once). If clusters are not counted a uniform number of times (e.g., cluster shard counts not divisible by the process count), the computed `used / available` ratio is skewed and `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage` hard backpressure will trigger too early or too late. It also multiplies the number of Redis INFO calls made on the consumer's submit path by the number of flusher processes.

_create_process_for_shard is dead code and would leak a duplicate process if used

`_create_process_for_shard` is never called anywhere. Worse, if it ever were used, it calls `_create_process_for_shards` without killing the existing process for that shard's group and without incrementing `process_restarts`, leaving two live processes flushing the same shards (duplicate segments produced, conflicting health values). It should be removed or fixed to go through the same kill-and-track path as `_ensure_processes_alive`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

false_positives.candidate:
Per-resource permission check in getGroupIdsWithViewPermission looks up resources by ID as if it were a name, and per-group resources are never typed

Inside the findByType visitor in GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission(), the code calls `hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), VIEW_MEMBERS, MANAGE_MEMBERS)`. However hasPermission(String groupId, ...) does `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)`, so it is passed a resource ID where a resource name is expected; the lookup returns null and evaluation silently falls back to the all-groups resource instead of evaluating the policies attached to that specific group resource. Additionally, resources created by AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource never have their type set (no setType call), so resourceStore.findByType(server, GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...) will not even iterate per-group resources — only the 'all groups' resource created in init() carries the type. Net effect: view-members/manage-members grants on individual groups are never detected by this method, and (combined with the getId() bug) the group-ID set used to filter user searches is wrong or empty.

No upgrade path for realms that enabled admin permissions before the Groups resource type existed

AdminPermissionsSchema.init() creates the 'Groups' all-resource and the group-specific scopes (manage-members, view-members, manage-membership) only when the admin-permissions client is first created for a realm. Realms that already have admin permissions enabled (resource server initialized by an earlier version) will never get the new resource type or scopes, and this PR adds no migration. Consequences for such realms: AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceTypeResource() returns null for 'Groups', and GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission then calls `policyStore.findByResource(server, null)`, which dereferences the null resource in the JPA store implementation and throws (500 on group admin endpoints); likewise creating any group permission fails because the scope lookups in getOrCreateResource find no 'manage-members'/'view-members' scopes and throw ModelException("No scopes found."). A migration/initialization step that adds the new resource type and scopes to existing admin-permissions resource servers is needed.

getResourceName does not resolve names for the new Groups resource type

AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceName() resolves human-readable names only for the Users resource type; for everything else it returns resource.getDisplayName(). Group resources created via getOrCreateResource are named by group ID and never have a display name set, so anywhere this method is used to present resources of a Groups-type policy (e.g. permission listings in the admin UI), the entry will show null/empty instead of the group's name or path. A GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE branch resolving the group (e.g. its name or path) should be added, analogous to the existing Users handling.

In testIncorrectGrantType, the factory's postInit() is never called, so its sessionFactory field is null. Decoding "ofrtac:5678" reaches DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.getGrantTypeByShortcut("ac"), which — not finding the shortcut in the manually populated map — calls sessionFactory.getProviderFactoriesStream(...) and throws a NullPointerException. The test catches plain RuntimeException, so it passes on the NPE rather than on the intended IllegalArgumentException("Unknown value 'ac' for grant type"). The test should assert the specific exception type/message (and ideally initialize the factory via postInit with a real or mocked session factory) so it actually verifies the unknown-shortcut handling.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same core problem as the golden comment: catching a generic RuntimeException in the test is too broad and should instead assert on the specific IllegalArgumentException. The candidate goes further to explain why catching RuntimeException is dangerous here (it currently masks a NullPointerException), which reinforces the exact concern raised in the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
New abstract getShortcut() breaks existing custom OAuth2 grant type providers

getShortcut() is added as a new abstract method with no default implementation on the OAuth2GrantTypeFactory interface. Any existing custom OAuth2 grant type provider (compiled against the previous interface) will fail with AbstractMethodError at runtime — and it will be hit during server startup, because DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit() unconditionally calls gtf.getShortcut() on every registered OAuth2GrantTypeFactory. A default method (e.g. returning null, or a shortcut derived from getId()) combined with null-handling in the encoder factory would keep backward compatibility for third-party grant providers.

Grant type only recorded for standard token exchange, not other exchange flows

The Constants.GRANT_TYPE attribute is set to the token-exchange grant type only inside StandardTokenExchangeProvider.exchangeClientToOIDCClient. Other token exchange providers built on AbstractTokenExchangeProvider (the legacy V1 token exchange behind the TOKEN_EXCHANGE feature, subject impersonation V2, federated exchange) never set this attribute, so access tokens minted through those flows will encode the grant type as "na" (unknown) even though they went through the token-exchange grant. Since recognizing the token-exchange grant is one of the stated goals of this PR (issue #37117), the attribute should be set in a shared place (e.g. TokenExchangeGrantType.process or AbstractTokenExchangeProvider) so all exchange variants are covered.

Public copy constructor Context(Context) removed from grant SPI class

The diff removes the public copy constructor OAuth2GrantType.Context(Context context). Nothing in the repository uses it anymore, but Context is a public static class of the OAuth2 grant type SPI, so any external custom grant implementation that built a derived context via this constructor will fail to compile or link after upgrade. Since the field set is otherwise identical, keeping the constructor (now also copying grantType) would avoid an unnecessary compatibility break for custom providers.

true_positives.golden_comment: After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
removeStoredCredentialById cannot remove a user-storage (federated) recovery-codes credential

After this change the credential looked up via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential may come from user storage (getFederatedCredentialsStream). If such a provider tracks used codes itself and returns a credential whose allCodesUsed() is true, the cleanup call authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(...) only removes credentials from the local store and silently does nothing for federated credentials — additionally, credential models built by a storage provider (as the test provider does with RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues) may carry a null or synthetic id, so the removal has no valid target. The exhausted credential then remains in user storage, isConfiguredFor keeps returning true, and the user continues to be challenged with recovery codes that can never succeed. Removal for federated credentials would need to go through the storage provider (e.g. updateCredential/disableCredentialType) instead of removeStoredCredentialById.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same underlying bug: the credential model built in the test storage provider (using createFromValues) has a null ID, which causes the downstream call to removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow to fail to remove the credential.

false_positives.candidate:
Recovery codes validated against user storage are never consumed and remain reusable

When the recovery-codes credential lives in local storage, the code that was just used is consumed as a side effect of validation (RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.isValid removes the used code and persists the credential). When the credential lives in user storage (the new path added by this PR), validation is delegated to the storage provider's CredentialInputValidator.isValid, and nothing afterwards marks the code as used: there is no updateCredential/disableCredentialType callback with the remaining codes. The test provider added in this PR demonstrates the gap — BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid only checks membership in the stored raw-code list and never removes the used entry, so the same recovery code can be presented again on every subsequent login. This silently weakens the one-time-use security property of recovery codes for exactly the scenario this PR enables, and the new test (testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin) never asserts that a used code is invalidated. Either Keycloak should push the remaining codes back via updateCredential after a successful user-storage validation, or the limitation should be explicitly handled/documented.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.

false_positives.candidate:
CAUTION overstates when the rolling-updates feature is required

The new CAUTION block states that the `rolling-updates` feature must be enabled, 'Otherwise, the Keycloak Operator will fail.' This is too broad. The companion test change in `UpgradeTest.createInitialDeployment` enables the feature only when `spec.update.strategy` is explicitly set; the default case (no update strategy) deliberately deploys the Keycloak CR without the feature and still expects rolling-upgrade behavior for configuration changes (`testCacheMaxCount` with a null strategy asserts `eventuallyRollingUpgradeStatus`). So the Operator only fails when `spec.update` is used without the feature, not in general. As written, the doc will scare users into enabling a preview feature they don't need for the default upgrade behavior. The caution should say the feature is required only when setting `spec.update.strategy`.

Feature-disabled exit code 4 and the check command path are not tested

This PR introduces a new exit code `FEATURE_DISABLED = 4` (and renumbers the recreate exit code from 4 to 3), making the exit code the documented contract for automation ('they should rely only on the exit code of the check command'). However, `testFeatureNotEnabled` only asserts the error message text for the `metadata` subcommand; it never asserts that the exit code is 4, and it does not exercise the `check` subcommand with the feature disabled at all. A regression that returns exit code 0 or 1 when the feature is disabled — which would silently break GitOps pipelines that branch on this code — would not be caught. The test should assert `cliResult.assertError(...)` plus the exit code 4, and cover `update-compatibility check` without `--features=rolling-updates`.

Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing null check and no migration for the new Clients resource/scopes on existing realms

In hasPermission(ClientModel, String), when no per-client resource exists the code loads the 'Clients' type resource via AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(...) and immediately calls authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource) without checking for null. getResourceTypeResource returns null whenever the admin-permissions resource server was initialized before this change: AdminPermissionsSchema.init() returns early when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() already exists, so realms that already had FGAP v2 enabled never get the new 'Clients' resource or the new scopes (configure, map-roles, map-roles-client-scope, map-roles-composite). For such realms every client admin operation that reaches this fallback throws an NPE (500), and creating any Clients-typed permission fails with 'Scope does not exist'. Add a null check here (mirroring the no-arg hasPermission) and provide an upgrade path that adds the new schema objects to existing admin-permissions resource servers.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies the exact same bug described in the golden comment: in `hasPermission`, `getResourceTypeResource` can return null, and passing it directly to `findByResource` without a null check leads to a NullPointerException.

false_positives.candidate:
Client removal fails with UnsupportedOperationException when V1 and V2 fine-grained-authz features are both enabled

AdminPermissions.registerListener now gates the ClientRemovedEvent handler only on Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (the V1 flag), which can be enabled at the same time as ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. When both are on, the listener calls AdminPermissions.management(session, realm).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false); management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2, clients() returns the new ClientPermissionsV2, and setPermissionsEnabled unconditionally throws UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2"). The exception propagates out of the event listener during session.clients().removeClient(...), so deleting any client — and by extension deleting a realm, which removes its clients — returns a 500. The same landmine exists for isPermissionsEnabled/resource/getPermissions. Either make the V2 overrides graceful no-ops for these legacy management methods, or make the listener skip when the V2 feature is active.

canMapRoles/canMapCompositeRoles/canMapClientScopeRoles ignore manage permission and MANAGE_CLIENTS role

These three methods only evaluate the explicit map-roles* scopes and, unlike canManage/canView in the same class, do not short-circuit on root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_CLIENTS) and do not treat a manage permission as implying map-roles. This is inconsistent with the rest of the class (canConfigure and canView both chain through canManage) and with UserPermissionsV2, where manage transitively grants map-roles (asserted by testTransitiveUserPermissions). Consequence: under V2, an admin holding the manage-clients role, or a manage permission on a specific client or on all clients, gets 403 when mapping client roles to users or adding composite roles — a regression compared to V1 behavior, where manage clients implied the ability to map its roles.

getResourceName does not resolve names for Clients-typed resources

getResourceName only special-cases the Users resource type, resolving the stored user id to the username. For the newly added Clients resource type it falls through to resource.getDisplayName(), which is never set for FGAP-created resources (getOrCreateResource only sets name/scopes), so admin REST responses and the admin console will show a null/empty name for client-typed permission resources instead of the client's clientId. Add a Clients branch mirroring the Users one that resolves ClientModel.getClientId().

Javadoc on void require methods incorrectly says "Returns {@code true}"

The newly added javadoc for requireView() ("Returns {@code true} if {@link #canView()} returns {@code true}.") and requireViewClientScopes() ("Returns {@code true} if {@link #canViewClientScopes()} returns {@code true}.") describes a boolean return, but both methods are void and throw ForbiddenException on failure. This contradicts the otherwise consistent 'Throws ForbiddenException if ...' wording used for the other require* methods and misleads implementers of the interface.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default keystore provider (SUN), not BouncyCastle

The CryptoProvider contract states this method returns the BouncyCastle security provider. AuthzClientCryptoProvider instead returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which is the SUN provider on standard JDKs. BouncyIntegration caches the returned provider's name globally (BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER) and keycloak-core code uses that name for explicit-provider JCA lookups (e.g., KeyStore/Cipher/Signature.getInstance(alg, BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER)); pinning those lookups to "SUN" will throw NoSuchAlgorithmException/NoSuchProviderException for anything SUN does not implement (e.g., PKCS12 keystores, which live in SunJSSE), even though the algorithms are available elsewhere in the JVM. It also needlessly instantiates a KeyStore on every call. The correct behavior for an environment without BouncyCastle is to return null, as WildFlyElytronProvider does.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue directly and accurately describes the exact same bug as the golden comment: `getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns the default keystore provider instead of BouncyCastle.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract method order() breaks all existing third-party CryptoProvider implementations

CryptoProvider is a public SPI loaded via ServiceLoader, and this PR adds a new abstract method `int order()` without a default implementation. Any existing out-of-tree implementation of CryptoProvider (custom crypto provider extensions compiled against the previous keycloak-common) will fail to compile against the new version and, worse, will throw AbstractMethodError at runtime when an old jar is used with the new keycloak-common, because CryptoIntegration.detectProvider now calls CryptoProvider::order on every ServiceLoader-discovered provider during sorting. This turns a previously working deployment into one that fails during CryptoIntegration.init. The method should be declared as `default int order() { return 0; }` (or similar) so existing implementations keep working.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same problem: adding a new abstract method `order()` to the `CryptoProvider` interface without a default implementation breaks backward compatibility for existing implementations.

false_positives.candidate:
Multiple equal-order providers are now resolved silently and arbitrarily instead of failing fast

Previously, having more than one CryptoProvider on the classpath was a hard configuration error ("Multiple crypto providers loaded..."). Now detectProvider sorts by order() descending and silently takes the first, only logging the ignored ones at debug level. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200, so if two server-side providers end up on the classpath together (a real misconfiguration, e.g. both elytron and fips jars present), the winner is determined by ServiceLoader encounter order, which depends on jar/classpath ordering and is effectively arbitrary — the server may run with the wrong crypto provider with no warning above debug level. Equal-order ties should still fail fast, or at least log a warning.

ES384/ES512 tests sign with a P-256 key and never verify the re-encoded DER with JCA

The test constructor creates a single key with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()`, whose default curve is P-256, and reuses it for all three tests. As a result testES384 and testES512 never process real 48-byte or 66-byte r/s values, so the padding/truncation logic in integerToBytes for those sizes is untested despite the test names suggesting otherwise. Additionally, the test only asserts that decode(encode(x)) == x, which is self-consistent by construction; the re-encoded DER signature is never passed to java.security.Signature.verify(), so an encoder bug that produces DER the JCA (or the server) rejects would still pass. Each test should generate a key for the matching curve (secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1) and verify the re-encoded signature with JCA.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reader thread is never joined, so the test can pass without ever exercising the race

In createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti, the background thread that repeatedly calls managedRealm.admin().groups().groups(...) is started but never joined. The main thread deletes the 100 groups, sets deletedAll=true, and immediately asserts caughtExceptions is empty. Because there is no thread.join() (and no guarantee the reader thread has executed even a single iteration before the deletes finish), the test can pass vacuously on a slow or busy CI runner without ever reproducing the concurrent read-during-delete scenario this PR is fixing. Additionally, the reader thread performs one more iteration after deletedAll becomes true (the flag is only checked at the top of the loop), so any exception thrown in that final in-flight request happens after the assertion has already executed and is silently lost. The test should join the reader thread before asserting (and ideally ensure a minimum number of read iterations occurred).
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue point out that the reader thread is never joined/waited for before asserting on the exceptions list after setting `deletedAll = true`. The candidate explicitly mentions that exceptions thrown in the final in-flight request after `deletedAll` becomes true will happen after the assertion has already executed and be silently lost, which directly matches the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
Fix only covers getSubGroupsCount; other cached read paths still NPE on concurrent group deletion

getSubGroupsCount() now null-checks modelSupplier.get() before use, but the identical concurrent-delete race remains in the sibling read paths of the same adapter: getSubGroupsStream(String, Integer, Integer), getSubGroupsStream(Integer, Integer), and getSubGroupsStream(String, Boolean, Integer, Integer) (lines 254-269) all call modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...) without a null check, and getAttributes/getFirstAttribute go through cached lazy loaders that dereference the supplied GroupModel. If the group is deleted from the database between cache read and delegate load, those paths still throw the same NullPointerException this PR set out to fix, so requests hitting them (e.g. paginated subgroup listing while a group is removed) remain broken. The behavior is also now inconsistent: when the adapter was invalidated, isUpdated() throws IllegalStateException("Not found in database") for a deleted group, while this method silently returns null for the same condition.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() violates the GroupModel contract (Javadoc says it never returns null) and may lead to NPEs in callers that expect a non-null count.

true_positives.golden_comment: In UsernameForm.authenticate(), isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() is called without passing the required UserModel parameter.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Call to isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments does not compile

UsernameForm.authenticate() calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments, but the only method with that name is the one added in this PR in the superclass UsernamePasswordForm: protected boolean isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user). There is no no-arg overload anywhere in the class hierarchy, so the services module fails to compile with 'no suitable method found: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()'. The call almost certainly should be isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()), matching how the same method is invoked in UsernamePasswordForm.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: in UsernameForm.authenticate(), the method isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() is called with no arguments instead of passing the required UserModel parameter.

true_positives.golden_comment: With isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) requiring user != null, authenticate(...) will not call webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) on the initial login page where context.getUser() is still null, so conditional passkey UI will not be set up for first-time passkey login. Consider whether this should also be enabled when no user has been selected yet so ID-less passkey authentication on the initial login form continues to work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requires a non-null user, which disables passkeys on all fresh logins

The new helper isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) returns webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() && user != null, and it now gates every call to webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context): in authenticate() (line 115) and in challenge(context, error, field) (line 137). On an initial login there is no user in the authentication context (context.getUser() == null), so fillContextForm is never invoked for first-time logins: the WebAuthn challenge note, the ENABLE_WEBAUTHN_CONDITIONAL_UI form attribute, and the webauth form markup are never set. true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` requires `user != null`, which prevents `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` from being called on the initial login page where `context.getUser()` is null, thereby breaking conditional passkey UI for first-time/fresh logins.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset branch passes a negative index to a Django QuerySet slice, which raises AssertionError

In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[cursor.offset : cursor.offset + limit + extra]`. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing — slicing with a negative start raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported`. The inline comment claiming 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false. Since cursor offsets are user-controlled (the `cursor` query string is parsed by Cursor.from_string with `int(bits[1])`, which accepts negatives), any privileged caller can supply e.g. `cursor=0:-5:0` with `optimized_pagination=true` and get a 500 AssertionError on every request. This is a reliable crash/DoS of the endpoint rather than a performance feature, and no boundary handling exists.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` attempts to slice a Django QuerySet with a negative offset, which is not supported by Django and raises an `AssertionError`.

true_positives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enable_advanced is computed unconditionally and dereferences organization_context.member, crashing for member-less auth

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated on every GET, even when the `optimized_pagination` query param is absent. `organization_context.member` is None for requests authenticated without an organization member (e.g., org API keys / auth tokens with the org:read scope that legitimately pass OrganizationAuditPermission). For such requests `request.user.is_superuser` is False, so the right-hand side evaluates `None.has_global_access` and raises AttributeError, returning a 500. This regresses the previously working default pagination path for those auth types. The expression should be computed lazily inside the `use_optimized` branch and guard against `member is None`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: accessing `organization_context.member.has_global_access` without checking if `member` is `None`, which causes an `AttributeError` when requests are authenticated via API keys or org auth tokens where `member` is `None`.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator crashes with TypeError when used with a datetime order_by key

The audit log endpoint instantiates OptimizedCursorPaginator with order_by="-datetime", but OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `int(math.floor(value) if ... else math.ceil(value))` on `getattr(item, self.key)`. For the audit logs endpoint that value is a `datetime` object, and `math.floor`/`math.ceil` on a datetime raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime.datetime`. This is called from build_cursor on the very first page of results (to compute the next cursor), so every request using `optimized_pagination=true` will 500 as soon as there is at least one audit log row. The code needed the DateTimePaginator-style conversion (`value.strftime("%s.%f") * multiplier`) or should have subclassed DateTimePaginator. There is also a secondary issue: even if get_item_key were fixed to return an int, `value_from_cursor` returns the raw integer cursor value and `build_queryset` would then compare the datetime column against an integer (`datetime <= %s` with an int param), which the database will reject.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: `get_item_key` in `OptimizedCursorPaginator` calls `math.floor`/`math.ceil` on the key, which raises a `TypeError` when the audit logs endpoint uses `order_by='-datetime'` because the value is a `datetime` object rather than a number.

false_positives.candidate:
Trim check compares against the raw negative offset instead of the slice actually fetched

In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, the `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra:` check uses the original `offset` variable, which in the negative-offset branch is negative. Since `queryset[negative:...]` raises before this is reached in Django, this is currently masked, but if the slicing ever 'worked' (e.g., on a list-backed queryset), the comparison would never match and the extra boundary row would not be trimmed, leaking an extra row into the page and producing wrong cursors. It should compare against the actual fetch size (`stop - start_offset` or `limit + extra`).

Comment claims negative offsets are a supported performance optimization, but no paginator actually supports them

The added comment in Cursor.__init__ states negative offsets are allowed for 'advanced pagination scenarios' and enable 'efficient reverse pagination'. No paginator actually handles negative offsets correctly — BasePaginator clamps non-prev offsets with max(0, offset), OffsetPaginator/MergingOffsetPaginator/ChainPaginator explicitly raise BadPaginationError on negative offsets, and OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset path crashes on Django's 'Negative indexing is not supported' assertion. The comment documents a capability that does not exist and is misleading to future maintainers.

No tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator or the new audit-logs pagination branch

The PR adds ~100 lines of new pagination logic (OptimizedCursorPaginator) plus a new conditional branch in OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint gated by the `optimized_pagination` query param and superuser/global-access checks, but adds no tests. Tests would have immediately caught the two crash bugs (datetime math.floor TypeError and negative-slice AssertionError). At minimum there should be tests covering: optimized_pagination=true for a superuser with audit log rows present, a prev/next cursor round-trip, a negative-offset cursor, and a non-member token request (to cover the member-None path).

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the build-wide lock allows concurrent duplicate builds of the same index

BuildIndex previously serialized all builds with cacheMu; now two goroutines can build the same NamespacedResource concurrently (getOrCreateIndex in search.go does a check-then-build with no synchronization, and its own comment acknowledges it does not block concurrent builders of the same key). Consequences: (1) for file-backed indexes (size > FileThreshold), both builders call bleve.New on the same directory path, and the second one fails on the bleve lock file, surfacing a spurious error to a search or watch-event request; (2) for memory-backed indexes both builds succeed and the second write to b.cache silently overwrites the first, leaking an open bleve.Index that is never closed and wasting the entire duplicate build. A per-key lock (or singleflight) is needed instead of the single global lock that was removed.

false_positives.candidate:
Shared FixedQueuePool is shut down by the old strategy on rebalance, causing silent message loss

The `FixedQueuePool` is created once in the factory's `__init__` and shared by every `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` produced by `create_with_partitions`. Arroyo closes and re-creates the strategy on every partition revocation/rebalance: the old strategy's `close()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which shuts down all queues and worker threads in the shared pool. The new strategy created after the rebalance still references the same pool. From then on, `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` calls `work_queue.put()`, which raises `queue.ShutDown` on a shut-down queue; this is caught by the broad `except Exception` in `submit`, which then calls `add_offset`/`complete_offset` on the message's offset. The result: every message after a rebalance is silently dropped (never processed) while its offset is marked complete and committed to Kafka. Since consumer groups rebalance on every deploy/scale event, running this mode in production would skip uptime results without any error surfacing beyond a log line. The pool needs to be created per `create_with_partitions` call, or `close()` must not shut down a pool it doesn't own.

Worker queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure and memory can grow without limit

`FixedQueuePool` creates each work queue with `queue.Queue()` (no maxsize), so `submit`/`put` never blocks. The docstring on `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` (line ~253) claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but that never happens: the Arroyo consumer thread will keep polling Kafka and appending `WorkItem`s faster than slow workers can drain them, buffering an unbounded number of decoded results in process memory. This is exactly the failure mode the PR is meant to mitigate (one slow item/group clogging processing) — a slow group now grows its queue until the consumer OOMs. The queues should have a `maxsize` (or `submit` should otherwise block/apply backpressure) to match the documented behavior.

join() ignores its timeout and shutdown abandons all queued items instead of draining them

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(timeout)` ignores the timeout and just calls `close()`, which immediately shuts down the queue pool. In `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` each worker's `shutdown` flag is set to True before `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` is called, so a worker that is woken with pending items still in its queue processes at most one more item and then exits its `while not self.shutdown` loop — everything remaining in the queues is discarded without being processed and without a final offset commit. Standard Arroyo strategies drain in-flight work and commit during `join` on graceful shutdown; here every deploy or rebalance abandons the entire in-memory backlog (which, given the unbounded queues, can be large) to be redelivered and reprocessed. At minimum `join` should wait for queues to drain up to the timeout and perform a final commit of completed offsets.

test_stats_reporting is flaky: asserts total_items > 0 after workers may have already drained the queue

The test submits 10 trivial work items (the processor just appends to a list under a lock) and then immediately asserts `stats["total_items"] > 0`. The three worker threads start consuming as soon as the first item is put, so on a fast machine all 10 items can be processed before the main thread reaches `get_stats()`, making `total_items` 0 and the assertion fail intermittently. The non-zero-depth assertion needs synchronization that blocks workers (e.g. an event the processor waits on) to be reliable.

If a Check is evaluated and denied before the permission grant is visible (e.g. a check that races the permission write at creation time, or read-replica lag on the permission query), the denial is cached for shortCacheTTL (30s) and every subsequent check for that exact resource returns Allowed=false without ever hitting the DB requery logic added in this PR. true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No re-check of cache after acquiring write lock causes duplicate loads

After the fast-path read returns nil, the code acquires the write lock and unconditionally reloads the assets from disk (or CDN) without re-checking `entryPointAssetsCache`. If several requests arrive before the first successful load (e.g. at startup), they will each take the write lock in turn and each perform a full file read/HTTP fetch, even though the first one already populated the cache. A simple `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` immediately after acquiring the write lock would avoid the redundant loads.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: an incomplete double-checked locking pattern where the code fails to re-check if the cache has been populated after acquiring the write lock.

false_positives.candidate:
Write lock held across file and network I/O serializes all callers

While the load is in progress, every other goroutine calling GetWebAssets — including ones that arrive after the load has started but before the cache write at line 69 — blocks on the write lock instead of doing their own I/O in parallel, and in dev mode every single request now serializes on this mutex. This is a behavior change worth being aware of; it is not a correctness bug, but a slow or hanging CDN call will now stall all callers on the mutex.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes derive their context from the request context, so they are canceled when the request completes

In Create (and identically in Delete line 110, Update line 135, and DeleteCollection line 163) the background goroutine does `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` where `ctx` is the incoming request context. The request context is canceled as soon as the API handler returns, which happens immediately after the synchronous unified-storage write — so the child context used for the 'safe measure' legacy write is typically canceled before or during the legacy SQL call. The legacy write will then fail with context canceled, silently diverging legacy and unified storage (only visible as a metric). The goroutine should detach from the request lifecycle first, e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)`, before applying the 10s timeout.

Update passes the original objInfo to the legacy store, so UpdatedObject is invoked a second time against a different old object

The previous implementation fetched the old object, computed the updated object once, and wrapped it in `updateWrapper` so both stores persisted the same object. The new code passes the raw `objInfo` to both `d.Storage.Update` and, asynchronously, to `d.Legacy.Update`. This means `objInfo.UpdatedObject()` is invoked twice: the second time (in the goroutine) it runs against the old object fetched from legacy storage, which may have a different resourceVersion or may not exist yet (see the create-ordering race). `UpdatedObjectInfo` implementations are not guaranteed to be idempotent or reusable across calls, and the resulting legacy object can diverge from what was written to unified storage. The legacy call should receive a wrapper holding the object already produced by the unified update.

Async legacy writes are unordered, so create-then-update/delete sequences can diverge legacy storage

Each write method spawns an independent goroutine with its own 10s timeout and no serialization. A client that creates an object and immediately updates or deletes it will have the create's legacy write and the update/delete's legacy write racing in separate goroutines: the update can reach legacy before the create has been applied (failing with not-found, since forceAllowCreate is false), or a delete can be applied before the create lands, leaving a stale object in legacy. Because reads in mode 3 come only from unified storage, this divergence is invisible to users and only shows up as error counters. If ordering matters for the 'safe measure' copy, the legacy writes need a queue/serialization per object.

Create and Update record a legacy-storage error metric when unified storage fails and legacy is never called

In Create (line 45), when `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` even though the legacy store was never invoked — this both inflates legacy error counts and loses the unified-storage error metric. The same mistake exists in Update at line 129, which records `recordLegacyDuration` on a `d.Storage.Update` failure. Both should call `recordStorageDuration`, as the error paths in Delete and DeleteCollection correctly do.

TestMode3_Create error case configures the failure on the legacy mock, but mode 3 calls unified storage first

The case 'error when creating object in the unified store fails' sets up only `setupLegacyFn` returning an error and provides no `setupStorageFn`. In mode 3, `dw.Create` calls `d.Storage.Create` first; with no expectation registered on the shared mock for that call, testify will panic with an unexpected-call failure rather than exercising the intended error path. The error expectation needs to be on the storage mock (and this worked in mode 1 only because mode 1 calls legacy first).

The added 'with dual write (file, mode 3)' and 'with dual write (unified storage, mode 3)' subtests reuse `doPlaylistTests`, which asserts legacy `/api/playlists` results immediately after k8s creates/updates/deletes (e.g. comparing `/api/playlists` list right after `client.Resource.Create`). This means any user.valid? call — including ones that never lead to a save, and repeated client-side-driven validation attempts — mutates persistent statistics, and the write happens outside the user's save transaction. If stats collection is intended, it would be safer to record the match only when a signup is actually rejected (e.g., in the controller or in an after-validation hook gated on the record being persisted), otherwise the counters can be inflated arbitrarily by repeatedly triggering validation without ever creating an account.

A spammer blocked as 'bad@spam.com' can register successfully as 'BAD@spam.com' or 'Bad@Spam.com' because the lookup won't match, and the user's own email uniqueness check is also case-sensitive so it won't collide with an existing account either. This PR makes `.small-action` a flex container via `@include flexbox()`. CSS specifies that `float` has no effect on flex items, so the `float: right` on the direct-child `button` (line 309) no longer does anything. Previously the button was pinned to the right edge of the small-action row; now it will render inline immediately after `.small-action-desc`, breaking the intended layout of small action posts (e.g. the edit/expand controls). The same applies to `float: left` on `.topic-avatar` (line 271), which is harmless only by accident of source order. The fix is to replace the button's float with `margin-left: auto` (or add `flex` spacing) so it is pushed to the end of the flex row.

align-items mixin emits -webkit-box-align, which does not support the 'baseline' value used by bullet badges

The new `align-items` mixin unconditionally emits `-webkit-box-align: $alignment` for the 2009 flexbox spec, but that old property only accepts start/end/center/stretch — `baseline` is invalid and the declaration is dropped. `.badge-wrapper.bullet` in badges.css.scss calls `@include align-items(baseline)`, so on browsers that only understand the old `-webkit-box` model (e.g. older iOS Safari, which Discourse's `display: -webkit-inline-box` fallback in `inline-flex()` explicitly targets) the invalid declaration is ignored and items fall back to stretch alignment, vertically misaligning the bullet color swatch against the category text. If old-WebKit support matters (the mixin's prefixes imply it does), the mixin needs a value mapping or a fallback for `baseline`.

Header panel alignment now depends entirely on flexbox with no fallback for non-flex browsers

`.panel` previously used `float: right`, which worked in any browser. It now relies on `margin-left: auto` inside the `.contents` flex container. In any browser where none of the `display` values emitted by the `flexbox()` mixin are supported, `.contents` stays a block container, an auto left margin on a block-level `.panel` computes to 0, and the panel (user menu, search, hamburger icons) collapses against the logo on the left instead of staying on the right, breaking the header layout. If the supported-browser matrix includes any non-flexbox browsers (or engines with buggy partial flex support such as IE10, where auto margins inside `-ms-flexbox` containers are unreliable), this needs a fallback such as retaining `float: right` alongside the flex rules.

Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.

include_website_name is missing the '?' suffix, so ActiveModelSerializers never calls it

ActiveModelSerializers filters attributes by calling `include_<attribute>?` (with a question mark) — every other filter in this file follows that convention (`include_email?`, `include_stats?`, etc.). The new method is defined as `def include_website_name` without the `?`, making it dead code: the `website.present?` guard never runs, and `website_name` is always serialized (as `nil` when the user has no website, and unconditionally in the restricted-TL0 case described above). Rename it to `include_website_name?`.

Although the golden comment also mentions a secondary issue about string concatenation, the core bug is matched with high precision.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name leaks the website field for TL0 users viewed anonymously, bypassing untrusted_attributes

The serializer deliberately hides `:website` (via `untrusted_attributes`, which checks `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)`) so that anonymous visitors cannot see a TL0 user's profile fields. The new `:website_name` attribute is declared in the plain `attributes` list (line 43), is derived directly from `object.user_profile.website`, and its inclusion check only tests `website.present?` — it never checks `restrict_user_fields?`. As a result, for a TL0 user viewed by an anonymous visitor, `website` is omitted from the JSON but `website_name` (containing the website host, and possibly path) is still serialized, leaking exactly the information the restriction is meant to hide. The existing 'TL0 user seen as anonymous' spec was not extended to cover `website_name`, so the test suite does not catch this. `website_name` should be added to `untrusted_attributes` or its include check should mirror `include_website?`.

Sibling subdomains are treated as the same domain as the instance

The middle branch compares hosts of equal label count by stripping the first label from both sides: `www.anything.com` vs `forum.anything.com` are considered 'the same domain' and the full URL path is displayed. A sibling subdomain is not the instance's domain — on multi-tenant or shared-domain setups (e.g. instance at `forum.example.com`, user website at `evil.example.com/phishing-page`) the profile will render the full path as if the link belonged to the site's own domain, which is exactly the misleading display this feature is supposed to avoid. The comparison should only show the path when the website host equals the instance host or is a parent domain of it (the first and third branches), not when it is merely a sibling.

true_positives.golden_comment: postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage targetOrigin is a full referer URL, which browsers reject, so iframe resizing never works

The layout calls `parent.postMessage({type: 'discourse-resize', height: ...}, '<%= request.referer %>')`. The targetOrigin argument to postMessage must be an origin (scheme://host[:port]) or '*'; passing a full URL with a path (e.g. `http://blog.example.com/2013/02/10/post.html`, which is what the referer will always be) causes the browser to throw a SyntaxError ('Invalid target origin') and the message is never delivered. Since embed.js only sets the iframe height when it receives this message, the embedded comments iframe stays at the browser default height (~150px) and the comments appear cut off. The origin should be derived from the referer (or `SiteSetting.embeddable_host`), not the full referer URL.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. `content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` assumes every feed item has a `content` element. false_positives.candidate:
raw_html cook method renders feed/imported HTML without any sanitization, enabling stored XSS

The new `cook` short-circuit returns `raw` verbatim when `cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`, bypassing the entire rendering/sanitization pipeline. This content originates from external sources: `Jobs::PollFeed` stores RSS/Atom item bodies (`CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)`) directly, and `TopicEmbed.import_remote` stores Readability output. Nothing sanitizes it, and it is rendered raw in `app/views/embed/best.html.erb` (`<%= raw post.cooked %>`) and in the normal topic UI. A malicious or compromised feed/article can therefore inject `<script>` or event-handler attributes that execute for every forum reader (stored XSS). The imported HTML should be run through the sanitizer (with an appropriate tag/attribute whitelist) before being stored as cooked.

TopicEmbed.import mutates the caller's contents string

`contents << "\n<hr>\n<small>..."` appends the 'Imported from' footer directly to the string object passed in by the caller. If the same string object is ever reused (e.g. a caller importing twice with one buffer, or passing a frozen string), the footer is appended multiple times — which also changes the computed content_sha1 and triggers spurious post revisions — or raises a RuntimeError on frozen strings. Use `contents = contents + ...` or `contents.dup` before appending.

setnx followed by expire is not atomic; a crash leaves the throttle key with no TTL

`retrieved_recently?` does `$redis.setnx(retrieved_key, "1")` and then `$redis.expire(retrieved_key, 60)` as two separate commands. If the process dies (or redis errors) between the two, the key is set with no expiry, and that embed URL is treated as 'retrieved recently' forever — `perform_retrieve` will never run for it again, so the topic for that URL is never imported. Use a single atomic command such as `$redis.set(retrieved_key, "1", ex: 60, nx: true)`.

The migration creates `t.string :embed_url, null: false` (255-char limit) with a unique index, while `TopicEmbed` only validates presence. Blog/feed URLs frequently exceed 255 characters (tracking parameters, long slugs). For such URLs, `TopicEmbed.create!` raises a database error (or RecordNotUnique-style failure) instead of a clean validation, and `EmbedController` will keep enqueueing retrieval jobs for a URL that can never be stored. Either use `text`/a larger limit or add a length validation and gracefully skip over-long URLs.

absolutize_urls raises URI::InvalidURIError for feed URLs that pass the loose scheme check

`TopicEmbed.import` accepts any URL matching `/^https?\:\/\//`, but `absolutize_urls` then calls `URI(url)`, which raises `URI::InvalidURIError` for strings with spaces, quotes, or other invalid characters that still match the prefix regex (feed-provided `link` values in `Jobs::PollFeed` are not otherwise validated). The exception is unrescued here, so one malformed feed item aborts the entire hourly `PollFeed` run (which has `retry: false`), preventing all other items from being imported. As written, end === start, so the check `end > workingHour.endTime` only verifies that the slot *starts* before the working-hours end. A slot that starts inside the fixed host's working hours but finishes after their end time (e.g. host available 09:00–12:00, a 60-minute slot at 11:30–12:30 contributed by another round-robin host's wider availability) passes the check and is bookable, letting invitees book time the fixed host is not available.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:

`if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes') === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, 'minutes'))` compares two distinct dayjs object instances by reference, which is always false (`.isSame()` was presumably intended). This branch exists to detect a blocked-day override (start === end, i.e. 'unavailable the whole day'). Because it never fires, a blocked day is only rejected incidentally via the before/after checks, and a slot starting exactly at the block's start instant satisfies none of them: the callback returns undefined, `dateOverrideExist` is already true, and the function returns `true` (available) — leaking a bookable slot on a day the host explicitly marked unavailable.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: comparing two dayjs objects using `===` compares object references (which is always false) instead of values, and both suggest using `.isSame()` instead.

false_positives.candidate:

In checkIfIsAvailable, when any date override matches the slot's day, `dateOverrideExist` is set to true and, if the slot falls inside the override window (so the `find` callback never returns true), the function hits `if (dateOverrideExist) { return true; }` — returning 'available' before the `busy.every(...)` check at the bottom ever runs. This means that on any day where a host has a date override, that host's existing bookings and calendar busy times are completely ignored. A fixed host (or a regular solo event user, since they are also isFixed) with a date override who already has a booking/meeting inside the override window will be shown as bookable, producing double bookings — the exact problem this PR claims to fix ('prevents round-robin events being booked where the fixed hosts are unavailable'). The busy check must still run when a date override exists; only the working-hours check should be bypassed.

Multiple same-day date-override windows veto each other

The `dateOverrides.find(...)` logic treats 'slot is outside this one override window' as grounds to return false (unavailable), but a user can have several override windows on the same date (cal.com's UI allows adding multiple time ranges to one date override, stored as separate rows). For a slot that falls inside window B, window A's callback hits `slotStartTime.isAfter(date.end)` (or `slotEndTime.isBefore(date.start)`) and returns true, so the slot is marked unavailable even though it is within window B — and vice versa. Net effect: on a day with two or more override windows, every window is rejected by the other and the host shows no availability at all. The find should only return a 'reject' verdict after confirming the slot is outside *all* same-day windows for that user.

Override decoding depends on the server running in UTC

The new code decodes the override's wall-clock-encoded Date back to a real instant with `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes')` and compares it against `slotStartTime`/`slotEndTime`, which are explicitly UTC (`time.utc()`). `dayjs(date.start)` parses the Date in the process's local timezone, so the decode math (wall time − organizer offset = real UTC instant) only holds when the Node process runs with TZ=UTC. On any non-UTC runtime (dev machines, some CI/self-hosted setups) the override window and day-matching comparisons are shifted by the server offset, making fixed-host override filtering silently wrong. Use `dayjs.utc(date.start)` for these comparisons, as the parallel code in packages/lib/slots.ts already does with `.utc()`.

Offset-shifted override times discard the day component

The invitee-timezone conversion computes `startTime`/`endTime` as `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, 'minute').hour() * 60 + ...minute()`. Taking `.hour()/.minute()` after the offset shift drops any day rollover: when the invitee/organizer offset difference pushes the override across midnight (e.g. organizer Asia/Kolkata override 01:00–02:00 = 19:30–20:30 the previous UTC day, viewed by a UTC invitee: offset = −330 min lands on the previous day, but hour() yields 1170 minutes), the slot is materialized at 19:30 on the *current* invitee day instead of the correct adjacent day. Since the activeOverrides filter keys on the unshifted date, cross-midnight overrides are placed on the wrong day — precisely the timezone-adjustment scenario this PR is fixing. The shifted value should be carried as a full timestamp (or the day delta applied to startOfInviteeDay), not reduced to minutes-since-midnight.

override.timeZone is optional in the type but required by the conversion

`dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()` assumes `override.timeZone` is set, but the `TimeRange` type declares `timeZone?: string` as optional and getSlots is a shared library function — nothing at the type level guarantees every caller supplies it (the slots router happens to add it in this PR). With `timeZone` undefined, dayjs's tz plugin falls back to the host system's timezone when computing `organizerUtcOffset`, so the offset correction is silently computed against the server timezone and override slots are shifted by a wrong amount. Either make the field required for date overrides passed to getSlots or guard/default it here.

The PR's primary purpose is making date overrides (and working hours) of *fixed hosts* apply to round-robin events via the new logic in checkIfIsAvailable, and the PR description lists a round-robin fixed-host scenario as the main test plan. However, the only test added exercises a single-user personal event with a different invitee timezone. None of the new checkIfIsAvailable behavior — fixed host availability gating, override-window filtering per host, interaction with busy times — is covered, which is how the regression where busy checks are skipped on override days (and the multi-window veto issue) went unnoticed. A round-robin scenario with one fixed host having a date override should be added, including a case where the fixed host is busy inside the override window.

If two cron executions overlap (possible when a run takes longer than the cron interval), both read the same retryCount and both write the same incremented value, so a failure is not counted and deletion is delayed. Using Prisma's atomic `retryCount: { increment: 1 }` avoids the lost update without changing the logic.
