retryCount update inside catch block can throw and abort the whole cron run

Previously the catch block only logged the error, so a failure for one reminder could never stop the loop. Now the catch block performs `prisma.workflowReminder.update` unguarded. If that update itself fails — e.g. the row was deleted concurrently by another cron execution or by a booking cancellation, or the DB connection is the very thing that failed — the exception propagates out of the catch, the for-loop terminates, all remaining unscheduled reminders are skipped for this run, and the handler returns a 500. The retry-count write in the catch should be wrapped in its own try/catch (or the loop should continue on failure) so one bad reminder cannot starve the rest.

This PR introduces user-facing behavioral changes — reminders are deleted after two failed scheduling attempts, including via the catch-all error path — but adds no tests. There is nothing verifying that a reminder is deleted exactly after two failures (retryCount boundary `gt: 1`), that a reminder that fails once is retried and can still succeed, or that deterministic errors (e.g. template rendering throwing) also count toward deletion. In `buildOrgAuthorizationCondition` (line 164 and 168) and `buildTeamAuthorizationCondition` (line 201) the code writes e.g. `Prisma.sql`("teamId" = ANY(${teamIds}))``. Prisma's tagged-template helper expands an interpolated JavaScript array into a comma-separated list of bound parameters — it does NOT serialize it as a single Postgres array parameter. So with `teamIds = [10, 20, 30]` the emitted SQL is `"teamId" = ANY($1, $2, $3)`, which Postgres rejects with `syntax error at or near "$2"` (ANY requires a single array expression or subquery). Every org-scope and team-scope query will therefore fail with a raw-query error at runtime; only the user-scope path (which has no ANY) is valid. The correct pattern is `"teamId" IN (${Prisma.join(teamIds)})` or passing a single array parameter with an explicit cast. The tests don't catch this because they only structurally compare Sql objects built with the same broken pattern.

The previous implementation exposed a public `findMany(findManyArgs)` method that combined authorization/filter conditions into a `bookingTimeStatusDenormalized.findMany` call. This PR deletes that method entirely and replaces it with `getBaseConditions(): Promise<Prisma.Sql>`, shifting query execution to callers via `$queryRaw`. No caller is updated in this PR (only the service and its test are changed), so any existing consumer that invokes `insightsBookingService.findMany(...)` — e.g. the insights tRPC procedures that fetch booking events/status/hourly data — will fail TypeScript compilation and lose functionality. Either keep a compatible `findMany` wrapper or update all callers in the same change.

The org-scope (line 332) and team-scope (line 295) tests assert conditions via `expect(conditions).toEqual(Prisma.sql`...`)`, which only deep-compares the Sql object's internal `strings`/`values` arrays — it never runs the SQL against the database. The only test that actually executes a query (`getBaseConditions`, line 481) uses scope `"user"`, the one code path that contains no `ANY(...)` array interpolation. As a result the tests pass while the org/team SQL is syntactically invalid (Prisma expands `ANY(${ids})` into `ANY($1, $2, ...)`, a Postgres syntax error). The org-scope test asserts exact equality with `Prisma.sql`... ("userId" = ANY(${[user.id, user2.id, user3.id]})) ...`. The service builds that array from `MembershipRepository.findAllByTeamIds`, a `findMany` with no `orderBy`, so Postgres does not guarantee the row order (the user also has two memberships — team and org — that get deduped via `Set`, preserving whatever order rows came back in). If the membership rows are returned in a different order, the Sql `values` array order differs and the deep-equality assertion fails spuriously. The assertion should compare order-insensitively or the repository query should impose a deterministic order.

false_positives.candidate:
Restarting a hung flusher in thread mode leaves the old thread running, producing duplicate segments for the same shards

When `produce_to_pipe` is set, flusher workers are `threading.Thread`s. In `_ensure_processes_alive`, if such a worker is judged hung (healthy_since stale), the restart path calls `process.kill()` only when `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`, so for threads nothing stops the old worker, and then `_create_process_for_shards` unconditionally starts a new thread for the same shards and overwrites `self.processes[process_index]`. The hung-but-alive thread and the replacement thread then concurrently call `buffer.flush_segments()` / `done_flush_segments()` for the same shards and both write to the same `process_backpressure_since`/`process_healthy_since` values, which can produce the same segment twice to the output and corrupts the health/backpressure bookkeeping. Either guard against restarting un-killable hung threads or document/handle the duplicate-flush window explicitly.

Redis memory check double-counts clusters shared by multiple per-process buffers, skewing the used/available ratio

Shards are assigned to processes round-robin (`process_index = i % num_processes`), so when `max_processes > 1` each per-process `SpansBuffer` typically holds shards that map to the same Redis cluster as other buffers. `submit()` now aggregates memory by calling `buffer.get_memory_info()` on every buffer and summing the results; a cluster's used/available memory is therefore counted once per covering buffer instead of once as before (previously a single buffer covered all assigned shards and could report each cluster once). If clusters are not counted a uniform number of times (e.g., cluster shard counts not divisible by the process count), the computed `used / available` ratio is skewed and `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage` hard backpressure will trigger too early or too late. It also multiplies the number of Redis INFO calls made on the consumer's submit path by the number of flusher processes.

_create_process_for_shard is dead code and would leak a duplicate process if used

`_create_process_for_shard` is never called anywhere. Worse, if it ever were used, it calls `_create_process_for_shards` without killing the existing process for that shard's group and without incrementing `process_restarts`, leaving two live processes flushing the same shards (duplicate segments produced, conflicting health values). It should be removed or fixed to go through the same kill-and-track path as `_ensure_processes_alive`.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the build-wide lock allows concurrent duplicate builds of the same index

BuildIndex previously serialized all builds with cacheMu; now two goroutines can build the same NamespacedResource concurrently (getOrCreateIndex in search.go does a check-then-build with no synchronization, and its own comment acknowledges it does not block concurrent builders of the same key). Consequences: (1) for file-backed indexes (size > FileThreshold), both builders call bleve.New on the same directory path, and the second one fails on the bleve lock file, surfacing a spurious error to a search or watch-event request; (2) for memory-backed indexes both builds succeed and the second write to b.cache silently overwrites the first, leaking an open bleve.Index that is never closed and wasting the entire duplicate build. A per-key lock (or singleflight) is needed instead of the single global lock that was removed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: narrowing cacheMu protection from the entire BuildIndex operation to the final cache assignment permits multiple goroutines to concurrently build an expensive index for the same key. The candidate adds consequences and a proposed fix without changing the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs reads b.cache map without holding cacheMu

TotalDocs() iterates over b.cache without acquiring b.cacheMu (it never did, but it matters now). Before this PR, BuildIndex held cacheMu for its entire duration and TotalDocs was effectively only reached after all init builds completed; now the lock is only taken for the final map insertion, and this PR adds a new call to TotalDocs in searchSupport.init (search.go line 216, the "search index initialized" log) that runs right after the watch-event goroutine is started. That goroutine calls getOrCreateIndex -> BuildIndex on events for unknown namespaces, which writes b.cache concurrently with the TotalDocs iteration. Concurrent map read/write in Go is a fatal runtime error ("concurrent map read and map write"), which will crash the process. TotalDocs should take b.cacheMu.RLock() before iterating.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: the new TotalDocs call iterates b.cache without synchronization after the event watcher starts, allowing concurrent BuildIndex map writes and a fatal concurrent map read/write panic.

false_positives.candidate:
Data race on shared err variable across errgroup goroutines in init

Inside searchSupport.init, every errgroup goroutine executes `_, _, err = s.build(ctx, ...)` assigning to the same outer `err` variable that is also read after group.Wait() and was previously assigned by GetResourceStats. With initWorkers > 1 (the exact scenario this PR is optimizing) these goroutines write err concurrently, which is a data race (flagged by -race) and can produce torn/ stale error values. Each goroutine should use a local error variable and return it, letting errgroup surface the first failure. The same loop also increments totalBatchesIndexed++ from multiple goroutines without synchronization (line 189), another race that can undercount the value reported in the span event.

NewResourceServer leaks resources when eager Init fails

When s.Init(ctx) fails, NewResourceServer returns nil, err but does not call s.cancel() to release the cancellable context created a few lines above, and does not close the blob bucket that may have been opened earlier in the function (OpenBlobBucket/NewCDKBlobSupport). Since Init now runs at construction time, init failures (e.g. index build errors) are a realistic path, and each failed construction leaks the context and the bucket handle. The error path should call cancel() and close any opened blob support before returning.

BuildIndex starts a span but drops the span context, inconsistent with the PR's trace-propagation fix

The PR fixes trace propagation by assigning the context returned from tracer.Start back to ctx in search.go and sql/backend.go, but bleveBackend.BuildIndex still does `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)` and discards the span-scoped context. Any operation inside BuildIndex that could use the context (e.g. passing it to the builder callback or future instrumented calls) would be detached from the BuildIndex span, so the bleve portion of index-building traces remains disconnected from its children. Use `ctx, span := b.tracer.Start(...)` for consistency with the rest of the change.

true_positives.golden_comment: MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler but only contains pass, failing to implement its required abstract methods: counter_names (property), get_dedupe_value(), get_group_key_values(), and build_occurrence_and_event_data(). This will cause a TypeError at runtime when the class is instantiated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
MetricAlertDetectorHandler can no longer be instantiated after switching to StatefulDetectorHandler

Previously the handler was instantiable and evaluate() returned an empty list. Either keep it on DetectorHandler or implement the abstract methods (even as stubs) so the class remains instantiable.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler without implementing the same four required abstract methods, causing a TypeError when instantiated. The candidate's additional runtime context does not change the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
test_dedupe in TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue builds the expected occurrence with the wrong group key

In TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe, the expected occurrence is built via build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "val1", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH), which sets the occurrence fingerprint to handler.build_fingerprint("val1") (i.e. ["<detector_id>:val1"]). true_positives.golden_comment: The function modifies the config variable to include display values but then returns the original monitor.config instead of the modified version.

false_positives.candidate:

Before this change, `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed` exposed `mark_failed_threshold`, `create_issue_platform_occurrence`, `get_failure_reason`, `get_monitor_environment_context`, `HUMAN_FAILURE_STATUS_MAP`, and the `SimpleCheckIn` TypedDict. true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at class definition time

In a dataclass, a plain default expression is evaluated once when the class body executes, not per instance. `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` therefore freezes `queued` to the module import time for every `AssignmentSource` created without an explicit value, instead of recording when the assignment was queued. Dataclasses only reject list/dict/set defaults, so this fails silently. The fix is `queued: datetime = field(default_factory=timezone.now)`. The field is currently unused, so the impact is limited to incorrect data, but it is a latent bug for any future consumer of the timestamp.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that timezone.now() is evaluated once at class definition time, causing all AssignmentSource instances without an explicit queued value to share the same timestamp rather than receiving a fresh one.

true_positives.golden_comment: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
AssignmentSource.to_dict() puts a non-JSON-serializable datetime into the Celery task payload

`sync_group_assignee_outbound` passes `assignment_source.to_dict()` as a kwarg to `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async`. `to_dict()` is `dataclasses.asdict(self)`, which includes `queued` as a raw `datetime` object. Celery's default task serializer is JSON (and Sentry's task payloads are generally expected to be JSON-safe), and a `datetime` is not JSON-serializable, so `apply_async` will raise `TypeError: Object of type datetime is not JSON serializable` at enqueue time. This failure occurs synchronously inside `GroupAssignee.objects.assign/deassign` whenever an assignment was triggered by an inbound integration webhook (which is exactly the new code path that always sets an `AssignmentSource`), so every inbound-triggered assignment would 500 the webhook handler and never enqueue any outbound sync. Even with an encoder that coerces datetimes to ISO strings, `from_dict` would then produce `queued` as a string rather than a datetime. The `queued` value should be serialized explicitly (e.g. `isoformat()` / timestamp) and parsed back in `from_dict`, or dropped from the payload. Note the new tests run tasks eagerly via `self.tasks()`, so no real serialization round-trip is exercised and this would not be caught by CI.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying issue: to_dict() includes queued as a raw datetime, which can fail JSON serialization when passed as task kwargs to apply_async and cause enqueue errors. The candidate overstates the certainty and scope of failure, but its core concern matches the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
New task kwarg is not backward compatible with workers running the previous code

`sync_assignee_outbound` now accepts `assignment_source_dict`, and `sync_group_assignee_outbound` immediately starts enqueuing messages containing that kwarg. During a rolling deploy (or a rollback), a worker still running the old function signature `sync_assignee_outbound(external_issue_id, user_id, assign)` will receive these messages and raise `TypeError: unexpected keyword argument 'assignment_source_dict'`; after the configured retries the assignee sync is lost. The standard mitigation is to stop passing the new kwarg until the new task signature is fully deployed (or guard it behind a feature/rollout), since the parameter was given a default only on the consumer side, which doesn't protect old consumers from new messages.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts the opposite of what the implementation does and only passes by timing luck

The test's docstring says "errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages", but the final assertion is `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` — i.e. it asserts that nothing was committed. In the actual implementation, `OrderedQueueWorker.run` completes the offset in a `finally` block even when `result_processor` raises, so both offsets (100 and 101) become committable and the commit loop commits them on its next 1-second tick. The test only passes because it finishes (processing is mocked and instant) before the commit thread's first 1s wake-up; wait a second longer and the offsets of the "failed" message would be committed. The test should either assert that the failed message's offset *is* committed (matching the implementation and the existing at-least-once semantics of the other modes) or the implementation should be changed — as written it documents behavior that is false and is fragile to scheduling.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the mismatch between the test's docstring and its assertion/implementation, which is the same concern as the golden comment. Its additional timing and implementation analysis does not change that match.

false_positives.candidate:
Shared FixedQueuePool is shut down by the old strategy on rebalance, causing silent message loss

The `FixedQueuePool` is created once in the factory's `__init__` and shared by every `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` produced by `create_with_partitions`. Arroyo closes and re-creates the strategy on every partition revocation/rebalance: the old strategy's `close()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which shuts down all queues and worker threads in the shared pool. The new strategy created after the rebalance still references the same pool. From then on, `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` calls `work_queue.put()`, which raises `queue.ShutDown` on a shut-down queue; this is caught by the broad `except Exception` in `submit`, which then calls `add_offset`/`complete_offset` on the message's offset. The result: every message after a rebalance is silently dropped (never processed) while its offset is marked complete and committed to Kafka. Since consumer groups rebalance on every deploy/scale event, running this mode in production would skip uptime results without any error surfacing beyond a log line. The pool needs to be created per `create_with_partitions` call, or `close()` must not shut down a pool it doesn't own.

Worker queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure and memory can grow without limit

`FixedQueuePool` creates each work queue with `queue.Queue()` (no maxsize), so `submit`/`put` never blocks. The docstring on `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` (line ~253) claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but that never happens: the Arroyo consumer thread will keep polling Kafka and appending `WorkItem`s faster than slow workers can drain them, buffering an unbounded number of decoded results in process memory. This is exactly the failure mode the PR is meant to mitigate (one slow item/group clogging processing) — a slow group now grows its queue until the consumer OOMs. The queues should have a `maxsize` (or `submit` should otherwise block/apply backpressure) to match the documented behavior.

join() ignores its timeout and shutdown abandons all queued items instead of draining them

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(timeout)` ignores the timeout and just calls `close()`, which immediately shuts down the queue pool. In `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` each worker's `shutdown` flag is set to True before `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` is called, so a worker that is woken with pending items still in its queue processes at most one more item and then exits its `while not self.shutdown` loop — everything remaining in the queues is discarded without being processed and without a final offset commit. Standard Arroyo strategies drain in-flight work and commit during `join` on graceful shutdown; here every deploy or rebalance abandons the entire in-memory backlog (which, given the unbounded queues, can be large) to be redelivered and reprocessed. At minimum `join` should wait for queues to drain up to the timeout and perform a final commit of completed offsets.

test_stats_reporting is flaky: asserts total_items > 0 after workers may have already drained the queue

The test submits 10 trivial work items (the processor just appends to a list under a lock) and then immediately asserts `stats["total_items"] > 0`. The three worker threads start consuming as soon as the first item is put, so on a fast machine all 10 items can be processed before the main thread reaches `get_stats()`, making `total_items` 0 and the assertion fail intermittently. The non-zero-depth assertion needs synchronization that blocks workers (e.g. an event the processor waits on) to be reliable.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset 'advanced pagination' path crashes: Django does not support negative slicing

The new branch `if self.enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0` passes a negative start directly into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, and the comment claims 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically'. That is false: Django's QuerySet slicing raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` for a negative start. Cursor offsets are user-controllable (Cursor.from_string happily parses `value:-100:0`), so any caller that enables this flag — the audit log endpoint does so via `enable_advanced_features=True` — can be forced into an unhandled exception and a 500 on every such request. The misleading comment in Cursor.__init__ (src/sentry/utils/cursors.py) about negative offsets being a supported optimization compounds this.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same negative-offset branch passing cursor.offset directly into queryset slicing when advanced features are enabled, and explains the resulting Django negative-slicing error.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot paginate datetime-ordered querysets, breaking the audit log endpoint path that uses it

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `int(math.floor(value))` on the raw model attribute, which only works for numeric keys. The new code in organization_auditlogs.py instantiates it with `order_by="-datetime"`, so `getattr(item, "datetime")` returns a datetime and `math.floor(datetime)` raises TypeError (this is exactly why DateTimePaginator overrides get_item_key to convert via strftime). Additionally, value_from_cursor returns the raw numeric cursor value, which build_queryset then compares against a datetime column. Every request with `optimized_pagination=true` will therefore 500 on the first page when build_cursor calls the key function. The optimized branch added to OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint is non-functional as written.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies math.floor to a datetime attribute when order_by='-datetime', causing a TypeError. Its additional discussion of cursor comparisons does not change this match.

false_positives.candidate:
organization_context.member can be None, causing AttributeError for non-member authentication

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` dereferences `organization_context.member` unconditionally whenever the user is not a superuser. RpcUserOrganizationContext.member is optional — requests authenticated with org-level auth tokens or other non-member principals have no member object — so those requests to the audit log endpoint will now raise AttributeError and return 500 instead of the audit log. This access is new in this PR; previously the endpoint never touched `.member`. Guard with `organization_context.member and organization_context.member.has_global_access`.

Segment keys change Redis type from SET to ZSET with no key rename or migration, causing WRONGTYPE errors during rollout

This PR changes the segment storage under the same key pattern `span-buf:s:{project:trace}:span_id` from a Redis SET (sadd/sscan/sunionstore) to a ZSET (zadd/zscan/zunionstore). Keys written by the old code live up to `redis_ttl` (default 3600s). After deploy, the Python `p.zadd(...)` and the new Lua script's `zcard`/`zunionstore` will hit pre-existing SET keys and Redis will raise WRONGTYPE, which propagates out of process_spans and fails the whole consumer batch (crash/retry loop) until all old keys expire. The key namespace should be versioned (e.g. `span-buf:sz:`) or a migration/compat path provided.

KeyError on spans missing end_timestamp_precise will fail the entire batch

`end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` uses direct indexing on the decoded span payload. Any message from an older Relay or a producer that omits this field raises KeyError inside process_batch, which fails the whole batch and leaves the consumer stuck retrying the same poison message. The pre-existing test payload (which lacked the field and had to be updated in this PR) shows such messages exist in practice. Use `val.get("end_timestamp_precise")` with a sensible fallback (e.g. 0 or the batch timestamp) so one malformed span cannot stall processing.

Segment span cap is hardcoded to 1000 in Lua while SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans (1001) is now dead config

The eviction logic `if span_count > 1000 then zpopmin(set_key, span_count - 1000)` hardcodes the limit in the Lua script instead of taking it as an ARGV, while `SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans: int = 1001` — a parameter that is no longer read anywhere after this PR removed the `max_segment_spans` check (and the `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` metric) from `_load_segment_data`. Operators tuning `max_segment_spans` will silently have no effect, and the two values (1000 vs 1001) already disagree. Either pass the limit into the script or remove the Python config.

Redirect-chain resolution limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000

The redirect-following loop was reduced from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000`, and the comment warning that segment trees deeper than the limit 'may not be joined together correctly' was deleted rather than updated. Segment trees with redirect chains deeper than 1000 will now silently fail to merge and be flushed as split/duplicated segments — a 10x tightening of a correctness-relevant limit with no mention in the PR and no remaining in-code warning. If intentional for performance, the comment should be kept (updated to 1000) and the behavior change documented; the redirect_depth metrics already emitted can verify impact.

Comment claims negative offsets are 'safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions' — queryset actually raises

The new comment above `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` says allowing negative offsets 'is safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions'. In fact Django raises AssertionError on negative slice starts, which is precisely why the clamp to max(0, offset) had to be added. The comment describes the opposite of what the code does and contradicts the identical false claim in OptimizedCursorPaginator; it should be corrected so future readers don't remove the clamp believing the ORM handles it.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling decision uses outer `dataset` instead of the `scoped_dataset` actually being queried

Inside `_get_event_stats`, the eligibility check calls `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` where `dataset` is the closure variable from `get()`, not the `scoped_dataset` argument that the query is actually executed against. In the dashboard-widget split path (`get_event_stats_factory`), `_get_event_stats` is invoked with `discover` as the scoped dataset and an errors-only query (`({query}) AND !event.type:transaction`) while the outer `dataset` is `metrics_performance`/`metrics_enhanced_performance`; `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` then returns False for the metrics dataset, so error counts for allowlisted (client-sampled) projects are never upsampled and are under-reported by the sampling factor. The check should use `scoped_dataset` (and ideally the actual query string being executed rather than `request.GET`).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: the upsampling eligibility check uses the outer dataset instead of scoped_dataset, causing upsampling to be skipped when dashboard-split queries run against discover while the outer dataset is metrics, even for allowlisted projects.

false_positives.candidate:
Accidental git submodule of the repository itself committed

The PR adds a new file `sentry-repo` containing `Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a` — this is a gitlink (embedded git repository) pointing at the base commit of this very repo, almost certainly created accidentally by running git commands inside a nested checkout. There is no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry, so this will leave the working tree in a confusing state for anyone who clones or checks out this branch (uninitialized submodule, dirty status, possible CI failures). It should be removed from the PR entirely.

Substring match treats negated `!event.type:error` queries as error-focused and upsamples transaction counts

_is_error_focused_query decides whether a discover query is error-only by checking `if "event.type:error" in query` on the lowercased raw query string. A query such as `!event.type:error` (everything *except* errors, i.e. transactions on the discover dataset) contains that substring, so it is classified as error-focused and count() is rewritten to `upsampled_count()` = `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. Transaction events do not carry a meaningful `sample_weight`, so their counts come back as 0/NULL instead of the true count — silently wrong results. The same false positive occurs for any query merely mentioning the text (e.g. `message:"event.type:error"`). The check should parse the query or at least account for negation rather than doing a raw substring match.

Cache key built with `hash()` can collide across different project sets

The eligibility cache key is `f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))}"`. Python's `hash()` produces a 64-bit value with no uniqueness guarantee: two different sets of project IDs that hash to the same value share a cache entry, so one set's allowlist eligibility would be returned for a different set of projects, producing wrong (upsampled or non-upsampled) counts for up to 60 seconds. Hash values are also not guaranteed stable across Python versions, causing silent key changes on deploys. The sorted project IDs themselves (e.g. joined with commas) should be used as the key instead of a hash.

Docstring claims fresh allowlist reads while the caller caches results for 60 seconds

The docstring for `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` states: "This function reads the allowlist configuration fresh each time, which means it can return different results between calls if the configuration changes during request processing. This is intentional to ensure we always have the latest configuration state." In reality the only caller, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`, caches the result for 60 seconds, so allowlist changes are explicitly *not* picked up fresh and stale eligibility is served for up to a minute. The docstring describes behavior the code does not have and contradicts the caching design documented in the caller; it should be corrected. Relatedly, `invalidate_upsampling_cache` (line 67) claims it "should be called when the allowlist configuration changes" but nothing in the codebase calls it, so there is no actual invalidation path.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key is ambiguous: fields joined with '_' can collide for UIDs containing underscores

userPermDenialCacheKey builds the key by concatenating namespace, userUID, action, name, and parent with '_' separators and no escaping or length prefixing. Resource and folder UIDs in Grafana can contain underscores, so distinct (name, parent) pairs produce identical keys: e.g. name="dash_a", parent="fold_b" and name="dash_a_fold", parent="b" both yield the same key. Because a cached entry means 'deny', a denial recorded for one dashboard/folder combination will incorrectly deny access to a different, unrelated dashboard for up to 30 seconds (shortCacheTTL). true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. If several requests arrive before the first successful load (e.g. at startup), they will each take the write lock in turn and each perform a full file read/HTTP fetch, even though the first one already populated the cache. A simple `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` immediately after acquiring the write lock would avoid the redundant loads.

While the load is in progress, every other goroutine calling GetWebAssets — including ones that arrive after the load has started but before the cache write at line 69 — blocks on the write lock instead of doing their own I/O in parallel, and in dev mode every single request now serializes on this mutex. This is a behavior change worth being aware of; it is not a correctness bug, but a slow or hanging CDN call will now stall all callers on the mutex.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes derive their context from the request context, so they are canceled when the request completes

In Create (and identically in Delete line 110, Update line 135, and DeleteCollection line 163) the background goroutine does `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` where `ctx` is the incoming request context. The request context is canceled as soon as the API handler returns, which happens immediately after the synchronous unified-storage write — so the child context used for the 'safe measure' legacy write is typically canceled before or during the legacy SQL call. The legacy write will then fail with context canceled, silently diverging legacy and unified storage (only visible as a metric). The goroutine should detach from the request lifecycle first, e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)`, before applying the 10s timeout.

The previous implementation fetched the old object, computed the updated object once, and wrapped it in `updateWrapper` so both stores persisted the same object. The new code passes the raw `objInfo` to both `d.Storage.Update` and, asynchronously, to `d.Legacy.Update`. This means `objInfo.UpdatedObject()` is invoked twice: the second time (in the goroutine) it runs against the old object fetched from legacy storage, which may have a different resourceVersion or may not exist yet (see the create-ordering race). `UpdatedObjectInfo` implementations are not guaranteed to be idempotent or reusable across calls, and the resulting legacy object can diverge from what was written to unified storage. The legacy call should receive a wrapper holding the object already produced by the unified update.

Async legacy writes are unordered, so create-then-update/delete sequences can diverge legacy storage

Each write method spawns an independent goroutine with its own 10s timeout and no serialization. A client that creates an object and immediately updates or deletes it will have the create's legacy write and the update/delete's legacy write racing in separate goroutines: the update can reach legacy before the create has been applied (failing with not-found, since forceAllowCreate is false), or a delete can be applied before the create lands, leaving a stale object in legacy. Because reads in mode 3 come only from unified storage, this divergence is invisible to users and only shows up as error counters. If ordering matters for the 'safe measure' copy, the legacy writes need a queue/serialization per object.

In Create (line 45), when `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` even though the legacy store was never invoked — this both inflates legacy error counts and loses the unified-storage error metric. The same mistake exists in Update at line 129, which records `recordLegacyDuration` on a `d.Storage.Update` failure. Both should call `recordStorageDuration`, as the error paths in Delete and DeleteCollection correctly do.

DeleteCollection records the legacy delete result against the storage metric

In the async goroutine of DeleteCollection, the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` instead of `recordLegacyDuration`. Legacy delete-collection latency/errors will be attributed to unified storage, corrupting both metrics (all other methods use `recordLegacyDuration` in this position).

The case 'error when creating object in the unified store fails' sets up only `setupLegacyFn` returning an error and provides no `setupStorageFn`. In mode 3, `dw.Create` calls `d.Storage.Create` first; with no expectation registered on the shared mock for that call, testify will panic with an unexpected-call failure rather than exercising the intended error path. The error expectation needs to be on the storage mock (and this worked in mode 1 only because mode 1 calls legacy first).

The added 'with dual write (file, mode 3)' and 'with dual write (unified storage, mode 3)' subtests reuse `doPlaylistTests`, which asserts legacy `/api/playlists` results immediately after k8s creates/updates/deletes (e.g. comparing `/api/playlists` list right after `client.Resource.Create`). The new `.map((query) => datasource.applyTemplateVariables(...))` runs before `partition(queries, querySupportsSplitting)` on line 300. `querySupportsSplitting` deliberately excludes queries containing `$__range` (lines 285-287) because the range variable must be resolved against the full, unsplit time range. true_positives.golden_comment: The `totalPages` calculation using `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` produces an extra page when `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit`, leading to incorrect pagination. Because showingLast compares currentPage to totalPages, the 'next' button stays enabled on the real last page; clicking it sets offset = min(offset + limit, user_count) = 100, and findMembers then fetches an empty page, leaving the admin looking at a blank 'page 3/3' of members with no way forward. The computation should be Math.ceil(user_count / limit) (with the zero case handled), and/or the next action should clamp offset to user_count - limit.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same off-by-one bug in Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1 for exact multiples of limit, including the same 100/50 example and navigation to an empty extra page.

false_positives.candidate:
'automatic' check resolves against the member, so the remove button always renders

This template is rendered as the itemView for each member in '{{each member in members itemView="group-member"}}', so its context is the individual user, not the group. '{{#unless automatic}}' therefore looks up 'automatic' on a User, which is undefined, so the condition always passes and the remove (×) link is shown even for automatic groups (admins, moderators, etc.). Clicking it fires the DELETE /admin/groups/:id/members request, which the server correctly rejects with 422 (can_not_modify_automatic), but the client-side removeMember action in the admin-group controller and the Group model's removeMember have no error handling, so the click fails silently and the member just stays in the list. The automatic check needs to come from the group/controller (e.g. passed via the each or referenced through the controller), and the failure case should surface an error to the admin.

Group create silently ignores the alias_level chosen in the form

The client sends alias_level on creation: Discourse.Group.asJSON() returns {name, alias_level, visible} and create() POSTs it to /admin/groups, and the alias level combo box in admin/templates/group.hbs is shown for new (unsaved) groups too. However the create action only assigns name and visible — params[:alias_level] is never applied — so every new group is created with the default alias_level of 0 ('nobody') regardless of what the admin selected, with no feedback. The admin must save the group and then save it again via update (which does handle alias_level) to get the intended setting.

Public group members page now truncates to 50 members with no pagination UI

The members action now always applies limit/offset (default limit 50) to every group; previously non-automatic groups returned their full member list and only automatic groups were capped. The public-facing group members page (discourse/routes/group-members.js.es6 and discourse/templates/group/members.hbs) was updated to read 'members' off the group model but has no pagination or load-more controls — only the admin group page got next/previous. As a result, any group with more than 50 members now shows only the first 50 (alphabetically) on its public members page, with no way for a visitor to see the rest.

members endpoint accepts an unbounded limit parameter

limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i places no upper bound on the page size for this publicly accessible endpoint (anyone who can see the group can call it). A request such as /groups/mods/members.json?limit=1000000 forces a COUNT plus a full SELECT and JSON serialization of that many users in one request. The limit should be clamped to a sane maximum (e.g. 200).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.
Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

This means any user.valid? call — including ones that never lead to a save, and repeated client-side-driven validation attempts — mutates persistent statistics, and the write happens outside the user's save transaction. If stats collection is intended, it would be safer to record the match only when a signup is actually rejected (e.g., in the controller or in an after-validation hook gated on the record being persisted), otherwise the counters can be inflated arbitrarily by repeatedly triggering validation without ever creating an account.

The candidate describes validation-driven counter inflation rather than emphasizing race conditions or misleading naming, but the core concern matches.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive, so blocks are trivially bypassed

BlockedEmail.should_block? performs an exact-match query: BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first. The email passed in comes straight from the signup form via User.new_from_params (which does no downcasing), and the blocked_emails table stores whatever case the admin entered. A spammer blocked as 'bad@spam.com' can register successfully as 'BAD@spam.com' or 'Bad@Spam.com' because the lookup won't match, and the user's own email uniqueness check is also case-sensitive so it won't collide with an existing account either. The block list should normalize (strip + downcase) both the stored value and the queried value, or the query should be case-insensitive.

false_positives.candidate:
float: right on .small-action button is silently ignored inside the new flex container

This PR makes `.small-action` a flex container via `@include flexbox()`. CSS specifies that `float` has no effect on flex items, so the `float: right` on the direct-child `button` (line 309) no longer does anything. Previously the button was pinned to the right edge of the small-action row; now it will render inline immediately after `.small-action-desc`, breaking the intended layout of small action posts (e.g. the edit/expand controls). The same applies to `float: left` on `.topic-avatar` (line 271), which is harmless only by accident of source order. The fix is to replace the button's float with `margin-left: auto` (or add `flex` spacing) so it is pushed to the end of the flex row.

The new `align-items` mixin unconditionally emits `-webkit-box-align: $alignment` for the 2009 flexbox spec, but that old property only accepts start/end/center/stretch — `baseline` is invalid and the declaration is dropped. `.badge-wrapper.bullet` in badges.css.scss calls `@include align-items(baseline)`, so on browsers that only understand the old `-webkit-box` model (e.g. older iOS Safari, which Discourse's `display: -webkit-inline-box` fallback in `inline-flex()` explicitly targets) the invalid declaration is ignored and items fall back to stretch alignment, vertically misaligning the bullet color swatch against the category text. If old-WebKit support matters (the mixin's prefixes imply it does), the mixin needs a value mapping or a fallback for `baseline`.

`.panel` previously used `float: right`, which worked in any browser. It now relies on `margin-left: auto` inside the `.contents` flex container. In any browser where none of the `display` values emitted by the `flexbox()` mixin are supported, `.contents` stays a block container, an auto left margin on a block-level `.panel` computes to 0, and the panel (user menu, search, hamburger icons) collapses against the logo on the left instead of staying on the right, breaking the header layout. If the supported-browser matrix includes any non-flexbox browsers (or engines with buggy partial flex support such as IE10, where auto margins inside `-ms-flexbox` containers are unreliable), this needs a fallback such as retaining `float: right` alongside the flex rules.

Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name is missing the '?' suffix, so ActiveModelSerializers never calls it

ActiveModelSerializers filters attributes by calling `include_<attribute>?` (with a question mark) — every other filter in this file follows that convention (`include_email?`, `include_stats?`, etc.). The new method is defined as `def include_website_name` without the `?`, making it dead code: the `website.present?` guard never runs, and `website_name` is always serialized (as `nil` when the user has no website, and unconditionally in the restricted-TL0 case described above). Rename it to `include_website_name?`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same missing '?' suffix on include_website_name and its effect on conditional attribute inclusion. It omits the golden comment's additional string-literal mutation concern, but matches the primary underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name leaks the website field for TL0 users viewed anonymously, bypassing untrusted_attributes

The serializer deliberately hides `:website` (via `untrusted_attributes`, which checks `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)`) so that anonymous visitors cannot see a TL0 user's profile fields. The new `:website_name` attribute is declared in the plain `attributes` list (line 43), is derived directly from `object.user_profile.website`, and its inclusion check only tests `website.present?` — it never checks `restrict_user_fields?`. As a result, for a TL0 user viewed by an anonymous visitor, `website` is omitted from the JSON but `website_name` (containing the website host, and possibly path) is still serialized, leaking exactly the information the restriction is meant to hide. The existing 'TL0 user seen as anonymous' spec was not extended to cover `website_name`, so the test suite does not catch this. `website_name` should be added to `untrusted_attributes` or its include check should mirror `include_website?`.

Sibling subdomains are treated as the same domain as the instance

The middle branch compares hosts of equal label count by stripping the first label from both sides: `www.anything.com` vs `forum.anything.com` are considered 'the same domain' and the full URL path is displayed. A sibling subdomain is not the instance's domain — on multi-tenant or shared-domain setups (e.g. instance at `forum.example.com`, user website at `evil.example.com/phishing-page`) the profile will render the full path as if the link belonged to the site's own domain, which is exactly the misleading display this feature is supposed to avoid. The comparison should only show the path when the website host equals the instance host or is a parent domain of it (the first and third branches), not when it is merely a sibling.

true_positives.golden_comment: postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage targetOrigin is a full referer URL, which browsers reject, so iframe resizing never works

The layout calls `parent.postMessage({type: 'discourse-resize', height: ...}, '<%= request.referer %>')`. The targetOrigin argument to postMessage must be an origin (scheme://host[:port]) or '*'; passing a full URL with a path (e.g. `http://blog.example.com/2013/02/10/post.html`, which is what the referer will always be) causes the browser to throw a SyntaxError ('Invalid target origin') and the message is never delivered. Since embed.js only sets the iframe height when it receives this message, the embedded comments iframe stays at the browser default height (~150px) and the comments appear cut off. The origin should be derived from the referer (or `SiteSetting.embeddable_host`), not the full referer URL.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify using the full referrer URL instead of its origin as postMessage's targetOrigin, preventing delivery of the resize message. The candidate's additional claim about a SyntaxError does not change the underlying issue identified.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
i.content can be nil for feeds without content:encoded, crashing the hourly job

`content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` assumes every feed item has a `content` element. SimpleRSS only populates `content` when the feed includes `content:encoded`; many RSS 2.0 feeds only provide `description`, and some Atom entries lack content entirely. For those items `i.content` is nil and `nil.scrub` raises NoMethodError, which aborts `rss.items.each` and kills the whole polling job (which has `retry: false`), so no topics are imported at all. Fall back to `i.description` or skip items with no content.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that calling scrub on a nil i.content crashes processing when feeds omit content, and recommend falling back to description.

false_positives.candidate:
raw_html cook method renders feed/imported HTML without any sanitization, enabling stored XSS

The new `cook` short-circuit returns `raw` verbatim when `cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`, bypassing the entire rendering/sanitization pipeline. This content originates from external sources: `Jobs::PollFeed` stores RSS/Atom item bodies (`CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)`) directly, and `TopicEmbed.import_remote` stores Readability output. Nothing sanitizes it, and it is rendered raw in `app/views/embed/best.html.erb` (`<%= raw post.cooked %>`) and in the normal topic UI. A malicious or compromised feed/article can therefore inject `<script>` or event-handler attributes that execute for every forum reader (stored XSS). The imported HTML should be run through the sanitizer (with an appropriate tag/attribute whitelist) before being stored as cooked.

TopicEmbed.import mutates the caller's contents string

`contents << "\n<hr>\n<small>..."` appends the 'Imported from' footer directly to the string object passed in by the caller. If the same string object is ever reused (e.g. a caller importing twice with one buffer, or passing a frozen string), the footer is appended multiple times — which also changes the computed content_sha1 and triggers spurious post revisions — or raises a RuntimeError on frozen strings. Use `contents = contents + ...` or `contents.dup` before appending.

setnx followed by expire is not atomic; a crash leaves the throttle key with no TTL

`retrieved_recently?` does `$redis.setnx(retrieved_key, "1")` and then `$redis.expire(retrieved_key, 60)` as two separate commands. If the process dies (or redis errors) between the two, the key is set with no expiry, and that embed URL is treated as 'retrieved recently' forever — `perform_retrieve` will never run for it again, so the topic for that URL is never imported. Use a single atomic command such as `$redis.set(retrieved_key, "1", ex: 60, nx: true)`.

embed_url is limited to 255 characters with no model-level length validation

The migration creates `t.string :embed_url, null: false` (255-char limit) with a unique index, while `TopicEmbed` only validates presence. Blog/feed URLs frequently exceed 255 characters (tracking parameters, long slugs). For such URLs, `TopicEmbed.create!` raises a database error (or RecordNotUnique-style failure) instead of a clean validation, and `EmbedController` will keep enqueueing retrieval jobs for a URL that can never be stored. Either use `text`/a larger limit or add a length validation and gracefully skip over-long URLs.

absolutize_urls raises URI::InvalidURIError for feed URLs that pass the loose scheme check

`TopicEmbed.import` accepts any URL matching `/^https?\:\/\//`, but `absolutize_urls` then calls `URI(url)`, which raises `URI::InvalidURIError` for strings with spaces, quotes, or other invalid characters that still match the prefix regex (feed-provided `link` values in `Jobs::PollFeed` are not otherwise validated). The exception is unrescued here, so one malformed feed item aborts the entire hourly `PollFeed` run (which has `retry: false`), preventing all other items from being imported. Validate with `URI.parse` up front and skip items that fail to parse.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.

Duplicate definition of OptimizedImage.downsize makes the width/height overload unreachable

The class now defines self.downsize twice: once as downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts) at line 145 and again as downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts) at line 149. In Ruby the second definition silently replaces the first, so the four-argument form is dead code. The two-APIs-in-one-method approach needs a different mechanism (e.g., a separate method name or a single signature).

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side upload size validation hardcoded to 10MB, ignoring site settings

validateUploadedFile previously read the limit from Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], which distinguishes max_image_size_kb from max_attachment_size_kb and respects admin configuration. The change replaces it with a hardcoded 10 * 1024. Consequences: sites that set a lower limit (e.g., 1MB images) will no longer block oversized files client-side, sites that set a higher limit will now wrongly reject valid uploads, attachments are incorrectly capped by the image-size logic, and the 'file too large' error message reports a max_size_kb that has no relation to the configured value.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the hardcoded 10 * 1024 upload limit replacing per-type Discourse.SiteSettings limits, causing client-side validation to diverge from configured server limits. The candidate matches the underlying issue despite not mentioning the 413 handler.

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Animated GIF path passes "80%" to gifsicle --resize-fit, which does not accept percentages

The new upload-downsizing code calls OptimizedImage.downsize(..., "80%", allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails). For GIFs with allow_animation set, optimize dispatches to downsize_instructions_animated, which delegates to resize_instructions_animated and emits `gifsicle ... --resize-fit 80%`. gifsicle's --resize-fit expects a WIDTHxHEIGHT geometry, not a percentage, so the command fails, convert_with returns false, and the controller's retry loop runs 5 times without shrinking the file. The result: animated GIFs larger than max_image_size_kb always fail to upload instead of being downsized, and the loop silently wastes 5 shell-outs before giving up.

false_positives.candidate:
413 error handler reports a hardcoded 10MB limit instead of the configured max image size

displayErrorForUpload used to show Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb in the file_too_large message when the web server returns 413. It now shows a hardcoded 10MB, so users are told the wrong maximum whenever the admin has configured max_image_size_kb to anything else, making the error message misleading.

FileHelper.download for API-provided URLs previously used SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes as the cap; it is now hardcoded to 10.megabytes. This download path is used for any file type, not just images, so attachment downloads via the API are now silently capped at 10MB regardless of max_attachment_size_kb, and sites with max_image_size_kb set above 10MB cannot fetch larger images even though the downsizing logic below was intended to shrink them.

The while loop never checks the boolean returned by OptimizedImage.downsize. If conversion fails (corrupt image, missing delegate, gifsicle geometry error), the loop burns all 5 attempts shelling out to a command that cannot succeed, then proceeds to Upload.create_for with the original oversized file, which then fails validation with a generic size error. A failed downsize should break out immediately (or surface a meaningful error) rather than retrying an unchanged file.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
unsubscribe crashes when the user has no topic_users row

In TopicsController#unsubscribe, `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` can legitimately return nil: users in mailing-list mode receive notification emails for topics they have never visited (the mailer itself handles this — `TopicUser.get` is used nil-tolerantly in send_notification_email), as do users emailed via a topic invite. false_positives.candidate: GET /t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe mutates state with no token or confirmation The new unsubscribe endpoint is a plain GET route that immediately changes the user's topic notification_level before rendering any page. Because GET requests carry no CSRF token, any third-party page that causes a logged-in user's browser to request the URL (e.g., an embedded pointing at the unsubscribe link) can silently mute or downgrade that user's subscription. Users who click the link will keep receiving emails for the topic, which is both a functional and messaging bug: either mute unconditionally or change the copy to say notifications are only reduced.

The route will therefore render with no template (or raise a missing-template error in development). Move the file to templates/topic-unsubscribe.hbs to match the route, controller, and view naming.

The only spec change in this PR adds an unsubscribe_url option to an existing message-builder test. There are no request specs for TopicsController#unsubscribe covering the notification-level transitions (watching/tracking → regular, regular → muted), the behavior when the user has no topic_users row, or the slug-mismatch redirect. A request spec for the missing-row case would have caught the nil-dereference crash on the primary path of this feature.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Script uses macOS-only sed syntax and a CWD-relative .env path

`sed -i '' -E ...` is the BSD/macOS form of in-place edit; on GNU sed (Linux, including CI containers and most dev VMs) the empty string is interpreted as a file name and the command errors out, so the script silently fails to update GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL for Linux users. true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:

`if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes') === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, 'minutes'))` compares two distinct dayjs object instances by reference, which is always false (`.isSame()` was presumably intended). This branch exists to detect a blocked-day override (start === end, i.e. 'unavailable the whole day'). Because it never fires, a blocked day is only rejected incidentally via the before/after checks, and a slot starting exactly at the block's start instant satisfies none of them: the callback returns undefined, `dateOverrideExist` is already true, and the function returns `true` (available) — leaking a bookable slot on a day the host explicitly marked unavailable.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: using === compares distinct dayjs object references rather than date values, making the condition always false. Both indicate .isSame() as the intended comparison.

false_positives.candidate:
Date-override days skip the busy-time check, enabling double bookings

In checkIfIsAvailable, when any date override matches the slot's day, `dateOverrideExist` is set to true and, if the slot falls inside the override window (so the `find` callback never returns true), the function hits `if (dateOverrideExist) { return true; }` — returning 'available' before the `busy.every(...)` check at the bottom ever runs. This means that on any day where a host has a date override, that host's existing bookings and calendar busy times are completely ignored. A fixed host (or a regular solo event user, since they are also isFixed) with a date override who already has a booking/meeting inside the override window will be shown as bookable, producing double bookings — the exact problem this PR claims to fix ('prevents round-robin events being booked where the fixed hosts are unavailable'). The busy check must still run when a date override exists; only the working-hours check should be bypassed.

Multiple same-day date-override windows veto each other

The `dateOverrides.find(...)` logic treats 'slot is outside this one override window' as grounds to return false (unavailable), but a user can have several override windows on the same date (cal.com's UI allows adding multiple time ranges to one date override, stored as separate rows). For a slot that falls inside window B, window A's callback hits `slotStartTime.isAfter(date.end)` (or `slotEndTime.isBefore(date.start)`) and returns true, so the slot is marked unavailable even though it is within window B — and vice versa. Net effect: on a day with two or more override windows, every window is rejected by the other and the host shows no availability at all. The find should only return a 'reject' verdict after confirming the slot is outside *all* same-day windows for that user.

Override decoding depends on the server running in UTC

The new code decodes the override's wall-clock-encoded Date back to a real instant with `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes')` and compares it against `slotStartTime`/`slotEndTime`, which are explicitly UTC (`time.utc()`). `dayjs(date.start)` parses the Date in the process's local timezone, so the decode math (wall time − organizer offset = real UTC instant) only holds when the Node process runs with TZ=UTC. On any non-UTC runtime (dev machines, some CI/self-hosted setups) the override window and day-matching comparisons are shifted by the server offset, making fixed-host override filtering silently wrong. Use `dayjs.utc(date.start)` for these comparisons, as the parallel code in packages/lib/slots.ts already does with `.utc()`.

The invitee-timezone conversion computes `startTime`/`endTime` as `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, 'minute').hour() * 60 + ...minute()`. Taking `.hour()/.minute()` after the offset shift drops any day rollover: when the invitee/organizer offset difference pushes the override across midnight (e.g. organizer Asia/Kolkata override 01:00–02:00 = 19:30–20:30 the previous UTC day, viewed by a UTC invitee: offset = −330 min lands on the previous day, but hour() yields 1170 minutes), the slot is materialized at 19:30 on the *current* invitee day instead of the correct adjacent day. Since the activeOverrides filter keys on the unshifted date, cross-midnight overrides are placed on the wrong day — precisely the timezone-adjustment scenario this PR is fixing. The shifted value should be carried as a full timestamp (or the day delta applied to startOfInviteeDay), not reduced to minutes-since-midnight.

`dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()` assumes `override.timeZone` is set, but the `TimeRange` type declares `timeZone?: string` as optional and getSlots is a shared library function — nothing at the type level guarantees every caller supplies it (the slots router happens to add it in this PR). With `timeZone` undefined, dayjs's tz plugin falls back to the host system's timezone when computing `organizerUtcOffset`, so the offset correction is silently computed against the server timezone and override slots are shifted by a wrong amount. Either make the field required for date overrides passed to getSlots or guard/default it here.

However, the only test added exercises a single-user personal event with a different invitee timezone. None of the new checkIfIsAvailable behavior — fixed host availability gating, override-window filtering per host, interaction with busy times — is covered, which is how the regression where busy checks are skipped on override days (and the multi-window veto issue) went unnoticed. A round-robin scenario with one fixed host having a date override should be added, including a case where the fixed host is busy inside the override window.

retryCount update inside catch block can throw and abort the whole cron run

Previously the catch block only logged the error, so a failure for one reminder could never stop the loop. Now the catch block performs `prisma.workflowReminder.update` unguarded. If that update itself fails — e.g. the row was deleted concurrently by another cron execution or by a booking cancellation, or the DB connection is the very thing that failed — the exception propagates out of the catch, the for-loop terminates, all remaining unscheduled reminders are skipped for this run, and the handler returns a 500. A regression here silently drops customer SMS reminders, so at least the retry-count boundary and the delete query scope should be covered.

In `buildOrgAuthorizationCondition` (line 164 and 168) and `buildTeamAuthorizationCondition` (line 201) the code writes e.g. `Prisma.sql`("teamId" = ANY(${teamIds}))``. Prisma's tagged-template helper expands an interpolated JavaScript array into a comma-separated list of bound parameters — it does NOT serialize it as a single Postgres array parameter. So with `teamIds = [10, 20, 30]` the emitted SQL is `"teamId" = ANY($1, $2, $3)`, which Postgres rejects with `syntax error at or near "$2"` (ANY requires a single array expression or subquery). Every org-scope and team-scope query will therefore fail with a raw-query error at runtime; only the user-scope path (which has no ANY) is valid. The correct pattern is `"teamId" IN (${Prisma.join(teamIds)})` or passing a single array parameter with an explicit cast. The tests don't catch this because they only structurally compare Sql objects built with the same broken pattern.

The previous implementation exposed a public `findMany(findManyArgs)` method that combined authorization/filter conditions into a `bookingTimeStatusDenormalized.findMany` call. This PR deletes that method entirely and replaces it with `getBaseConditions(): Promise<Prisma.Sql>`, shifting query execution to callers via `$queryRaw`. No caller is updated in this PR (only the service and its test are changed), so any existing consumer that invokes `insightsBookingService.findMany(...)` — e.g. the insights tRPC procedures that fetch booking events/status/hourly data — will fail TypeScript compilation and lose functionality. Either keep a compatible `findMany` wrapper or update all callers in the same change.

The org-scope (line 332) and team-scope (line 295) tests assert conditions via `expect(conditions).toEqual(Prisma.sql`...`)`, which only deep-compares the Sql object's internal `strings`/`values` arrays — it never runs the SQL against the database. The only test that actually executes a query (`getBaseConditions`, line 481) uses scope `"user"`, the one code path that contains no `ANY(...)` array interpolation. As a result the tests pass while the org/team SQL is syntactically invalid (Prisma expands `ANY(${ids})` into `ANY($1, $2, ...)`, a Postgres syntax error). At least one test per scope should execute the produced conditions with `$queryRaw` against the real database so invalid generated SQL is caught.

The org-scope test asserts exact equality with `Prisma.sql`... ("userId" = ANY(${[user.id, user2.id, user3.id]})) ...`. The service builds that array from `MembershipRepository.findAllByTeamIds`, a `findMany` with no `orderBy`, so Postgres does not guarantee the row order (the user also has two memberships — team and org — that get deduped via `Set`, preserving whatever order rows came back in). If the membership rows are returned in a different order, the Sql `values` array order differs and the deep-equality assertion fails spuriously. The assertion should compare order-insensitively or the repository query should impose a deterministic order.

In non-sync mode, `refreshTokenResponseSchema` transforms `expires_in` (seconds) into an absolute epoch timestamp via `.transform()`.
