Since `getToken` decides to refresh based on `isExpired(o365AuthCredentials.expires_in)`, every single `getToken()` call triggers another POST to the sync endpoint — one extra HTTP round-trip (plus a DB write) per calendar operation, and the stored `refresh_token` is also clobbered with the placeholder string.

Webex refresh bypasses parseRefreshTokenResponse, so sync-mode responses always fail schema validation

Unlike the other apps, the Webex adapter was wrapped with `refreshOAuthTokens` but still validates the result with the strict `webexRefreshedTokenSchema.safeParse(responseBody)` instead of `parseRefreshTokenResponse`. That schema requires `scope` to be the exact literal "spark:kms meeting:schedules_read meeting:schedules_write", `token_type: "Bearer"`, `refresh_token`, and `refresh_token_expires_in`. Per the PR's own contract (comment in `refreshOAuthTokens`: 'The response should only contain the access token and expiry date'), the sync endpoint returns a minimal payload, so validation fails and every Webex token refresh rejects with 'Invalid refreshed tokens were returned' whenever credential sync is enabled.

Salesforce now refreshes the token on every service instantiation and ignores the credential-sync endpoint

The new code in `getClient` unconditionally POSTs to `https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` and writes to the DB every time a `SalesforceCalendarService` is constructed — previously jsforce lazily refreshed only on a 401. This adds an external HTTP call plus a DB write to every Salesforce calendar operation. Additionally, this is the only modified app that does not route through `refreshOAuthTokens`, so when credential syncing is the source of truth, the stored `refresh_token` may be the placeholder `"refresh_token"` (or absent), making this direct Salesforce refresh fail with invalid_grant and breaking the integration entirely.

findFirst-then-create upsert has a race that creates duplicate credentials

The handler does `prisma.credential.findFirst({ userId, appId })` and then either updates or creates. Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same user/app (retries are typical for webhooks) can both observe no existing credential and both execute `prisma.credential.create`, leaving duplicate credential rows for the same user and app. Other parts of the codebase use `findFirst` when reading credentials, so duplicates silently shadow each other and can cause the wrong (stale) credential to be used. Since `(userId, appId)` is not unique in the schema, this should at least be serialized (e.g. transaction with locking, or a unique constraint) rather than a check-then-act.

No tests for the credential-sync webhook or the sync-mode token refresh paths

The PR checklist explicitly states no tests were added. The new endpoint writes third-party credentials directly into the database and the modified refresh paths in ~10 app integrations (Google, Zoom, Office365, HubSpot, Zoho, Webex, Lark, Salesforce) now branch on `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` — several of which are broken in sync mode (shape mismatches, NaN expiry, wrapper object persisted). At minimum, tests covering the webhook (auth failure, create vs update, bad payload) and one representative sync-mode refresh per response-shape family (fetch Response vs SDK object vs axios) would have caught the regressions in this PR.

The `cancelled: true` update (or row delete) therefore happens in the background after the response may already have been sent; in a serverless deployment the lambda can be frozen once the response completes, so the flag may never be written — in which case the cron never cancels the SendGrid send and the reminder email is still delivered, re-creating the bug this PR fixes. The calls should be collected and awaited (the same applies to the identical new pattern in `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx` requestReschedule and `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/workflows.tsx`).

That path POSTs the `status: "cancel"` to SendGrid right away — for reminders that may be scheduled days in the future — which is exactly the behavior this PR identifies as the root cause of hitting SendGrid's max of 100 pending cancellations (pending cancellations accumulate until the scheduled date). Additionally, the immediateDelete path neither deletes the `WorkflowReminder` row nor sets `cancelled: true`, so the row lingers with `scheduled: true` and is invisible to the cron's `cancelled: true` cleanup; it only disappears when the generic `scheduledDate <= now` deleteMany runs after the send date. Also note the whole forEach is fire-and-forget, so the surrounding try/catch can never catch errors from these async calls.

If the SendGrid request fails for any one reminder (e.g. a stale/invalid `referenceId` batch_id, which returns an error from SendGrid), the loop exits immediately: (a) all remaining `remindersToCancel` never get their SendGrid cancellation posted, so those emails will still be sent even though the bookings were cancelled — the exact bug this PR is meant to fix; and (b) the `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` promises collected in `workflowRemindersToDelete` are never awaited, and since Prisma promises are lazy, those deletes never execute. Because the failing row is never deleted, it will abort the loop again on every subsequent cron run (every 15 min), permanently blocking cancellations for all reminders that happen to sort after it (the query has no orderBy). Each reminder's SendGrid call and DB delete needs its own error handling so a single bad record can't block the batch.

When a paid booking is cancelled, the handler refunds the payment, sets the booking status to REJECTED, and returns early at `return { message: "Booking successfully cancelled." }` — before reaching the new "Workflows - cancel all reminders for cancelled bookings" block further down (which calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` / `deleteScheduledSMSReminder`). In the `requestReschedule` mutation, the old code collected `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany` promises and awaited them via `Promise.all(remindersToDelete)`. The mutation can complete and the serverless invocation can be torn down before the `cancelled: true` updates / deletes commit, leaving reminders active for a booking that was cancelled for rescheduling, so the cron never cancels them and emails may still be sent. If clusters are not counted a uniform number of times (e.g., cluster shard counts not divisible by the process count), the computed `used / available` ratio is skewed and `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage` hard backpressure will trigger too early or too late. Consequence: under V2, an admin holding the manage-clients role, or a manage permission on a specific client or on all clients, gets 403 when mapping client roles to users or adding composite roles — a regression compared to V1 behavior, where manage clients implied the ability to map its roles.

getResourceName does not resolve names for Clients-typed resources

getResourceName only special-cases the Users resource type, resolving the stored user id to the username. For the newly added Clients resource type it falls through to resource.getDisplayName(), which is never set for FGAP-created resources (getOrCreateResource only sets name/scopes), so admin REST responses and the admin console will show a null/empty name for client-typed permission resources instead of the client's clientId. Add a Clients branch mirroring the Users one that resolves ClientModel.getClientId().

Javadoc on void require methods incorrectly says "Returns {@code true}"

The newly added javadoc for requireView() ("Returns {@code true} if {@link #canView()} returns {@code true}.") and requireViewClientScopes() ("Returns {@code true} if {@link #canViewClientScopes()} returns {@code true}.") describes a boolean return, but both methods are void and throw ForbiddenException on failure. This contradicts the otherwise consistent 'Throws ForbiddenException if ...' wording used for the other require* methods and misleads implementers of the interface.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() grants manage rights to admins holding only the view scope on all groups

In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() the fallback permission check is `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`, i.e. it returns true when the caller has either the VIEW or the MANAGE scope on the all-groups resource. This appears to be a copy-paste of canView() directly above it. As a result, an admin who is granted only a 'view' permission for all groups (e.g. via an all-groups scope permission with the view scope) is treated as being able to manage groups globally: the no-arg canManage()/requireManage() is what GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup() uses to authorize creating top-level groups, so a view-only admin can create groups. Per-group manage (canManage(GroupModel)) correctly checks only MANAGE, so the no-arg variant should drop AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW from the expected scopes.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() falls back to checking both the VIEW and MANAGE scopes, so a user with only VIEW permission passes the manage check. Both say the fix is to check MANAGE only.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns authz resource IDs instead of group IDs

In GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission(), the granted set is populated with `groupResource.getId()`, which is the authorization-store Resource UUID. In the V2 schema the group ID is stored as the resource *name* (AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup returns group.getId() and getOrCreateResource creates the resource with that name). Callers of this method — UsersResource.searchForUser, BruteForceUsersResource.searchForUser and UsersResource.getUsersCount — feed the returned IDs into the UserModel.GROUPS session attribute / group-filtered count queries, which expect real group IDs. Concretely: an admin whose only user visibility comes from a view-members/manage-members permission on all groups will get a non-empty set containing a resource UUID, the GROUPS session attribute is set with it, and searchForUserStream filters by membership in a non-existent group, so the admin sees zero users. The method should add groupResource.getName() (the group ID), mirroring what the V1 implementation did by stripping the prefix from the resource name.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say getGroupIdsWithViewPermission adds groupResource.getId(), the resource UUID, when it should add the group ID stored as the resource name. Both note this breaks the UserModel.GROUPS filtering and the count queries. This is the same issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Per-resource permission check in getGroupIdsWithViewPermission looks up resources by ID as if it were a name, and per-group resources are never typed

Inside the findByType visitor in GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission(), the code calls `hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), VIEW_MEMBERS, MANAGE_MEMBERS)`. However hasPermission(String groupId, ...) does `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)`, so it is passed a resource ID where a resource name is expected; the lookup returns null and evaluation silently falls back to the all-groups resource instead of evaluating the policies attached to that specific group resource. Additionally, resources created by AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource never have their type set (no setType call), so resourceStore.findByType(server, GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...) will not even iterate per-group resources — only the 'all groups' resource created in init() carries the type. Net effect: view-members/manage-members grants on individual groups are never detected by this method, and (combined with the getId() bug) the group-ID set used to filter user searches is wrong or empty.

No upgrade path for realms that enabled admin permissions before the Groups resource type existed

AdminPermissionsSchema.init() creates the 'Groups' all-resource and the group-specific scopes (manage-members, view-members, manage-membership) only when the admin-permissions client is first created for a realm. Realms that already have admin permissions enabled (resource server initialized by an earlier version) will never get the new resource type or scopes, and this PR adds no migration. Consequences for such realms: AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceTypeResource() returns null for 'Groups', and GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission then calls `policyStore.findByResource(server, null)`, which dereferences the null resource in the JPA store implementation and throws (500 on group admin endpoints); likewise creating any group permission fails because the scope lookups in getOrCreateResource find no 'manage-members'/'view-members' scopes and throw ModelException("No scopes found."). A migration/initialization step that adds the new resource type and scopes to existing admin-permissions resource servers is needed.

getResourceName does not resolve names for the new Groups resource type

AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceName() resolves human-readable names only for the Users resource type; for everything else it returns resource.getDisplayName(). Group resources created via getOrCreateResource are named by group ID and never have a display name set, so anywhere this method is used to present resources of a Groups-type policy (e.g. permission listings in the admin UI), the entry will show null/empty instead of the group's name or path. A GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE branch resolving the group (e.g. its name or path) should be added, analogous to the existing Users handling.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default keystore provider (SUN), not BouncyCastle

The CryptoProvider contract states this method returns the BouncyCastle security provider. AuthzClientCryptoProvider instead returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which is the SUN provider on standard JDKs. BouncyIntegration caches the returned provider's name globally (BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER) and keycloak-core code uses that name for explicit-provider JCA lookups (e.g., KeyStore/Cipher/Signature.getInstance(alg, BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER)); pinning those lookups to "SUN" will throw NoSuchAlgorithmException/NoSuchProviderException for anything SUN does not implement (e.g., PKCS12 keystores, which live in SunJSSE), even though the algorithms are available elsewhere in the JVM. It also needlessly instantiates a KeyStore on every call. The correct behavior for an environment without BouncyCastle is to return null, as WildFlyElytronProvider does.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same bug as the golden comment: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default keystore provider instead of BouncyCastle.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract method order() breaks all existing third-party CryptoProvider implementations

CryptoProvider is a public SPI loaded via ServiceLoader, and this PR adds a new abstract method `int order()` without a default implementation. Any existing out-of-tree implementation of CryptoProvider (custom crypto provider extensions compiled against the previous keycloak-common) will fail to compile against the new version and, worse, will throw AbstractMethodError at runtime when an old jar is used with the new keycloak-common, because CryptoIntegration.detectProvider now calls CryptoProvider::order on every ServiceLoader-discovered provider during sorting. This turns a previously working deployment into one that fails during CryptoIntegration.init. The method should be declared as `default int order() { return 0; }` (or similar) so existing implementations keep working.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments raise the same concern: the new abstract order() method on CryptoProvider breaks backward compatibility with existing implementations.

false_positives.candidate:
Multiple equal-order providers are now resolved silently and arbitrarily instead of failing fast

Previously, having more than one CryptoProvider on the classpath was a hard configuration error ("Multiple crypto providers loaded..."). Now detectProvider sorts by order() descending and silently takes the first, only logging the ignored ones at debug level. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200, so if two server-side providers end up on the classpath together (a real misconfiguration, e.g. both elytron and fips jars present), the winner is determined by ServiceLoader encounter order, which depends on jar/classpath ordering and is effectively arbitrary — the server may run with the wrong crypto provider with no warning above debug level. Equal-order ties should still fail fast, or at least log a warning.

ES384/ES512 tests sign with a P-256 key and never verify the re-encoded DER with JCA

The test constructor creates a single key with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()`, whose default curve is P-256, and reuses it for all three tests. As a result testES384 and testES512 never process real 48-byte or 66-byte r/s values, so the padding/truncation logic in integerToBytes for those sizes is untested despite the test names suggesting otherwise. Additionally, the test only asserts that decode(encode(x)) == x, which is self-consistent by construction; the re-encoded DER signature is never passed to java.security.Signature.verify(), so an encoder bug that produces DER the JCA (or the server) rejects would still pass. Each test should generate a key for the matching curve (secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1) and verify the re-encoded signature with JCA.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reader thread is never joined, so the test can pass without ever exercising the race

In createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti, the background thread that repeatedly calls managedRealm.admin().groups().groups(...) is started but never joined. The main thread deletes the 100 groups, sets deletedAll=true, and immediately asserts caughtExceptions is empty. Because there is no thread.join() (and no guarantee the reader thread has executed even a single iteration before the deletes finish), the test can pass vacuously on a slow or busy CI runner without ever reproducing the concurrent read-during-delete scenario this PR is fixing. Additionally, the reader thread performs one more iteration after deletedAll becomes true (the flag is only checked at the top of the loop), so any exception thrown in that final in-flight request happens after the assertion has already executed and is silently lost. The test should join the reader thread before asserting (and ideally ensure a minimum number of read iterations occurred).
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say the reader thread is never joined. Both also note that asserting right after setting deletedAll lets exceptions from the in-flight iteration be lost, which makes the test flaky. Same underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Fix only covers getSubGroupsCount; other cached read paths still NPE on concurrent group deletion

getSubGroupsCount() now null-checks modelSupplier.get() before use, but the identical concurrent-delete race remains in the sibling read paths of the same adapter: getSubGroupsStream(String, Integer, Integer), getSubGroupsStream(Integer, Integer), and getSubGroupsStream(String, Boolean, Integer, Integer) (lines 254-269) all call modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...) without a null check, and getAttributes/getFirstAttribute go through cached lazy loaders that dereference the supplied GroupModel. If the group is deleted from the database between cache read and delegate load, those paths still throw the same NullPointerException this PR set out to fix, so requests hitting them (e.g. paginated subgroup listing while a group is removed) remain broken. The behavior is also now inconsistent: when the adapter was invalidated, isUpdated() throws IllegalStateException("Not found in database") for a deleted group, while this method silently returns null for the same condition.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() violates the GroupModel contract (Javadoc says it never returns null) and may lead to NPEs in callers that expect a non-null count.

true_positives.golden_comment: In UsernameForm.authenticate(), isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() is called without passing the required UserModel parameter.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Call to isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments does not compile

UsernameForm.authenticate() calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments, but the only method with that name is the one added in this PR in the superclass UsernamePasswordForm: protected boolean isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user). There is no no-arg overload anywhere in the class hierarchy, so the services module fails to compile with 'no suitable method found: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()'. The call almost certainly should be isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()), matching how the same method is invoked in UsernamePasswordForm.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same issue: UsernameForm.authenticate() calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() without the required UserModel argument.

true_positives.golden_comment: With isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) requiring user != null, authenticate(...) will not call webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) on the initial login page where context.getUser() is still null, so conditional passkey UI will not be set up for first-time passkey login. Consider whether this should also be enabled when no user has been selected yet so ID-less passkey authentication on the initial login form continues to work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requires a non-null user, which disables passkeys on all fresh logins

The new helper isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) returns webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() && user != null, and it now gates every call to webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context): in authenticate() (line 115) and in challenge(context, error, field) (line 137). On an initial login there is no user in the authentication context (context.getUser() == null), so fillContextForm is never invoked for first-time logins: the WebAuthn challenge note, the ENABLE_WEBAUTHN_CONDITIONAL_UI form attribute, and the webauth form markup are never set. Previously fillContextForm was called precisely in the user == null branch. This inverts the behavior and removes passkey autofill/auto-login from the normal (non re-authentication) username/password page, regressing the primary passkeys scenario. The tests retained/added in this very PR confirm the expected behavior and would fail: PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest.webauthnLoginWithDiscoverableKey expects automatic passkey login when opening a fresh login form, and passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey (in both PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest and PasskeysOrganizationAuthenticationTest) asserts that //form[@id='webauth'] is present on the fresh login page. The condition must also be true when the user is null (fresh login); requiring user != null makes passkeys available only during re-authentication.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requires user != null, so fillContextForm is skipped on the initial login page where the user is null. That breaks conditional passkey login on the fresh login form.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset branch passes a negative index to a Django QuerySet slice, which raises AssertionError

In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[cursor.offset : cursor.offset + limit + extra]`. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing — slicing with a negative start raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported`. The inline comment claiming 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false. Since cursor offsets are user-controlled (the `cursor` query string is parsed by Cursor.from_string with `int(bits[1])`, which accepts negatives), any privileged caller can supply e.g. `cursor=0:-5:0` with `optimized_pagination=true` and get a 500 AssertionError on every request. This is a reliable crash/DoS of the endpoint rather than a performance feature, and no boundary handling exists.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator slices a Django queryset with a negative offset, which Django does not support and which raises an AssertionError.

true_positives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enable_advanced is computed unconditionally and dereferences organization_context.member, crashing for member-less auth

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated on every GET, even when the `optimized_pagination` query param is absent. `organization_context.member` is None for requests authenticated without an organization member (e.g., org API keys / auth tokens with the org:read scope that legitimately pass OrganizationAuditPermission). For such requests `request.user.is_superuser` is False, so the right-hand side evaluates `None.has_global_access` and raises AttributeError, returning a 500. This regresses the previously working default pagination path for those auth types. The expression should be computed lazily inside the `use_optimized` branch and guard against `member is None`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: organization_context.member is None for API key/org token auth, so accessing has_global_access raises AttributeError. The candidate says the crash happens on every GET, while the golden ties it to optimized_pagination=true. That is a difference in scope, but the underlying issue is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator crashes with TypeError when used with a datetime order_by key

The audit log endpoint instantiates OptimizedCursorPaginator with order_by="-datetime", but OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `int(math.floor(value) if ... else math.ceil(value))` on `getattr(item, self.key)`. For the audit logs endpoint that value is a `datetime` object, and `math.floor`/`math.ceil` on a datetime raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime.datetime`. This is called from build_cursor on the very first page of results (to compute the next cursor), so every request using `optimized_pagination=true` will 500 as soon as there is at least one audit log row. The code needed the DateTimePaginator-style conversion (`value.strftime("%s.%f") * multiplier`) or should have subclassed DateTimePaginator. There is also a secondary issue: even if get_item_key were fixed to return an int, `value_from_cursor` returns the raw integer cursor value and `build_queryset` would then compare the datetime column against an integer (`datetime <= %s` with an int param), which the database will reject.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug. get_item_key calls math.floor/ceil on a datetime value because the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in audit logs, which raises a TypeError.

false_positives.candidate:
Trim check compares against the raw negative offset instead of the slice actually fetched

In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, the `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra:` check uses the original `offset` variable, which in the negative-offset branch is negative. Since `queryset[negative:...]` raises before this is reached in Django, this is currently masked, but if the slicing ever 'worked' (e.g., on a list-backed queryset), the comparison would never match and the extra boundary row would not be trimmed, leaking an extra row into the page and producing wrong cursors. It should compare against the actual fetch size (`stop - start_offset` or `limit + extra`).

Comment claims negative offsets are a supported performance optimization, but no paginator actually supports them

The added comment in Cursor.__init__ states negative offsets are allowed for 'advanced pagination scenarios' and enable 'efficient reverse pagination'. No paginator actually handles negative offsets correctly — BasePaginator clamps non-prev offsets with max(0, offset), OffsetPaginator/MergingOffsetPaginator/ChainPaginator explicitly raise BadPaginationError on negative offsets, and OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset path crashes on Django's 'Negative indexing is not supported' assertion. The comment documents a capability that does not exist and is misleading to future maintainers.

No tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator or the new audit-logs pagination branch

The PR adds ~100 lines of new pagination logic (OptimizedCursorPaginator) plus a new conditional branch in OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint gated by the `optimized_pagination` query param and superuser/global-access checks, but adds no tests. Tests would have immediately caught the two crash bugs (datetime math.floor TypeError and negative-slice AssertionError). At minimum there should be tests covering: optimized_pagination=true for a superuser with audit log rows present, a prev/next cursor round-trip, a negative-offset cursor, and a non-member token request (to cover the member-None path).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Importing non-existent OptimizedCursorPaginator

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the build-wide lock allows concurrent duplicate builds of the same index

BuildIndex previously serialized all builds with cacheMu; now two goroutines can build the same NamespacedResource concurrently (getOrCreateIndex in search.go does a check-then-build with no synchronization, and its own comment acknowledges it does not block concurrent builders of the same key). Consequences: (1) for file-backed indexes (size > FileThreshold), both builders call bleve.New on the same directory path, and the second one fails on the bleve lock file, surfacing a spurious error to a search or watch-event request; (2) for memory-backed indexes both builds succeed and the second write to b.cache silently overwrites the first, leaking an open bleve.Index that is never closed and wasting the entire duplicate build. A per-key lock (or singleflight) is needed instead of the single global lock that was removed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same issue. Narrowing the cacheMu lock in BuildIndex lets multiple goroutines build the same index for the same key at the same time.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs reads b.cache map without holding cacheMu

TotalDocs() iterates over b.cache without acquiring b.cacheMu (it never did, but it matters now). Before this PR, BuildIndex held cacheMu for its entire duration and TotalDocs was effectively only reached after all init builds completed; now the lock is only taken for the final map insertion, and this PR adds a new call to TotalDocs in searchSupport.init (search.go line 216, the "search index initialized" log) that runs right after the watch-event goroutine is started. That goroutine calls getOrCreateIndex -> BuildIndex on events for unknown namespaces, which writes b.cache concurrently with the TotalDocs iteration. Concurrent map read/write in Go is a fatal runtime error ("concurrent map read and map write"), which will crash the process. TotalDocs should take b.cacheMu.RLock() before iterating.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug. TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, while the watcher goroutine can call BuildIndex and write to the map concurrently. That can cause a concurrent map read/write panic.

false_positives.candidate:
Data race on shared err variable across errgroup goroutines in init

Inside searchSupport.init, every errgroup goroutine executes `_, _, err = s.build(ctx, ...)` assigning to the same outer `err` variable that is also read after group.Wait() and was previously assigned by GetResourceStats. With initWorkers > 1 (the exact scenario this PR is optimizing) these goroutines write err concurrently, which is a data race (flagged by -race) and can produce torn/ stale error values. Each goroutine should use a local error variable and return it, letting errgroup surface the first failure. The same loop also increments totalBatchesIndexed++ from multiple goroutines without synchronization (line 189), another race that can undercount the value reported in the span event.

NewResourceServer leaks resources when eager Init fails

When s.Init(ctx) fails, NewResourceServer returns nil, err but does not call s.cancel() to release the cancellable context created a few lines above, and does not close the blob bucket that may have been opened earlier in the function (OpenBlobBucket/NewCDKBlobSupport). Since Init now runs at construction time, init failures (e.g. index build errors) are a realistic path, and each failed construction leaks the context and the bucket handle. The error path should call cancel() and close any opened blob support before returning.

BuildIndex starts a span but drops the span context, inconsistent with the PR's trace-propagation fix

The PR fixes trace propagation by assigning the context returned from tracer.Start back to ctx in search.go and sql/backend.go, but bleveBackend.BuildIndex still does `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)` and discards the span-scoped context. Any operation inside BuildIndex that could use the context (e.g. passing it to the builder callback or future instrumented calls) would be detached from the BuildIndex span, so the bleve portion of index-building traces remains disconnected from its children. Use `ctx, span := b.tracer.Start(...)` for consistency with the rest of the change.

true_positives.golden_comment: MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler but only contains pass, failing to implement its required abstract methods: counter_names (property), get_dedupe_value(), get_group_key_values(), and build_occurrence_and_event_data(). This will cause a TypeError at runtime when the class is instantiated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
MetricAlertDetectorHandler can no longer be instantiated after switching to StatefulDetectorHandler

MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler but implements none of its abstract methods (counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, build_occurrence_and_event_data). Because StatefulDetectorHandler is an ABC with unimplemented abstractmethods, calling MetricAlertDetectorHandler(detector) raises TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class. This class is wired as MetricAlertFire.detector_handler, so any time Detector.detector_handler is accessed for a detector of type 'metric_alert_fire' (e.g. inside process_detectors, which has no exception handling around handler construction), the entire detector processing loop will crash with an unhandled TypeError. false_positives.candidate:
Shared FixedQueuePool is shut down by the old strategy on rebalance, causing silent message loss

The `FixedQueuePool` is created once in the factory's `__init__` and shared by every `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` produced by `create_with_partitions`. Arroyo closes and re-creates the strategy on every partition revocation/rebalance: the old strategy's `close()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which shuts down all queues and worker threads in the shared pool. The new strategy created after the rebalance still references the same pool. From then on, `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` calls `work_queue.put()`, which raises `queue.ShutDown` on a shut-down queue; this is caught by the broad `except Exception` in `submit`, which then calls `add_offset`/`complete_offset` on the message's offset. The result: every message after a rebalance is silently dropped (never processed) while its offset is marked complete and committed to Kafka. Since consumer groups rebalance on every deploy/scale event, running this mode in production would skip uptime results without any error surfacing beyond a log line. The pool needs to be created per `create_with_partitions` call, or `close()` must not shut down a pool it doesn't own.

Worker queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure and memory can grow without limit

`FixedQueuePool` creates each work queue with `queue.Queue()` (no maxsize), so `submit`/`put` never blocks. The docstring on `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` (line ~253) claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but that never happens: the Arroyo consumer thread will keep polling Kafka and appending `WorkItem`s faster than slow workers can drain them, buffering an unbounded number of decoded results in process memory. This is exactly the failure mode the PR is meant to mitigate (one slow item/group clogging processing) — a slow group now grows its queue until the consumer OOMs. The queues should have a `maxsize` (or `submit` should otherwise block/apply backpressure) to match the documented behavior.

join() ignores its timeout and shutdown abandons all queued items instead of draining them

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(timeout)` ignores the timeout and just calls `close()`, which immediately shuts down the queue pool. In `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` each worker's `shutdown` flag is set to True before `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` is called, so a worker that is woken with pending items still in its queue processes at most one more item and then exits its `while not self.shutdown` loop — everything remaining in the queues is discarded without being processed and without a final offset commit. Standard Arroyo strategies drain in-flight work and commit during `join` on graceful shutdown; here every deploy or rebalance abandons the entire in-memory backlog (which, given the unbounded queues, can be large) to be redelivered and reprocessed. At minimum `join` should wait for queues to drain up to the timeout and perform a final commit of completed offsets.

The test submits 10 trivial work items (the processor just appends to a list under a lock) and then immediately asserts `stats["total_items"] > 0`. The three worker threads start consuming as soon as the first item is put, so on a fast machine all 10 items can be processed before the main thread reaches `get_stats()`, making `total_items` 0 and the assertion fail intermittently. The non-zero-depth assertion needs synchronization that blocks workers (e.g. an event the processor waits on) to be reliable.

The new `.map((query) => datasource.applyTemplateVariables(...))` runs before `partition(queries, querySupportsSplitting)` on line 300. `querySupportsSplitting` deliberately excludes queries containing `$__range` (lines 285-287) because the range variable must be resolved against the full, unsplit time range. true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: Math.floor(user_count/limit)+1 yields an extra page when user_count is an exact multiple of limit (100/50 gives 3 pages), which lets the user navigate to an empty page.

false_positives.candidate:
'automatic' check resolves against the member, so the remove button always renders

This template is rendered as the itemView for each member in '{{each member in members itemView="group-member"}}', so its context is the individual user, not the group. '{{#unless automatic}}' therefore looks up 'automatic' on a User, which is undefined, so the condition always passes and the remove (×) link is shown even for automatic groups (admins, moderators, etc.). Clicking it fires the DELETE /admin/groups/:id/members request, which the server correctly rejects with 422 (can_not_modify_automatic), but the client-side removeMember action in the admin-group controller and the Group model's removeMember have no error handling, so the click fails silently and the member just stays in the list. The automatic check needs to come from the group/controller (e.g. passed via the each or referenced through the controller), and the failure case should surface an error to the admin.

Group create silently ignores the alias_level chosen in the form

The client sends alias_level on creation: Discourse.Group.asJSON() returns {name, alias_level, visible} and create() POSTs it to /admin/groups, and the alias level combo box in admin/templates/group.hbs is shown for new (unsaved) groups too. However the create action only assigns name and visible — params[:alias_level] is never applied — so every new group is created with the default alias_level of 0 ('nobody') regardless of what the admin selected, with no feedback. The admin must save the group and then save it again via update (which does handle alias_level) to get the intended setting.

Public group members page now truncates to 50 members with no pagination UI

The members action now always applies limit/offset (default limit 50) to every group; previously non-automatic groups returned their full member list and only automatic groups were capped. The public-facing group members page (discourse/routes/group-members.js.es6 and discourse/templates/group/members.hbs) was updated to read 'members' off the group model but has no pagination or load-more controls — only the admin group page got next/previous. As a result, any group with more than 50 members now shows only the first 50 (alphabetically) on its public members page, with no way for a visitor to see the rest.

members endpoint accepts an unbounded limit parameter

limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i places no upper bound on the page size for this publicly accessible endpoint (anyone who can see the group can call it). A request such as /groups/mods/members.json?limit=1000000 forces a COUNT plus a full SELECT and JSON serialization of that many users in one request. The limit should be clamped to a sane maximum (e.g. 200).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.
Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
should_block? writes to the database from inside a model validation

EmailValidator#validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block?(value), which increments match_count and saves the blocked_emails row as a side effect of running validations. This means any user.valid? call — including ones that never lead to a save, and repeated client-side-driven validation attempts — mutates persistent statistics, and the write happens outside the user's save transaction. If stats collection is intended, it would be safer to record the match only when a signup is actually rejected (e.g., in the controller or in an after-validation hook gated on the record being persisted), otherwise the counters can be inflated arbitrarily by repeatedly triggering validation without ever creating an account.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same problem: the should_block check method has side effects, updating the match stats in the database during what should be a read-only check. The candidate does not mention race conditions, but it identifies the same core issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive, so blocks are trivially bypassed

BlockedEmail.should_block? performs an exact-match query: BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first. The email passed in comes straight from the signup form via User.new_from_params (which does no downcasing), and the blocked_emails table stores whatever case the admin entered. A spammer blocked as 'bad@spam.com' can register successfully as 'BAD@spam.com' or 'Bad@Spam.com' because the lookup won't match, and the user's own email uniqueness check is also case-sensitive so it won't collide with an existing account either. The block list should normalize (strip + downcase) both the stored value and the queried value, or the query should be case-insensitive.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: BlockedEmail.should_block? does a case-sensitive lookup, so a blocked email can be bypassed by changing its letter case.

false_positives.candidate:
Moved whitelist/blacklist email validation has no specs in the new validator spec

The email_domains_whitelist / email_domains_blacklist logic was moved out of User#email_validator into the new EmailValidator class, but the newly added spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb only covers the BlockedEmail branch — there are no tests exercising the whitelist or blacklist paths of the moved code. If no existing user specs cover those site settings, a regression there (e.g., in email_in_restriction_setting?) would go unnoticed; the spec file should include cases for whitelist-allowed, whitelist-rejected, and blacklist-rejected emails.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

true_positives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Header panel alignment now depends entirely on flexbox with no fallback for non-flex browsers

`.panel` previously used `float: right`, which worked in any browser. It now relies on `margin-left: auto` inside the `.contents` flex container. In any browser where none of the `display` values emitted by the `flexbox()` mixin are supported, `.contents` stays a block container, an auto left margin on a block-level `.panel` computes to 0, and the panel (user menu, search, hamburger icons) collapses against the logo on the left instead of staying on the right, breaking the header layout. If the supported-browser matrix includes any non-flexbox browsers (or engines with buggy partial flex support such as IE10, where auto margins inside `-ms-flexbox` containers are unreliable), this needs a fallback such as retaining `float: right` alongside the flex rules.
true_positives.reasoning: Both flag that removing float:right on .panel can break right alignment. The candidate attributes this to non-flex browsers, while the golden attributes it to .panel not being a flex item in the noscript header. Same code change and consequence, different cause.

false_positives.candidate:
float: right on .small-action button is silently ignored inside the new flex container

This PR makes `.small-action` a flex container via `@include flexbox()`. CSS specifies that `float` has no effect on flex items, so the `float: right` on the direct-child `button` (line 309) no longer does anything. Previously the button was pinned to the right edge of the small-action row; now it will render inline immediately after `.small-action-desc`, breaking the intended layout of small action posts (e.g. the edit/expand controls). The same applies to `float: left` on `.topic-avatar` (line 271), which is harmless only by accident of source order. The fix is to replace the button's float with `margin-left: auto` (or add `flex` spacing) so it is pushed to the end of the flex row.

align-items mixin emits -webkit-box-align, which does not support the 'baseline' value used by bullet badges

The new `align-items` mixin unconditionally emits `-webkit-box-align: $alignment` for the 2009 flexbox spec, but that old property only accepts start/end/center/stretch — `baseline` is invalid and the declaration is dropped. `.badge-wrapper.bullet` in badges.css.scss calls `@include align-items(baseline)`, so on browsers that only understand the old `-webkit-box` model (e.g. older iOS Safari, which Discourse's `display: -webkit-inline-box` fallback in `inline-flex()` explicitly targets) the invalid declaration is ignored and items fall back to stretch alignment, vertically misaligning the bullet color swatch against the category text. If old-WebKit support matters (the mixin's prefixes imply it does), the mixin needs a value mapping or a fallback for `baseline`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name is missing the '?' suffix, so ActiveModelSerializers never calls it

ActiveModelSerializers filters attributes by calling `include_<attribute>?` (with a question mark) — every other filter in this file follows that convention (`include_email?`, `include_stats?`, etc.). The new method is defined as `def include_website_name` without the `?`, making it dead code: the `website.present?` guard never runs, and `website_name` is always serialized (as `nil` when the user has no website, and unconditionally in the restricted-TL0 case described above). Rename it to `include_website_name?`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate flags the same core problem as the golden comment: include_website_name is missing its '?' suffix, so the conditional inclusion never runs. It does not mention the string concatenation concern, but the primary issue matches.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name leaks the website field for TL0 users viewed anonymously, bypassing untrusted_attributes

The serializer deliberately hides `:website` (via `untrusted_attributes`, which checks `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)`) so that anonymous visitors cannot see a TL0 user's profile fields. The new `:website_name` attribute is declared in the plain `attributes` list (line 43), is derived directly from `object.user_profile.website`, and its inclusion check only tests `website.present?` — it never checks `restrict_user_fields?`. As a result, for a TL0 user viewed by an anonymous visitor, `website` is omitted from the JSON but `website_name` (containing the website host, and possibly path) is still serialized, leaking exactly the information the restriction is meant to hide. The existing 'TL0 user seen as anonymous' spec was not extended to cover `website_name`, so the test suite does not catch this. `website_name` should be added to `untrusted_attributes` or its include check should mirror `include_website?`.

Sibling subdomains are treated as the same domain as the instance

The middle branch compares hosts of equal label count by stripping the first label from both sides: `www.anything.com` vs `forum.anything.com` are considered 'the same domain' and the full URL path is displayed. A sibling subdomain is not the instance's domain — on multi-tenant or shared-domain setups (e.g. instance at `forum.example.com`, user website at `evil.example.com/phishing-page`) the profile will render the full path as if the link belonged to the site's own domain, which is exactly the misleading display this feature is supposed to avoid. The comparison should only show the path when the website host equals the instance host or is a parent domain of it (the first and third branches), not when it is merely a sibling.

true_positives.golden_comment: postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage targetOrigin is a full referer URL, which browsers reject, so iframe resizing never works

The layout calls `parent.postMessage({type: 'discourse-resize', height: ...}, '<%= request.referer %>')`. The targetOrigin argument to postMessage must be an origin (scheme://host[:port]) or '*'; passing a full URL with a path (e.g. `http://blog.example.com/2013/02/10/post.html`, which is what the referer will always be) causes the browser to throw a SyntaxError ('Invalid target origin') and the message is never delivered. Since embed.js only sets the iframe height when it receives this message, the embedded comments iframe stays at the browser default height (~150px) and the comments appear cut off. The origin should be derived from the referer (or `SiteSetting.embeddable_host`), not the full referer URL.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: the postMessage targetOrigin is set to the full referrer URL rather than its origin, so the message never arrives and the iframe is not resized. The candidate's claim that the browser throws an error rather than silently dropping the message is a minor detail and does not change the issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
i.content can be nil for feeds without content:encoded, crashing the hourly job

`content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` assumes every feed item has a `content` element. SimpleRSS only populates `content` when the feed includes `content:encoded`; many RSS 2.0 feeds only provide `description`, and some Atom entries lack content entirely. For those items `i.content` is nil and `nil.scrub` raises NoMethodError, which aborts `rss.items.each` and kills the whole polling job (which has `retry: false`), so no topics are imported at all. Fall back to `i.description` or skip items with no content.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same bug: i.content being nil causes a NoMethodError on .scrub. Both suggest falling back to description.

false_positives.candidate:
raw_html cook method renders feed/imported HTML without any sanitization, enabling stored XSS

The new `cook` short-circuit returns `raw` verbatim when `cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`, bypassing the entire rendering/sanitization pipeline. This content originates from external sources: `Jobs::PollFeed` stores RSS/Atom item bodies (`CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)`) directly, and `TopicEmbed.import_remote` stores Readability output. Nothing sanitizes it, and it is rendered raw in `app/views/embed/best.html.erb` (`<%= raw post.cooked %>`) and in the normal topic UI. A malicious or compromised feed/article can therefore inject `<script>` or event-handler attributes that execute for every forum reader (stored XSS). The imported HTML should be run through the sanitizer (with an appropriate tag/attribute whitelist) before being stored as cooked.

TopicEmbed.import mutates the caller's contents string

`contents << "\n<hr>\n<small>..."` appends the 'Imported from' footer directly to the string object passed in by the caller. If the same string object is ever reused (e.g. a caller importing twice with one buffer, or passing a frozen string), the footer is appended multiple times — which also changes the computed content_sha1 and triggers spurious post revisions — or raises a RuntimeError on frozen strings. Use `contents = contents + ...` or `contents.dup` before appending.

setnx followed by expire is not atomic; a crash leaves the throttle key with no TTL

`retrieved_recently?` does `$redis.setnx(retrieved_key, "1")` and then `$redis.expire(retrieved_key, 60)` as two separate commands. If the process dies (or redis errors) between the two, the key is set with no expiry, and that embed URL is treated as 'retrieved recently' forever — `perform_retrieve` will never run for it again, so the topic for that URL is never imported. Use a single atomic command such as `$redis.set(retrieved_key, "1", ex: 60, nx: true)`.

embed_url is limited to 255 characters with no model-level length validation

The migration creates `t.string :embed_url, null: false` (255-char limit) with a unique index, while `TopicEmbed` only validates presence. Blog/feed URLs frequently exceed 255 characters (tracking parameters, long slugs). For such URLs, `TopicEmbed.create!` raises a database error (or RecordNotUnique-style failure) instead of a clean validation, and `EmbedController` will keep enqueueing retrieval jobs for a URL that can never be stored. Either use `text`/a larger limit or add a length validation and gracefully skip over-long URLs.

absolutize_urls raises URI::InvalidURIError for feed URLs that pass the loose scheme check

`TopicEmbed.import` accepts any URL matching `/^https?\:\/\//`, but `absolutize_urls` then calls `URI(url)`, which raises `URI::InvalidURIError` for strings with spaces, quotes, or other invalid characters that still match the prefix regex (feed-provided `link` values in `Jobs::PollFeed` are not otherwise validated). The exception is unrescued here, so one malformed feed item aborts the entire hourly `PollFeed` run (which has `retry: false`), preventing all other items from being imported. Validate with `URI.parse` up front and skip items that fail to parse.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate definition of OptimizedImage.downsize makes the width/height overload unreachable

The class now defines self.downsize twice: once as downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts) at line 145 and again as downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts) at line 149. In Ruby the second definition silently replaces the first, so the four-argument form is dead code. Any existing or future caller that passes max_width and max_height (the established API of this method) will now raise ArgumentError: wrong number of arguments (4 for 3). The two-APIs-in-one-method approach needs a different mechanism (e.g., a separate method name or a single signature).
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same problem. downsize is defined twice, the second definition overrides the first, and callers that pass separate width and height arguments break.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side upload size validation hardcoded to 10MB, ignoring site settings

validateUploadedFile previously read the limit from Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], which distinguishes max_image_size_kb from max_attachment_size_kb and respects admin configuration. The change replaces it with a hardcoded 10 * 1024. Consequences: sites that set a lower limit (e.g., 1MB images) will no longer block oversized files client-side, sites that set a higher limit will now wrongly reject valid uploads, attachments are incorrectly capped by the image-size logic, and the 'file too large' error message reports a max_size_kb that has no relation to the configured value.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same problem: the 10MB limit is hardcoded and ignores the per-type site settings, so client-side checks can diverge from configured server limits. The candidate does not mention the 413 handler, but the core issue is identical.

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Animated GIF path passes "80%" to gifsicle --resize-fit, which does not accept percentages

The new upload-downsizing code calls OptimizedImage.downsize(..., "80%", allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails). For GIFs with allow_animation set, optimize dispatches to downsize_instructions_animated, which delegates to resize_instructions_animated and emits `gifsicle ... --resize-fit 80%`. gifsicle's --resize-fit expects a WIDTHxHEIGHT geometry, not a percentage, so the command fails, convert_with returns false, and the controller's retry loop runs 5 times without shrinking the file. The result: animated GIFs larger than max_image_size_kb always fail to upload instead of being downsized, and the loop silently wastes 5 shell-outs before giving up.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same issue as the golden comment. With allow_animated_thumbnails enabled, '80%' is passed to gifsicle --resize-fit, which expects WxH geometry, so downsizing silently fails.

false_positives.candidate:
413 error handler reports a hardcoded 10MB limit instead of the configured max image size

displayErrorForUpload used to show Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb in the file_too_large message when the web server returns 413. It now shows a hardcoded 10MB, so users are told the wrong maximum whenever the admin has configured max_image_size_kb to anything else, making the error message misleading.

URL download limit hardcoded to 10MB, breaking API uploads for other limits and non-image files

FileHelper.download for API-provided URLs previously used SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes as the cap; it is now hardcoded to 10.megabytes. This download path is used for any file type, not just images, so attachment downloads via the API are now silently capped at 10MB regardless of max_attachment_size_kb, and sites with max_image_size_kb set above 10MB cannot fetch larger images even though the downsizing logic below was intended to shrink them.

Downsize retry loop ignores failure and silently gives up after 5 attempts

The while loop never checks the boolean returned by OptimizedImage.downsize. If conversion fails (corrupt image, missing delegate, gifsicle geometry error), the loop burns all 5 attempts shelling out to a command that cannot succeed, then proceeds to Upload.create_for with the original oversized file, which then fails validation with a generic size error. A failed downsize should break out immediately (or surface a meaningful error) rather than retrying an unchanged file.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
unsubscribe crashes when the user has no topic_users row

In TopicsController#unsubscribe, `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` can legitimately return nil: users in mailing-list mode receive notification emails for topics they have never visited (the mailer itself handles this — `TopicUser.get` is used nil-tolerantly in send_notification_email), as do users emailed via a topic invite. The very next lines dereference `tu.notification_level`, so clicking the new per-topic unsubscribe link from such an email raises NoMethodError and returns a 500 instead of unsubscribing. The action should handle the missing row, e.g. by creating it via `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, topic.id, notification_level: TopicUser.notification_levels[:muted])`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: TopicUser.find_by can return nil, and the code then calls methods on tu without a check, causing a crash.

false_positives.candidate: GET /t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe mutates state with no token or confirmation The new unsubscribe endpoint is a plain GET route that immediately changes the user's topic notification_level before rendering any page. Because GET requests carry no CSRF token, any third-party page that causes a logged-in user's browser to request the URL (e.g., an embedded pointing at the unsubscribe link) can silently mute or downgrade that user's subscription. Additionally, antivirus link scanners and browser/email prefetchers that fetch links from incoming mail will unsubscribe users without them ever clicking anything. State-changing actions should require POST, or the link should land on a confirmation page / use a signed token like the digest unsubscribe key.

Unsubscribe downgrades watching/tracking users to 'regular', contradicting the 'stop notifications' copy

For users whose notification_level is watching or tracking, the unsubscribe action sets the level to regular rather than muted. At 'regular' the user still receives notifications — and notification emails — whenever someone replies to them or mentions them in that topic. Yet the email link text says 'To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, click here' and the landing page says 'You will stop receiving notifications for <topic>'. Users who click the link will keep receiving emails for the topic, which is both a functional and messaging bug: either mute unconditionally or change the copy to say notifications are only reduced.

Template path does not match the route name, so the unsubscribe UI will not render

The client route is registered as a top-level route named `topicUnsubscribe` in app-route-map.js.es6, and the controller and view are named `topic-unsubscribe.js.es6`, so Ember resolves the template for that route under the name 'topicUnsubscribe'. The template added here lives at templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs, which registers as 'topic/unsubscribe' — a name only a child route `topic.unsubscribe` of the topic resource would look up. The route will therefore render with no template (or raise a missing-template error in development). Move the file to templates/topic-unsubscribe.hbs to match the route, controller, and view naming.

No request specs for the new unsubscribe endpoint

The only spec change in this PR adds an unsubscribe_url option to an existing message-builder test. There are no request specs for TopicsController#unsubscribe covering the notification-level transitions (watching/tracking → regular, regular → muted), the behavior when the user has no topic_users row, or the slug-mismatch redirect. A request spec for the missing-row case would have caught the nil-dereference crash on the primary path of this feature.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Script uses macOS-only sed syntax and a CWD-relative .env path

`sed -i '' -E ...` is the BSD/macOS form of in-place edit; on GNU sed (Linux, including CI containers and most dev VMs) the empty string is interpreted as a file name and the command errors out, so the script silently fails to update GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL for Linux users. Additionally ENV_FILE="../.env" only resolves correctly if the script happens to be invoked from inside the scripts/ directory; running it from the repo root creates/updates a .env one level above the repository. Use a portable sed invocation (e.g. `sed -i.bak` plus cleanup, or detect GNU vs BSD) and resolve ENV_FILE relative to the script's own location.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly flags the macOS-only `sed -i ''` syntax failing on GNU/Linux, which is the same issue as the golden comment. The extra point about the .env path does not change that.

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Handler throws a generic Error, surfacing as HTTP 500 instead of a proper tRPC error code

When the credential does not exist or belongs to another user, the handler throws `new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. In tRPC a plain Error is converted into an INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (500) response, which misleads clients and error monitoring into treating an expected authorization/not-found case as a server crash. true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))

`if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes') === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, 'minutes'))` compares two distinct dayjs object instances by reference, which is always false (`.isSame()` was presumably intended). This branch exists to detect a blocked-day override (start === end, i.e. 'unavailable the whole day'). Because it never fires, a blocked day is only rejected incidentally via the before/after checks, and a slot starting exactly at the block's start instant satisfies none of them: the callback returns undefined, `dateOverrideExist` is already true, and the function returns `true` (available) — leaking a bookable slot on a day the host explicitly marked unavailable.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate flags the same bug as the golden comment: dayjs objects are compared with ===, which checks references, so the result is always false and .isSame() is the fix.

false_positives.candidate:
