In checkIfIsAvailable, when any date override matches the slot's day, `dateOverrideExist` is set to true and, if the slot falls inside the override window (so the `find` callback never returns true), the function hits `if (dateOverrideExist) { return true; }` — returning 'available' before the `busy.every(...)` check at the bottom ever runs. This means that on any day where a host has a date override, that host's existing bookings and calendar busy times are completely ignored. A fixed host (or a regular solo event user, since they are also isFixed) with a date override who already has a booking/meeting inside the override window will be shown as bookable, producing double bookings — the exact problem this PR claims to fix ('prevents round-robin events being booked where the fixed hosts are unavailable'). The busy check must still run when a date override exists; only the working-hours check should be bypassed.

Multiple same-day date-override windows veto each other

The `dateOverrides.find(...)` logic treats 'slot is outside this one override window' as grounds to return false (unavailable), but a user can have several override windows on the same date (cal.com's UI allows adding multiple time ranges to one date override, stored as separate rows). For a slot that falls inside window B, window A's callback hits `slotStartTime.isAfter(date.end)` (or `slotEndTime.isBefore(date.start)`) and returns true, so the slot is marked unavailable even though it is within window B — and vice versa. Net effect: on a day with two or more override windows, every window is rejected by the other and the host shows no availability at all. The find should only return a 'reject' verdict after confirming the slot is outside *all* same-day windows for that user.

Override decoding depends on the server running in UTC

The new code decodes the override's wall-clock-encoded Date back to a real instant with `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes')` and compares it against `slotStartTime`/`slotEndTime`, which are explicitly UTC (`time.utc()`). `dayjs(date.start)` parses the Date in the process's local timezone, so the decode math (wall time − organizer offset = real UTC instant) only holds when the Node process runs with TZ=UTC. On any non-UTC runtime (dev machines, some CI/self-hosted setups) the override window and day-matching comparisons are shifted by the server offset, making fixed-host override filtering silently wrong. Use `dayjs.utc(date.start)` for these comparisons, as the parallel code in packages/lib/slots.ts already does with `.utc()`.

Offset-shifted override times discard the day component

The invitee-timezone conversion computes `startTime`/`endTime` as `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, 'minute').hour() * 60 + ...minute()`. Taking `.hour()/.minute()` after the offset shift drops any day rollover: when the invitee/organizer offset difference pushes the override across midnight (e.g. organizer Asia/Kolkata override 01:00–02:00 = 19:30–20:30 the previous UTC day, viewed by a UTC invitee: offset = −330 min lands on the previous day, but hour() yields 1170 minutes), the slot is materialized at 19:30 on the *current* invitee day instead of the correct adjacent day. Since the activeOverrides filter keys on the unshifted date, cross-midnight overrides are placed on the wrong day — precisely the timezone-adjustment scenario this PR is fixing. The shifted value should be carried as a full timestamp (or the day delta applied to startOfInviteeDay), not reduced to minutes-since-midnight.

override.timeZone is optional in the type but required by the conversion

`dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()` assumes `override.timeZone` is set, but the `TimeRange` type declares `timeZone?: string` as optional and getSlots is a shared library function — nothing at the type level guarantees every caller supplies it (the slots router happens to add it in this PR). With `timeZone` undefined, dayjs's tz plugin falls back to the host system's timezone when computing `organizerUtcOffset`, so the offset correction is silently computed against the server timezone and override slots are shifted by a wrong amount. Either make the field required for date overrides passed to getSlots or guard/default it here.

However, the only test added exercises a single-user personal event with a different invitee timezone. A round-robin scenario with one fixed host having a date override should be added, including a case where the fixed host is busy inside the override window.

In `buildOrgAuthorizationCondition` (line 164 and 168) and `buildTeamAuthorizationCondition` (line 201) the code writes e.g. `Prisma.sql`("teamId" = ANY(${teamIds}))``. Prisma's tagged-template helper expands an interpolated JavaScript array into a comma-separated list of bound parameters — it does NOT serialize it as a single Postgres array parameter. So with `teamIds = [10, 20, 30]` the emitted SQL is `"teamId" = ANY($1, $2, $3)`, which Postgres rejects with `syntax error at or near "$2"` (ANY requires a single array expression or subquery). Every org-scope and team-scope query will therefore fail with a raw-query error at runtime; only the user-scope path (which has no ANY) is valid. The correct pattern is `"teamId" IN (${Prisma.join(teamIds)})` or passing a single array parameter with an explicit cast. The org-scope (line 332) and team-scope (line 295) tests assert conditions via `expect(conditions).toEqual(Prisma.sql`...`)`, which only deep-compares the Sql object's internal `strings`/`values` arrays — it never runs the SQL against the database. The only test that actually executes a query (`getBaseConditions`, line 481) uses scope `"user"`, the one code path that contains no `ANY(...)` array interpolation. As a result the tests pass while the org/team SQL is syntactically invalid (Prisma expands `ANY(${ids})` into `ANY($1, $2, ...)`, a Postgres syntax error). The service builds that array from `MembershipRepository.findAllByTeamIds`, a `findMany` with no `orderBy`, so Postgres does not guarantee the row order (the user also has two memberships — team and org — that get deduped via `Set`, preserving whatever order rows came back in). Per the PR's own contract (comment in `refreshOAuthTokens`: 'The response should only contain the access token and expiry date'), the sync endpoint returns a minimal payload, so validation fails and every Webex token refresh rejects with 'Invalid refreshed tokens were returned' whenever credential sync is enabled.

Salesforce now refreshes the token on every service instantiation and ignores the credential-sync endpoint

The new code in `getClient` unconditionally POSTs to `https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` and writes to the DB every time a `SalesforceCalendarService` is constructed — previously jsforce lazily refreshed only on a 401. This adds an external HTTP call plus a DB write to every Salesforce calendar operation. Additionally, this is the only modified app that does not route through `refreshOAuthTokens`, so when credential syncing is the source of truth, the stored `refresh_token` may be the placeholder `"refresh_token"` (or absent), making this direct Salesforce refresh fail with invalid_grant and breaking the integration entirely.

findFirst-then-create upsert has a race that creates duplicate credentials

The handler does `prisma.credential.findFirst({ userId, appId })` and then either updates or creates. Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same user/app (retries are typical for webhooks) can both observe no existing credential and both execute `prisma.credential.create`, leaving duplicate credential rows for the same user and app. Other parts of the codebase use `findFirst` when reading credentials, so duplicates silently shadow each other and can cause the wrong (stale) credential to be used. Since `(userId, appId)` is not unique in the schema, this should at least be serialized (e.g. transaction with locking, or a unique constraint) rather than a check-then-act.

No tests for the credential-sync webhook or the sync-mode token refresh paths

The PR checklist explicitly states no tests were added. The new endpoint writes third-party credentials directly into the database and the modified refresh paths in ~10 app integrations (Google, Zoom, Office365, HubSpot, Zoho, Webex, Lark, Salesforce) now branch on `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` — several of which are broken in sync mode (shape mismatches, NaN expiry, wrapper object persisted). At minimum, tests covering the webhook (auth failure, create vs update, bad payload) and one representative sync-mode refresh per response-shape family (fetch Response vs SDK object vs axios) would have caught the regressions in this PR.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. The `cancelled: true` update (or row delete) therefore happens in the background after the response may already have been sent; in a serverless deployment the lambda can be frozen once the response completes, so the flag may never be written — in which case the cron never cancels the SendGrid send and the reminder email is still delivered, re-creating the bug this PR fixes. The calls should be collected and awaited (the same applies to the identical new pattern in `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx` requestReschedule and `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/workflows.tsx`).

The async deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder calls run inside forEach without await, so reminders may never actually be cancelled. The candidate also covers the same locations: booking cancellation, reschedule, and the workflows router.

When a booking is rescheduled, the old booking's email reminders are cancelled via `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)` with `immediateDelete=true`. That path POSTs the `status: "cancel"` to SendGrid right away — for reminders that may be scheduled days in the future — which is exactly the behavior this PR identifies as the root cause of hitting SendGrid's max of 100 pending cancellations (pending cancellations accumulate until the scheduled date). Additionally, the immediateDelete path neither deletes the `WorkflowReminder` row nor sets `cancelled: true`, so the row lingers with `scheduled: true` and is invisible to the cron's `cancelled: true` cleanup; it only disappears when the generic `scheduledDate <= now` deleteMany runs after the send date. Also note the whole forEach is fire-and-forget, so the surrounding try/catch can never catch errors from these async calls.

The golden comment's point about the omitted SendGrid DELETE call is not addressed, but the main issue matches.

One failing SendGrid cancel aborts the whole cancellation batch and drops all DB deletes

If the SendGrid request fails for any one reminder (e.g. a stale/invalid `referenceId` batch_id, which returns an error from SendGrid), the loop exits immediately: (a) all remaining `remindersToCancel` never get their SendGrid cancellation posted, so those emails will still be sent even though the bookings were cancelled — the exact bug this PR is meant to fix; and (b) the `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` promises collected in `workflowRemindersToDelete` are never awaited, and since Prisma promises are lazy, those deletes never execute. Because the failing row is never deleted, it will abort the loop again on every subsequent cron run (every 15 min), permanently blocking cancellations for all reminders that happen to sort after it (the query has no orderBy). Each reminder's SendGrid call and DB delete needs its own error handling so a single bad record can't block the batch.

When a paid booking is cancelled, the handler refunds the payment, sets the booking status to REJECTED, and returns early at `return { message: "Booking successfully cancelled." }` — before reaching the new "Workflows - cancel all reminders for cancelled bookings" block further down (which calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` / `deleteScheduledSMSReminder`). The mutation can complete and the serverless invocation can be torn down before the `cancelled: true` updates / deletes commit, leaving reminders active for a booking that was cancelled for rescheduling, so the cron never cancels them and emails may still be sent. Calendar update uses the requester's credentials instead of the organizer's

The handler builds `new EventManager({ ...user, credentials: [...credentials] })` from `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` — i.e. the credentials of whoever called the endpoint — even though the booking's organizer (with credentials) was already loaded via `booking.user.credentials`. Worse, this call is outside any try/catch and runs after the DB update, so the attendees are already persisted but the mutation throws and the calendar event is never updated — attendees get no calendar invite on the real event and the client shows an error despite the guests having been added.

After fetching the booking, the handler never checks `booking.status` or whether the booking has already ended. Guests can therefore be added to CANCELLED or REJECTED bookings (receiving CONFIRMED ics invites and scheduled emails for an event that does not exist) and to bookings in the past. The UI partially hides this (the edit menu is rendered for past confirmed bookings too, via the `isBookingInPast && isConfirmed` branch in BookingListItem.tsx), and the API itself enforces nothing, so cancelled/past events can have attendees appended and calendar/email notifications sent out.

The permission check grants access to any existing attendee (`isAttendee`), and there is no limit on how many guests can be added or how often. Anyone who books a public event can then submit an arbitrary list of victim email addresses, and the handler will persist them as attendees and send them AttendeeScheduledEmail invitations containing the event details, organizer identity, and video meeting URL. This turns the endpoint into an unauthenticated-content email relay abusing Cal.com's sender reputation. The UI added in this PR only exposes the dialog on the organizer's bookings list, so the attendee permission appears broader than the feature requires; if attendee-added guests are intentional, they at least need rate limiting / a count cap.

For seated events, every attendee is expected to have a BookingSeat record (seat reference) — the handler even copies `seatsPerTimeSlot`/`seatsShowAttendees` onto the CalendarEvent, but it only creates plain Attendee rows via `createMany` and never creates BookingSeat entries. The subject is built with `name: this.calEvent.attendees[0].name`. The scheduled-email flow this copies assumes attendees[0] is the booker with a real name.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code single-use guarantee is racy (read-modify-write)

Backup code consumption decrypts the stored codes, checks indexOf, then nulls the entry and re-encrypts in a separate `prisma.user.update`. Two concurrent login requests presenting the same backup code will both read the pre-consumption state, both find the code, and both succeed before either writes back. Backup codes are documented to the user as 'can be used exactly once', but this check-then-act sequence allows parallel reuse. The consumption should be made atomic (e.g., conditional update/transaction) or the finding at least acknowledged.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same race condition: backup codes are decrypted, checked, and updated non-atomically, so concurrent requests can reuse a single backup code.

The show/hide password button in PasswordField now has `tabIndex={-1}`, making it unreachable via keyboard navigation in every form that uses PasswordField (login, password change, 2FA setup, etc.). The PR's core feature — logging in with a backup code via 'Lost access' — has no test coverage; the file only adds a TODO comment acknowledging this. true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Calendar/video deletions run un-awaited inside async forEach; surrounding try/catch is now dead

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) })` fires off async callbacks that nothing awaits, and the function proceeds to send the reschedule email and return immediately. Previously `getCalendar` was synchronous so `deleteEvent` was at least initiated synchronously; with the new `await getCalendar(...)` the deletion isn't even started until the dynamic import resolves, which races with the function returning (risky in serverless, where the process can freeze after the response). Additionally, errors thrown inside these async callbacks — including dynamic-import failures — reject outside the surrounding try/catch (lines 124–139), producing unhandled rejections rather than the logged errors the catch block intends. Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))` inside the try block.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same bug: forEach with async callbacks running calendar/video deletions without being awaited. Both describe the resulting race conditions and the unhandled rejections that escape the surrounding try/catch. Both recommend replacing it with Promise.all and map.

false_positives.candidate:
Dynamic imports are evaluated eagerly at module load, so nothing is actually lazy-loaded

Each entry like `applecalendar: import("./applecalendar")` is evaluated when the `@calcom/app-store` module itself is first imported, which immediately kicks off loading of every app's chunk. Because the import() expressions run at object-literal evaluation time (not on property access), importing this module anywhere starts fetching all ~28 app bundles at once — there is no per-app deferral, only code splitting. If the intent of the PR is to defer loading apps until they are used, the values need to be lazy thunks (e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`) with call sites adjusted. As written, the change also converts app-module load failures into rejected promises stored in this object, which will surface as unhandled rejections for any app that is never explicitly awaited.
